topicinfo.text: National Park Estate (Great Koala National Park Reservations) Bill 2026

p.span: National Park Estate (Great Koala National Park Reservations) Bill 2026
Second Reading Debate
Debate resumed from an earlier hour.

The Hon. JEREMY BUCKINGHAM ( 19:31 :44 ): I contribute to debate on the National Park Estate (Great Koala National Park Reservations) Bill 2026, which is an incredibly important bill and is incredibly good news for the ecology, the environment and the people of the Mid North Coast. It has been a long road to get here. It took decades of work from community members, environmentalists and this Government to build the support needed to create the framework for this incredibly important addendum to our natural estate. I congratulate our excellent Minister for the Environment on shepherding the park through to fruition. She is incredibly humble, but it is a testament to her tenacity that she got the bill up in a way that has built a lot of support in the community. I should know—I live in Bellingen, and there are no protests in the street.

The timber industry workers there recognise that they have to move out of hardwood native forest logging and into plantations. There is a transition package for people to move to the National Parks and Wildlife Service, and there are hundreds of millions of dollars coming down range for investment in the Dorrigo Rainforest Centre and the walks along the Dorrigo escarpment. Now there is the Great Koala National Park, which will be a jewel in the crown of the North Coast. The Hon. Mark Latham said that no-one goes to those parks. What a joke! Close to 175,000 people a year go to the Dorrigo National Park. With the addition of the Great Koala National Park, it will increase to more than one-quarter of a million people.

The people on the Mid North Coast recognise that tourism is the backbone and lifeblood of their economy. Around 70 per cent of the visitors to those national parks are from outside of the region, and now it is not just the Big Banana or the fantastic surf beaches that are magnets for those tourists. The Bongil Bongil National Park and the various interconnected reserves will do the work of protecting our natural heritage estate. The Government has erred—I think rightly—on the side of allowing different tenures so different access opportunities and uses for those forests can be offered. They are absolutely chock-a-block full of people all the time, swimming in the rivers, walking dogs in certain areas and birdwatching.

One of my favourite things to do is to look for wompoo pigeons and spangled drongos. If members have never seen a male spangled drongo in the wild, they must go and see one. I am not talking about the Hon. Wes Fang; I am talking about the beautiful rainforest bird. The plethora of birds in the forests is incredible. One of the most biodiverse places for avian species on this earth is in that part of the Mid North Coast, at the intersection of the mountains, the riverine ecosystems, the wetlands and the coastal ecosystems. There are also many migratory birds. Birdwatchers should definitely go there. It is an absolute hotspot for a range of species, and they are coming back in big numbers. There are raptors, peregrine falcons, goshawks, eagles, sea eagles—I could go on and on, but I will not.

As I said, the park has been a long time coming. I must acknowledge the work of the North East Forest Alliance, the Bellingen Environment Centre, Ashley Love, Dailan Pugh and Susie Russell, to name a few. I acknowledge the local community up there, and also the Hon. Luke Foley. Who can forget the front page of The Daily Telegraph with an illustration of him as "Luke Foliage" the koala—I have got to rate that headline; whoever wrote it gets 10 out of 10—when it announced the then Opposition members' commitment to the Great Koala National Park. Now in government, here they are delivering it.

A lot of people said, "They'll never deliver it. They'll back away. They won't deliver it in full." But 176,000 hectares has been added to the estate, creating links between those nature reserves. It is absolutely fantastic. It is not without an economic cost. There is no doubt the taxpayers of New South Wales will have to chip in. With the moratorium on native timber harvesting, the timber industry will have to restructure. As a former sawmiller, I know a little bit about the timber industry. My family ran a sawmill in Tasmania of a minor species.
The Hon. Wes Fang: You sold out your mates.

The Hon. JEREMY BUCKINGHAM: We didn't sell out or anything like that. People decided to use timber from species other than our rainforest species and our hardwood species for construction. This place is probably built out of hardwood, but there are no frames of homes being built out of Australian oak and Australian hardwoods in New South Wales. It is heavy, hard to nail and more expensive than the product that we get from the softwood plantations. About 91 per cent of timber used in this State comes from plantations, and 84 per cent of that comes from softwood plantations. The majority of the rest is not coming from Indonesian rainforests or the Siberian taiga; it is coming from New Zealand radiata pine plantations.

The builders and the construction industry have voted with their feet. They wanted a softer, easier to handle timber for their construction, and that is what they have chosen. Furniture-grade timber can be sourced from our plantations. Foresty Corporation is logging in Pine Creek State Forest at a place the community calls Forest Bridge. I recognise the concerns the community have about Pine Creek, as they do with the Tarkeeth. But we have to recognise that we cannot tell the timber industry that it has to go to plantations, as we move out of native forest logging, and then at the first juncture say, "Except this one here, which is absolutely critical to you keeping up with sawlogs". That is why, despite some intensive lobbying locally, I have not supported that. I have been up there and had a look.

I also put on record that State forests are not always open for use, as some members have said. In a forest that is earmarked for logging, you cannot always do the things that you can do in a State forest, because it is a working forest. Often there is heavy machinery there, trucks are coming and going, and it is not the sort of place where you want to go for a bushwalk, walk the dog or look for a spangled drongo or a wompoo pigeon. The bill will result in there being more uses for these forests. There is recognition of the Gumbaynggirr people, making sure that Aboriginal cultural values and joint management are enshrined in the bill. There is a range of different reserve land tenures in the bill.

The Forestry NSW workforce transition is a key element. The bill contains provisions to support employment transition for affected Forestry Corporation employees by enabling appointments to the National Parks and Wildlife Service. Those people know the forests. They know the roads. It will not be the case that, when they are part of the national park, those forests will not be managed and will all of a sudden be at risk of burning down. As I am prone to do, I digress momentarily into the area of ecological transition. These forests have not burnt down. They did not burn down in the 2019 Black Summer fires because a lot of them have transitioned, in terms of ecological succession, into rainforest.
The Hon. Wes Fang: It has nothing to do with the fact that there were Forestry Corporation employees there that put the fires out.

The Hon. JE REMY BUCKINGHAM: It had nothing to do with the fact that the Forestry Corporation was there. We did not cut them down for 80 years and they turned into rainforest. They went from closed eucalypt forests into subtropical rainforests, which stay pretty wet and do not burn down as easily because they are not dominated by eucalypt species. That can be seen a lot. Members who might be flying up and down the coast should have a look.
The Hon. Wes Fang: Koalas live on eucalypts!
The Hon. JEREMY BUCKINGHAM: Keep an eye out for a spangled drongo and its call from the wild. In those areas koalas can be heard. If you want to be alarmed in the middle of the night—
[Interruption]

There you go! That is a very good impression of a koala from Ms Sue Higginson. It is of course a hotspot of 12,000 koalas, a key population there. But it is not just the koalas. My favourite bird, the coastal emu, does not rate much of a mention, but it is an endangered species that is genetically located only in that area. They are struggling to survive with the fragmentation caused by agriculture, roads and the incursion of dogs. It is fantastic we now have this park on the books for operation. I have expressed my interest in the operational elements of this park. The community wants to know the who, what, when, where and how of the operations of it, where the structures are going to be built and all the rest. This is the jewel in the crown. There are not many places in this State where you can swim in clean wild rivers. If you swim in the Wilsons River and the Richmond River on the North Coast, you will come out covered with mud, silt and acid sulphate.

But it is not so for the Bellinger River, Kalang River and Crystal Creek. If members ever get the chance, they should get up to Crystal Creek. It is like Tahiti up there; it is unbelievable. It is getting a reputation around the world. These are clean beaches. As a result of this bill, people will be able to go from the Bongil Bongil, the beaches down there at the Wenonah Headland, all the way up to Dorrigo. It is all protected; it is all recovering. Our southern greater glider; glossy black cockatoos; rare spider orchids, including Dendrobium melaleucaphilum; the cryptic forest twiner, Tylophora woollsii; Floyd's grass; Beadle's grevillea—the list goes on and on. If you are a plant buff, you will absolutely love it up there. You may never have seen these plants, but now you will. The king orchids are in the wild and are absolutely amazing. People will be coming from all around the world. There is also the opportunity for Aboriginal-led tourism, with specific reserves for the Gumbaynggirr people.

Being on country with some of the Gumbaynggirr Elders, it is absolutely amazing to hear some of the stories they tell about their interactions with the Dunghutti people, their oral histories remembering Captain Cook going past, gliding up Smoky Cape—"Off you go, Captain Cook. We know what you're about"—and their stories of the history of colonisation. White fellas got up into that country only in the 1860s. We have had a massive impact there. Photos of Bellingen and Dorrigo in the 1920s show that not a stick was left there. They absolutely denuded the place for forestry, dairying and cattle. There were no trees left. What is there now is almost entirely regeneration and recovery, and the stewardship of many generations. I finish with the words of Sir David Attenborough, who said, "Surely we have a responsibility to leave for future generations a planet that is healthy and inhabitable by all species."

That is what the creation of this park does. It delivers intergenerational equity, an ecological asset for all time, protected by legislation and welcomed by the vast majority of people. There is no campaign on the ground in Bellingen to overturn this. The businesses know that tourism is the future. They know that having clean water, a healthy environment and those thriving ecosystems are the reasons people live there. That is what they want protected, and that is what this bill does. I commend the Government for the work it has done, including the Minister for Primary Industries, the Hon. Tara Moriarty. It has been a full team effort to bring the community along to build the social licence for what will be one of the most fantastic parks in Australia. I commend the bill to the House.

Ms CATE FAEHRMANN ( 19:46 :20 ): I speak in debate on and wholeheartedly support the National Park Estate (Great Koala National Park Reservations) Bill 2026. I begin by honouring the contribution of my wonderful colleague Ms Sue Higginson—her longstanding advocacy for forests, for nature, and working and campaigning with all the wonderful Northern Rivers, Mid North Coast, Coffs Harbour and Bellingen forest folk over so many years. It is truly incredible that we are finally here after so much effort and attention. Hundreds of really dedicated people have worked incredibly hard, and thousands of people have been passionate about protecting the koala and have worked tirelessly for many years. Groups of hundreds have spent hundreds of hours, if not thousands or tens of thousands of hours—I point to Dailan Pugh in the President's gallery—raising awareness about the plight of the koala, which is representative of their habitat, the forests.

I know something of how hard the work has been: the strategy meetings; the full-day workshops; the full‑day meetings where campaigners came together, so frustrated about the ongoing logging and destruction of forests, to come up with tactics and lobbying strategies and ways to get the message into the media; and the desperation that comes from witnessing so much destruction over so many decades. Tonight I think about how much effort and frustration it has taken to get to this point. People talk about blood, sweat and tears. There really have been a lot of tears involved—tears when standing in forests and seeing such beautiful nature that we know is koala habitat being destroyed. After campaigning and campaigning, I remember quite a few discussions about whether anything would be left.

The first time I was in Parliament, from 2010 to 2013, I had the environment portfolio. We campaigned hard to protect forests, end broadscale land clearing and stop development in the habitats of threatened species. At that time we did not have a dedicated koala focus. When I came back to Parliament in 2018, along with the environment portfolio there was a dedicated koala portfolio. That was a result of the dedicated koala habitat protection campaign that Ms Sue Higginson outlined in wonderful detail. Dawn Walker, a former colleague, held that portfolio for The Greens because of her work on the Northern Rivers.

After the 2019 State election I was elected chair of Portfolio Committee No. 7 – Planning and Environment. I had a discussion with my team that led to the first inquiry that committee ran, which was about koalas and the protection of their habitat. I had a moment where I thought, "Oh, my God, of course that is what we need to do. If we just talk about forests, I don't think we're going to get far. But everybody loves koalas, right?" We were protecting forests for the beautiful wildlife, but so many people could not see the forest for the trees. Many people do not get the beauty and the integrity of nature. Australians who are not really into nature need help to understand, and that is what we did with the koala inquiry. Before then, the movement made the very strategic decision to say, "This is what's at stake; this is why we need to protect the forests. This is just one creature that we will protect." The koala was the only one that would turn hearts and minds for us, so I thank our gorgeous koalas for being so adorable.

Koalas were in a lot of trouble when we got the inquiry underway. Matt Kean was the Coalition environment Minister, and he talked a lot about the need to save koalas and put a lot of money into the Koala Strategy. The NSW Chief Scientist and Engineer's report in 2016 found that to maintain koala viability, large areas of connected habitat were needed, but that did not lead to the former Coalition Government doing anything at all to protect that habitat. Of course, we know what an impossible task that would have been with The Nationals as the junior Coalition partner. For the record, the Hon. Wes Fang is nodding furiously. On 20 June 2019 we launched the koala populations and habitat in New South Wales inquiry. It was the start of the bushfire season that year. At least 5,000 koalas were estimated to be lost in those fires—potentially more. We all remember those images: the woman who used the shirt off her back to rescue a poor burnt koala from an active fireground and a firefighter giving a stressed koala a drink of water from a water bottle. It was heartbreaking, and it put the focus on the nation's koalas like never before.

The committee did a wonderful job. The community was incredible. They were really into that inquiry and saw it as the vehicle to hopefully give voice to the Great Koala National Park proposal, among others. The committee found that without urgent government intervention to protect habitats and address all other threats, the koala would become extinct in New South Wales before 2050. I acknowledge the efforts of the current Minister for the Environment, who was on that committee with me and former Liberal member the Hon. Catherine Cusack. We all worked extremely well together. The final report got us to a very good place. One of the recommendations from that report—recommendation 41—was that the Government investigate the establishment of the Great Koala National Park. Obviously, every member who knows the committee process will realise that recommendation was a compromise. It was probably drafted without the word "investigate" in there, but that is what we got. That report was handed down more than six years ago, now.

In the last term of Parliament, as Ms Sue Higginson mentioned, we introduced a bill to create the Great Koala National Park. The Coalition and the Labor Party voted that bill down. At that time, in 2022, the koala was listed as endangered at both State and Federal levels. Some 7,185 hectares of the proposed Great Koala National Park was logged in the 21 months following the Minns Government coming to power, according to data by the good folk at the North East Forest Alliance. A moratorium on logging within the proposed boundaries of the park was finally announced in September 2025. We have two weeks of Parliament left in the year and we are probably sitting until midnight tomorrow. I wish we had done this in 2023 or 2024, so those parks could have been protected for a couple of years by now and some of the thousands of hectares would not have been logged.

However, this is a very positive bill. I put on record some of the wonderful actions that have taken place to protect koalas over the years. The community loves koalas so much that I could barely believe it during the committee inquiry. Members will remember the koala wars and what we called the koala killing bill—the koala State environmental planning policy that the Coalition Government wanted to introduce in the previous Parliament. It nearly brought down the Coalition. Barilaro called koalas "tree rats". Catherine Cusack got 11,000 emails urging her to cross the floor, which she did. Those emails were from a lot of people in her area on the Northern Rivers and the Mid North Coast, as well as people from other parts of the country and even internationally.

I should probably give a shout-out to some of those people, who really love their koalas, because I am sure they are watching. During COVID, we held a Save Our Koalas national day of action. People turned out all over the State in their masks and held socially distanced events in parks. They held up placards all across the State about saving the koala. We thought we might get only a few people participating—"Who are all these people?" I think koalas are cute, but I love that people are obsessed. We have created protected habitats and protected areas of nature via those beautiful animals, so I thank the koalas for being so cute.

Wonderful local environment groups like the North East Forest Alliance, Bellingen Environment Centre, Nambucca Valley Conservation Association, Forest Ecology Alliance, Knitting Nannas and others have regularly held events outside the offices of local members and of Forestry. It has been such a hard slog to get the attention of mainstream and local media. That does not come from nowhere; it comes from everybody's deep value of and love for nature and koalas. It is very heartwarming to be here because of their efforts.

I mentioned the efforts of local environmental and conservation organisations, and everybody knows and has talked about what the bill does. But, as my colleague Ms Sue Higginson has said, it is a pity that Labor had to create the park off the back of carbon credits. It should not have been that way. It is the first time a national park had to be created with carbon credits. The park was at risk without a carbon credit scheme. Our wonderful and diverse environmental movement is still healing from the impact of having that held over its head. I echo the contribution of Ms Sue Higginson that it has been a very frustrating and challenging moment for the movement. But now the bill is passing. We are protecting those wonderful forests for koalas, nature and the community. I acknowledge the hurt that a lot of people have felt about the decision to require a carbon credit scheme for the national park. We continue to fight for the forests together, but things should not have been that way.

I also acknowledge that a lot of people are still fighting for the protection of forests. The campaigners are out trying to protect forests right now. Ms Sue Higginson spoke about the Forest Bridge proposal, Pine Creek State Forest and Tuckers Knob. I visited the Pine Creek forest with the Friends of Pine Creek, John Pile and all the wonderful people who have spent their lives protecting their forests. Yes, Pine Creek forest may not be a particular classification of forest, but it certainly has ecological values and ecological integrity, and provides vital koala habitat. I thank the campaigners who are planning to go to protect the sacred country of the Gumbaynggirr people there.

I wish we could say that all those wonderful, beautiful areas with big, gorgeous trees were also protected. We will not stop campaigning and working with the community until they are. It is also important to remember, as Ms Sue Higginson and other members have also mentioned, the campaign for the beautiful forests in the proposed Great Southern Forest Park, which are the habitat of the greater glider, platypus and other animals. We will not stop until those absolutely wonderful forests are also protected.

We know that the campaign to protect koala habitat goes further. The koala inquiry did not just talk about a Great Koala National Park; it talked about the need to protect habitat wherever koalas exist, particularly where there are important populations. I cannot fail to mention the decimation of the population of koalas on the roads in Campbelltown in Sydney's south-west. Slaughter would be a better word for it. As I have spoken about a lot in this place, koala habitat has been completely cleared for housing development. Because of the feud between developers and the Government over who will build a wildlife crossing or six, not enough area has been protected. For goodness sake, it is not that hard to protect that population of koalas.

There have been coalmine expansions every other week. The planning department is signing off on a plan to expand coalmines that destroy koala habitat. In fact, in 2025 there was a report released by a range of NGOs, including Mudgee District Environment Group, Nature Conservation Council and Lock the Gate, called Koalas or Coal Mines. It identified 24 proposed coalmines that will clear important koala habitat, resulting in a combined loss of 400 hectares of koala habitat. That includes coalmine expansions such as Yancoal's proposed Moolarben OC3 expansion near Mudgee. That alone will impact on 113 hectares of koala habitat. The Minister's own Environment and Heritage Group said the expansion:

… threatens koala habitat that is "critical to the survival of the species" and "would significantly contribute" to four other animal species and one critically endangered ecological community becoming extinct in NSW.

We know we are on a losing ticket with coalmines and coalmine expansions under this Government. I will keep it positive: Yay for the Great Koala National Park! We are here with a very good news story from this Labor Government. I acknowledge the efforts by the Minister for the Environment, who has put in incredibly hard work to get us here today. It is also great that the Opposition has acknowledged all the hard work of The Greens in getting us here today because, listening to the Opposition, this is all our doing. I thank Dailan Pugh of North East Forest Alliance for all his incredible work. He is in the gallery today. I also acknowledge Susie Russell, Paula Flack, Ashley Love, Deanna Markovina and our wonderful Bellingen crew. I thank former CEO of the National Parks Association, Kevin Evans, for his amazing work. I commend the bill to the House.

Ms ABIGAIL BOYD ( 20:06 :29 ): I contribute to debate on the National Park Estate (Great Koala National Park Reservations) Bill 2026. Firstly, I echo the thanks and appreciation already so ably conferred by my colleagues Ms Sue Higginson and Ms Cate Faehrmann—both of whom have had a long history with the campaign for this Great Koala National Park—to all of the countless climate, ecology and forest campaigners, both within and outside Parliament, who have advocated and fought over decades for the formation of a Great Koala National Park. As my colleague alluded to just now, for some of us, including me, this is a truly bittersweet moment.

When the bill is passed later today—or perhaps some time tomorrow—it will be a moment for celebration, but for me it will also be a time of grieving. I grieve for the forest destruction that has been allowed to occur in the time that people have been calling for this action. I grieve for the forest destruction that has occurred since Labor, in opposition, joined The Greens in adopting as its policy the declaration of the Great Koala National Park. I grieve for the forest destruction that has occurred and escalated every single day since this Government came to power, dangling the declaration over the heads of communities and activists desperate and distraught at the ecological devastation being perpetrated before their eyes. That it took until today, with only four days of Government business remaining for this entire parliamentary term, for the bill to even arrive in this Chamber is a damning indictment on the Minns Labor Government and its Ministers.

I also grieve for the people and animals of this planet, both current and future generations, who will pay the cruel price of the climate vandalism being perpetrated by this Government. It has added to its sad and sorry rap sheet of a litany of climate-destroying decisions by making the park contingent on the Government's ability to create and sell carbon credits to polluting industries, based on the utterly falsified and unmeritorious claim that the reservation represents genuine additional avoided deforestation. NSW Labor first promised to establish the Great Koala National Park in 2015 and promised to do so again in early 2023. That election promise was not contingent on the registration of a carbon offsets project. Subsequent policy announcements by the Minns Labor Government in late 2023 likewise did not indicate any such contingency.

That all started to change, however, once Labor came to power and started work on developing what is now called the improved native forest management method, a carbon crediting methodology that was ultimately adopted by the Commonwealth Government under its Australia Carbon Credit Unit Scheme in June this year. That methodology is profoundly and fundamentally flawed and will only serve as a net negative when it comes to action on climate change. First, the method will allow abatement projects, like the Great Koala National Park, that are not genuinely additional to what would have occurred in the ordinary course of events. The method substitutes the two relevant default additionality requirements under the Act with a new additionality requirement and simultaneously exempts States from the new requirement in circumstances that are tailored precisely to the New South Wales Great Koala National Park. As the Koalas for Coal working paper so aptly states:
The regulatory reverse-engineering entailed in this exemption makes a mockery of the additionality criterion, which is foundational to any attempt to demonstrate carbon credit integrity …

Regulatory reverse engineering is quite simply par for the course with Labor governments, perhaps most recently and devastatingly encapsulated by the Minns Labor Government's plans to directly overwrite the ruling of a landmark High Court decision and write bespoke legislation permitting the Mount Pleasant coalmine to increase its coal production by 32 per cent. Premier Chris Minns has been clear that his intention and that of the Government is to go against the ruling of the High Court and authorise MACH Energy to increase the annual coal output at its Mount Pleasant coalmine by four megatonnes to 16.5 megatonnes per year until 2032. These are the climate credentials of this reckless, feckless and hopelessly captured Labor Government. Like government, like carbon credit methodology, they are entirely without credibility or integrity when it comes to the urgent action required to do our part to prevent the most catastrophic impacts of climate change.

This week the United Nations Environment Programme announced that the world needs to cut carbon emissions by nearly one-fifth in the next four years and by close to half within a decade to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. Although the window has closed on holding temperature rises to 1.5 degrees Celsius, in line with scientific advice, limiting the overshoot of that target is still possible, according to the latest United Nations report. But that would require cutting greenhouse gases by 18 per cent by 2030 and by 45 per cent by 2035 to yield a good chance of limiting temperature rises to 1.7 degrees Celsius above pre‑industrial levels. That would still allow events such as the record heatwaves and climate devastation and disasters of the last few months to become frequent and common but could help prevent them from getting drastically worse.

The executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, Inger Andersen, has condemned governments such as this one and the ones that preceded it for their failure to act despite being warned for years that time was running out. She said that the United Nations used to say there was still an opportunity if the world made a herculean effort to stay within the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit. She also stated:
It's now clear the herculean effort was not made. We procrastinated, and now we are saying this window has closed.
Nevertheless, she has urged countries to keep the 1.5 degrees Celsius goal—the centrepiece of the Paris climate agreement—stating:
We can make the overshoot as brief and as short as possible. It's not time to throw in the towel and give up. This is about how to find our way back, as shortly and quickly as possible.

Allowing the carbon stored temporarily in the trees supporting the existence of our precious koala population to be monetised through the creation of carbon offsets that will make it easier for heavy climate polluters to cause more of the climate pollution that is burning down those same trees and devastating ecological communities is not finding our way back. It is an active choice to forge deeper into a terrifyingly dangerous and unpredictable climate future. A carbon credit is supposed to represent the equivalent of one tonne of avoided carbon dioxide equivalent that would otherwise have been released into the atmosphere. If carbon credits are generated from the Great Koala National Park, it is estimated it will create about 3.7 million carbon credits. Once sold, they will allow 3.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide to be released into the atmosphere while purporting to be carbon neutral. That is a farce.

For the Labor Government to make the protection of the park contingent on that level of climate destruction is unconscionable, and it sets a terrible precedent. Why would any government beset with the same rotten neoliberal ideological mindset as this one elect to do any other climate mitigation measure at all unless and until it can identify a method, or create a new one, that will enable it to generate financially valuable carbon credits via the Federal Government's Australian carbon credit units scheme? The commodification of nature will be utterly complete, and, with it, its death sentence surely written. Neoliberal economic ideology that seeks to commodify nature is at the root of that destruction and harm. Let the uprisings in France be a warning to this Government and all who seek to form government. Student protests over education underfunding and racialisation soon developed into a national mobilisation on 6 October, involving half a million students, teachers, parents and trade unions taking to the streets in protest against the French Government's campaign of austerity and repression.

A key complaint of the student protest was excessively high temperatures in classrooms, which exceeded 40 degrees Celsius with no air conditioning or adequate ventilation during the 2026 European heatwaves that were turbocharged by climate change. Professional firefighters joined the national protests in large numbers, saying that a lack of firefighting resources was laid bare during the summer's huge wildfires. Years of funding cuts have left schools crumbling, but those exceptional temperatures provided the spark. The demand for more school funding is also a demand for climate adaptation. The national mobilisation that has risen up is a rejection of the deeply flawed and failing leadership of neoliberalism's final boss, French President Emmanuel Macron.

Terrifyingly, but in keeping with historical precedent, the failures of economic liberalism breed fascism, providing legitimacy to capitalist dictatorship and the unbridled power of capital. In France, fascist candidate Marine Le Pen threatens to win the upcoming presidential elections. That prospect should serve as a dire warning to the Labor Government, which is pursuing a similarly flawed, austerity-ridden neoliberal agenda, with right-wing reactionaries breathing down its neck. It is the wrong way. Go back. The people demand climate and economic justice. They demand ecological restoration and care, and a rejection of the dehumanisation of capitalist excess. I say this in good faith and in the hope of a better outcome and a better future: It is not too late to sever the link between the Great Koala National Park and the carbon credit unit production industry.

I rejoice in the creation of the Great Koala National Park. I am in awe of and eternal gratitude to the brave environmental and forest defenders who have dedicated their lives, sweat and passion towards its creation. I take immense pride in being a very small part of that movement of people who have taken the beautiful idea of nature preservation forward from imagination to what will soon be reality. I am endlessly inspired by the ability of people to come together in selfless defence of nature and one another to organise for and deliver real change in this world. There is truly no greater force on earth than the collective will of good people working together in common cause. Here is to many more victories for the people. I proudly join my colleagues in supporting the bill.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 20:16 :27 ): I contribute to debate on the National Park Estate (Great Koala National Park Reservations) Bill 2026. I acknowledge the contribution of Ms Abigail Boyd, who eloquently approached the issue of carbon credits. Let us be honest, the first thing I say about the bill and the park is that they have nothing to do with koalas. That is pretty clear, despite the name, because the 4 per cent of koalas who are in the park that exists at the moment will not magically fill the 170,000-plus hectares of land that will be swallowed up and locked away by that koala sanctuary, which it effectively is under the legislation. The park is not about koalas, but it is also built on a lie. A number of members have spoken about that today. The Great Koala National Park exists because the State Government has provided that name. It has effectively gone to the Federal Government and sought—
Ms Cate Faehrmann: No, it was the National Parks Association.

The Hon. WES FANG: I listened to members' contributions to debate in silence. If Ms Cate Faehrmann wishes to contribute, she may do so in the Committee stage. The Great Koala National Park is that in name only. It is really a carbon credit Ponzi scheme that will fall down at some point in future. Ms Abigail Boyd was quite accurate in her assessment of the way the scheme was developed. Those carbon credits did not exist before the Minister decided she was going to create a way to fund the park. Effectively, the Government is doing so by saying, "We're not cutting down these trees. Therefore, there's additionality." That is not the case. Even members of The Greens acknowledge that is not the case.

I know that there was an internal war at the Federal level about the way this process was being examined and legislated because—let's be honest—if the goal of carbon credits is to reduce carbon emissions, that is not going to happen with this scheme. These carbon credits are being created out of nothing. If that is the case—and it is—it shows that the whole issue of carbon credits and the net zero scheme in Australia is built on a lie. We are not cutting carbon emissions by selling those credits. That just does not happen. Members who support this legislation can lie to themselves that these carbon credits are real and that selling them will make a difference to the environment, but they know it is a lie. It is a lie because those carbon credits did not exist beforehand. The Government created a new scheme that does not really exist, and the contributions to this second reading debate have demonstrated that.

That is the problem with a lot of this stuff. The Government says, "This is a carbon credit," but is it really? I would suggest that it is not. Even members of The Greens, who want to see another national park, acknowledge that the way the Government has gone about this is a lie. That cannot be escaped. The scheme is further demonstrated to be based on a lie when the Government says it will not sell those carbon credits to industries involved with fossil fuel. It will only sell the carbon credits to certain industries. That is not how a carbon credit scheme works. If the carbon credits were genuine, they would go into the market. The whole idea of a market is that carbon credits can be purchased. When the Government artificially creates a circumstance where only certain industries can purchase those credits, it has effectively admitted that the whole thing is a lie.

Given that we know this is a lie and the whole carbon credit scheme has been cooked up to try to generate enough money to fund the national park, why are we doing it? It would seem to hark back to election commitments that were made. I accept that. I am not desensitised to the politics of this. Some members of this House, particularly The Greens, are ecstatic about the bill because they have been campaigning for that national park for quite a while. Fair play to them. They have been consistent, at least, in advocating for and seeking to encourage this national park to be declared. Linking it to koalas was a clever strategy. Fair play to whoever decided to link this national park to koalas.

But it is not really about koalas. It is about shutting down native timber forestry in New South Wales. Labor did it in Victoria but went down a different path, just saying, "We are no longer going to have native forestry in Victoria." Labor is trying something different here, calling it the Great Koala National Park. Somehow that will save the koalas, even though the science indicates that that is completely absurd. Following the science, I think Brad Law said that koala numbers in forestry areas tend to do better because they prefer smaller trees with fresh growth. They survive well in those areas because they are well maintained, normally free of pests and weeds and all of those issues that create a risk for koalas, and ultimately the maintenance of roads and fire equipment means that the areas tend to be more protected from fire. The Hon. Jeremy Buckingham shot himself in the foot when he said that the wetter areas are much better in the Great Koala National Park because there are species other than eucalyptus. I thought the whole point of having the Great Koala National Park was to protect eucalyptus species because that is what koalas eat. I do not know what he was smoking there. One can only suggest.

We have heard from members in this place today that this park will be great because it will protect koalas and be a great tourist attraction and that all these wonderful things will come out of locking up all of this land. But, bar one or two members—such as Ms Sue Higginson, who comes from around that area, and the Hon. Jeremy Buckingham, who suggests that he does as well, although there may be some question about that—all of the people who are looking to shut down this area live in Sydney. People in rural and regional New South Wales are sick to death of people from Sydney telling them how to live.

There is absolute disgust from regional people because, every time people in Sydney want to make a change, it impacts us. It is not industry in Sydney they are shutting down. It is not in industry in Sydney where we see job losses. We do not build the transmission lines and the solar and wind farms in Sydney. We are not shutting down industry here in Sydney. It is always in rural and regional New South Wales. I hear the laughing from members of the Labor Party. I note that most of them live in Sydney. All of them are laughing at those rural and regional people as I am telling them that this is an issue. The Hon. Anthony D'Adam loves to laugh at it. He is having a great old laugh at those people who have lost their jobs in the forestry industry.
The Hon. Anthony D'Adam: I'm laughing at you because you live in Sydney, LARPing as a rural MP.
The Hon. WES FANG: You pretended to be somebody who fought for workers, mate.
The Hon. Mark Banasiak: Point of order—
The Hon. PETER PRIMROSE: Order! I will hear the point of order.

The Hon. Mark Banasiak: There is far too much chatter in the House. There seems to be a toing and froing. The Hon. Wes Fang is directing his comments to the Hon. Anthony D'Adam rather than through the Chair and the Hon. Anthony D'Adam is responding to those comments. It is a shemozzle.

The ASSISTANT PRESIDENT ( The Hon. Peter Primrose ): I uphold the point of order. We have had a well-organised debate so far. I remind members to direct their comments through the Chair. Members will be respectful and allow the Hon. Wes Fang to be heard in silence.

The Hon. WES FANG: I struggle with the idea that it is the Labor Party that has shut down the forestry industry. It was supposed to be the party of the worker, but now it is the party of the activist and the greenie. That is a shame. Now it is the National Party that represents timber and forestry workers. We represent those people who have lost their jobs. We are the party they talk to because they could not get an audience with the Minister. I do not know how many times I met with forestry workers in Parliament who said they could not get a meeting with Minister Sharpe. She would not meet with them.

We have to ask ourselves, what sort of Minister does not meet with workers from the industry that will be impacted and shut down through legislation? What sort of Minister would do that? What sort of Labor Minister would not meet with the industry she is going to shut down? That is a disgrace. It goes to show how far Labor is from its mandate. It has moved away from being the party of the workers towards being the party of the activist. We need only to look at the Hon. Anthony D'Adam on that side of the House to work out exactly what the party's priorities are.

Rural and regional communities deserve to have good jobs that, at the end of the day, make them feel proud. They deserve jobs that for a hard day's work give them a fair day's pay. That used to be the Labor Party's mantra. But now we are supposed to tell those forestry workers that they can go and be baristas, Uber drivers and tour guides. What are they going to do? How many more industries do we need to shut down in New South Wales? Manufacturing has already gone by the wayside. Jobs that are reliant on affordable energy, reasonable housing and that require workers to be involved in and engaged with machinery, like forestry, are all going by the wayside. Somehow this Labor Government thinks we can just give those workers jobs in cafes. That was until we forced re-usable cups on cafes, which we did earlier today.

I have already explained to the House that locking up land in a national park is not always the best way to manage it. During the 2020 bushfires in my area, I saw firsthand when the Kosciuszko National Park burned, it burned big and hard. It was the case that a number of the animals that resided in that national park were lost. Unfortunately, perhaps that is the future of this national park, because we know that when land is locked up and we allow National Parks to manage it instead of Forestry, pests and weeds are not managed and there are worse outcomes when there are bushfires. That has been demonstrated time and again. I suspect history may show the suggestions that this park is going to protect koalas to be incorrect.

The final thing I will touch on in the minute or so that I have left—unfortunately, we only get 20 minutes in the second reading debate—is that there are separate positions on this bill in the Coalition. The National Party has continually stood up for and represented forestry workers. Unfortunately, The Nationals will be separating from our Liberal Party colleagues on this bill, and I know that there are certain Liberal Party colleagues of mine who are disappointed that is the case. I acknowledge that I am not sure everybody in the Liberal Party is as steadfastly locked behind that decision as perhaps the vote will indicate. There is one person in particular who I single out: Mark Speakman. I may not be long for this place, Mr Assistant President, and I may or may not have a number of legacies. But the shortness of the Hon. Mark Speakman's leadership of the Opposition is one legacy I will claim. Noting his comments in debate on this bill in the other place, the fact he was happy to throw forestry workers under the bus and that he did so as a sopping wet left Liberal, I am glad that he is gone from the leadership. I conclude my remarks there.

The ASSISTANT PRESIDENT ( The Hon. Peter Primrose ): I welcome to the President's gallery Mr Johnson Hsiung, president of the World Taiwanese Chamber of Commerce, his executive team and Jordan Lane, MP. They are guests of the Hon. Natalie Ward. They are very welcome to Parliament.
The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 20:37 :13 ): Mr Assistant President, I wish to speak to the amendments moved during debate.

The ASSISTANT PRESIDENT ( The Hon. Peter Primrose ): Having consulted the Clerk, under the standing orders you can speak on another amendment at this point of the debate but not the amendment you moved.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK: I briefly speak to the amendment moved by my colleague the Hon. Robert Borsak, which seeks to refer the bill to an inquiry. It is wise that we do so, given the concerns that have been raised in this debate thus far, particularly around the carbon credit accounting scheme. Those matters are unresolved and are causing angst amongst a wide selection of members of this House, including those from The Greens. In her contribution to debate Ms Cate Faehrmann talked about how that has torn apart both her party and a lot of the environmental organisations. That is disappointing, I guess, from their perspective. From the outside looking in, it seems that environmental organisations are always quite united in their causes. To hear that they have been torn apart by this Government's decision is, I think, worth exploring in the inquiry. More importantly, it is worth exploring and getting more details about how the carbon credit accounting scheme is actually supposed to work in the delivery of the park, and to really test the Government's theories and accounting standards. With those brief words, I throw my full support behind the amendment to refer the bill to an inquiry.

Ms SUE HIGGINSON ( 20:40 :12 ): The Greens vehemently oppose the amendment to send the bill to a committee for inquiry. I remind the Hon. Mark Banasiak that, during the selection of bills process, we tried all those sorts of things and none of it came about. That involved the whole crossbench and representatives from both sides of Parliament. At this point it is a ridiculous ploy to suggest that the bill should now be referred to an inquiry. I remind the Hon. Mark Banasiak that the Selection of Bills Committee has a very democratic process. Every part of the crossbench has a representative there, as does the Opposition and the Government. We were all there, and we voted not to send the bill to a committee.

The member also made a very poor attempt to suggest that he is acting on behalf of The Greens and our movement because we are torn. The contribution of my colleague Ms Cate Faehrmann was that we are well and truly a recovering movement. The reality is that the Improved Native Forest Management [INFM] method has been done. Not only was the INFM done, but this project was submitted and approved. There is nothing relevant now for this House to explore. The carbon credit scheme and the Great Koala National Park project have been submitted to the Commonwealth under the Commonwealth scheme. It is done and dusted. This is not even an attempt at being opportunistic. Let us be honest: It is just a massive waste of time. Some members want to pass this bill in good faith. The numbers are on the side of the Government. The amendment is just in bad faith. It is unfair. It is more than a waste of people's time. I ask members to please cease and desist, and let the House do its business.
The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 20:42 :21 ): I speak on behalf of The Nationals on the two amendments moved during the course of debate, if I am able to do that now. I think I can speak to both.

The ASSISTANT PRESIDENT ( The Hon. Peter Primrose ): For the information of members, if a member contributed to debate before the amendments were moved, as the Hon. Sarah Mitchell did, they may speak a second time on the amendments. Other members spoke in debate after the amendments were moved and therefore cannot speak a second time.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL: Thank you for that clarification, Mr Assistant President. I place on record the views of The Nationals in relation to both amendments. One amendment was moved by the Hon. Mark Banasiak and one by the Hon. Robert Borsak. The Nationals will support both amendments. The first amendment, moved by the Hon. Mark Banasiak, basically punts the bill into the never‑never. I do not know the parliamentary term but that is probably how I would describe it, in very ineloquent terms. The Nationals are very opposed to the bill. We do not want it to pass. As I said in my contribution to the second reading debate—and I will not reiterate those remarks—we are concerned about the impact on the local community and the timber industry in particular. We would, of course, support any motion that stops this bill from passing.

The second amendment, to refer the bill to a committee—after the first amendment presumably fails, because I can count the numbers—also presents a good opportunity. I was not going to engage with what Ms Sue Higginson said, and I do not mean that in a disrespectful way, but members in this place have been told to cease and desist. This Parliament actually does good work with committees. Ms Sue Higginson is entitled to have her view, and I speak from my perspective. I listened to the contributions even after I spoke, and I have had my own engagement with people on the ground who are in the industry.

As the Hon. Wes Fang said in his contribution to the second reading debate, people from the timber industry and their families have wanted to meet with the Government to understand this better. They have not been happy with the packages. We have asked so many questions about it in the House throughout the course of this year. Those people do not get to stand in front of Government Ministers and members and put their case. We have to do that on their behalf. If everything the Government says stacks up, that will come to light in a committee inquiry into the bill. An inquiry would also give people in our communities a voice on how the bill impacts them. They have not had that chance.

The one way that they have been able to give some sort of indication of what they think of the bill is through their vote at elections. When Labor took this proposal as an election commitment to the last election, not one Labor MP was put in up there. Who did those communities put in place in those electorates? They put in National Party MPs in Coffs Harbour, Clarence, Oxley and Myall Lakes. The people who are directly impacted by the park would have voted for Labor if they wanted it, but they did not. A committee inquiry would give them a chance to have their voices heard. The Parliament does some of its best work when it hears directly from the people who will be impacted by the legislation we are about to pass. The Nats absolutely support the referral of the bill to a committee if that opportunity arises through a vote of this House.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 20:45 :55 ): On behalf of the Liberal Party, I indicate that we do not support the amendment moved by the Hon. Mark Banasiak, nor the amendment moved by the Hon. Robert Borsak. I acknowledge that the members may wish to utilise any mechanism available in this House to delay the bill. The Liberal Party would like to see the bill passed, although during the Committee stage we will move amendments that we think will improve it. Fundamentally, as the Hon. Sarah Mitchell said, this is a numbers matter and the bill will be passed. The Liberal Party made a commitment, and we want to see it through. Therefore, we do not support any delay, whether by way of committee referral or otherwise.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 20:46 :55 ): In reply: I thank all members for their contributions to debate on the National Park Estate (Great Koala National Park Reservations) Bill 2026. The bill establishes the legislative framework for the creation of the Great Koala National Park [GKNP] in north-eastern New South Wales. It has been decades in the making. Premier Wran and the Labor Government protected the rainforests of the north-east—some of which will become part of the GKNP—working in partnership with those who campaigned for them for a long time.

The environmental vision of the Labor Government under Premier Bob Carr led to record-breaking creation of national parks across the State. Again, they worked closely with those who sought to protect nature, and they found a way to do so. With today's bill, the Minns Government now joins that important legacy. The debate contained a lot of discussion about the Improved Native Forest Management [INFM] carbon project. I am thrilled that we found a way to support forests and value them for their carbon, water and biodiversity, rather than extracting from them.

Creating the Great Koala National Park is one of the most important things we can do to save koalas in New South Wales. It is about protecting the places where koalas live. They cannot survive without the trees to support them. It is also about creating an area that people can explore and enjoy for generations, where they can walk through the trees, camp with their family, ride their bikes, take holidays and just spend time in nature. The importance of the park cannot be understated. It will protect is one of the most environmentally and culturally significant landscapes in Australia. The park will connect existing reserves to create a vast protected area of over 475,000 hectares, the second largest in New South Wales after Kosciuszko. It represents a new era of landscape-scale conservation in New South Wales. Protecting large areas of land means wildlife has room to move, breed and grow in strength and genetic diversity. With a changing climate and more compounding threats than ever before, our precious wildlife needs large and interconnected protected areas to survive and thrive for generations to come.

The park paves a new way for Aboriginal leadership and management in New South Wales. For the first time, a whole-of-country approach will be taken across this vast landscape, supported by the creation of eight Aboriginal ranger positions within Aboriginal community controlled organisations, which is a first for the State. The Great Koala National Park has been a dream for more than a decade, and today—or maybe tomorrow—it will become a reality. I ask for the indulgence of the House while I pay tribute to some of the hundreds of people who have worked towards this moment for many years. I apologise in advance to anyone that I miss.

I acknowledge Uncle John Kelly, Auntie Jennie Rosser and all of the Gumbaynggirr and Dunghutti people who have advocated for the park, been a part of the Aboriginal advisory panel and generously shared their cultural knowledge, including Amie Jacky, Angela Brown, Cathy Thomas, Cheryl Brown, Ciaron Dunn, Darren Skinner, Dean Kelly, Narelle Wilson, Michele Donovan, Michael Donovan, Milly Webb, Shirley Duroux, Tony Perkins and many more. I acknowledge the original work of Ashley Love, who worked closely with the former leader of the Labor Party Luke Foley and staff from his office, including Felicity Wade. They put forward a network of State forests that they thought should be considered for the creation of the Great Koala National Park, and their work led to Labor's original commitment to move forward with the project.

I acknowledge the team from the National Parks Association, including Gary Dunnett, Liz Jeremy, Danielle Ryan and Grahame Douglas. Gary had his last day at the National Parks Association last week, after decades of work. I hope that he feels some satisfaction when the bill is passed tonight. I thank staff from the Nature Conservation Council, particularly Jacqui Mumford and Clancy Barnard. I thank Lyndon Schneiders, Warrick Jordan, Wilson Harris, Skye Laris and the tenacious Ken Henry from the Australian Climate and Biodiversity Foundation. I thank the team from World Wildlife Fund for Nature Australia, including Dermot O'Gorman and Stuart Blanch. I put on record that the koalas they have been handing around look a bit weird.

I thank the passionate people from the Labor Environment Action Network. The Labor Party has some incredible people who are strong advocates for the environment, and they push us to do better all the time. In particular, I acknowledge Felicity Wade, Penny Pedersen and David Mason. I acknowledge Dailan Pugh from North East Forest Alliance. I have walked in the forests with Dailan, and I have some of his pictures. He has been a persistent nagger and an important guide and mentor to me. I acknowledge the many years he has worked to save those forests. I also acknowledge Susie Russell from the North Coast Environment Council, who never takes a backward step. I thank Susie for being willing to trust me and trust that we would eventually get there.

I acknowledge Jeff Angel from the Total Environment Centre, who was here when Wran protected the forests and is still here today. He is happy about both this bill and the plastics bill. I acknowledge Patricia Edwards from the Clarence Environment Centre, Ashley Love from the Bellingen Environment Centre and Paula Flack from the Nambucca Valley Conservation Association. I acknowledge the Labor Party members from around the Coffs and Mid North Coast regions who, I have been advised, have been watching this debate today. In particular, I acknowledge Susan Jenvey, Tony Judge, Wendy Backhous, Paul Sekfy, Bill Smith and the late June Smith, a Labor candidate who ran in the Coffs Harbour electorate and supported the creation of the Great Koala National Park. June will be missed tonight. I also thank Asren Pugh, who will hopefully be elected as a new member of this place, for all of his work on the project.

I acknowledge the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water and the National Parks and Wildlife Service, and I particularly thank the team at the Coffs Harbour branch. They have been on the ground building the park and working with stakeholders and Aboriginal organisations to do something quite amazing, and they have also become Australian Carbon Credit Unit Scheme policy experts. I am so glad that they are here today. This was a lot of work and, as a Minister, I am profoundly grateful to them. The work they have done is incredible. Unfortunately, because of the world we now live in, I am not able to name all of the public servants on my list. People find them online and go after them, and I will not expose them to that. I tell them that they all rock and they are all excellent. I cannot wait to join them so they can show me some more koalas.

The Government does not support the amendments of the Hon. Robert Borsak and the Hon. Mark Banasiak. It is their right to put those amendments forward, but one of the amendments basically kills the bill and the other tries to send the bill into the never-never before the election. The bill has been a long time coming. There has been a lot of consultation. The bill is carefully structured. We have listened to what people have told us. The bill is one of the largest conservation actions taken since the creation of the regional forest agreements over 25 years ago. The creation of this national park has taken a long time; it does not need to be any longer. We should pass the bill.

I understand some of the carbon credit work has been challenging, but the bill is about valuing forests for a range of different things. We should use the ability to sequester carbon. If we can find ways for polluters who are killing the planet to contribute to its care and upkeep, I am totally okay with that. This Government is okay with that. I am very grateful we have found a way to move through that. I understand the legitimate concerns around monetising nature, but we are valuing nature for what it provides to nature and our planet in a way where taxpayers do not have to pay for all of it. That does not fix all of the problems.

I correct the record. There have been some allegations and misrepresentations throughout the debate. The Government has been very clear about the way in which it will use the income from carbon credits. It will be for manufacturing industries. We have had a lot of talk about jobs over the past couple of weeks. The State is going through a rapid energy transition. That is challenging, and we want jobs to do that. The income from carbon credits is not going to fossil fuel companies. It is going to manufacturing industries and others, and that is a good thing. We will continue to do that. Finally, there are big passions and people have big feelings about the bill. At the end of the day, when I look back on this in 20 years time, I will always remember what Neville Wran said. The greatest thing he thought he did was save the rainforests. We are going to save some koalas today. I commend the bill to the House.
