These amendments do a number of things. They would reserve the remaining State forest land within the Forest Bridge proposal as national park. Friends of Pine Creek have spent more than five years developing and defending this proposal, drawing on decades of research into the koala population south of Coffs Harbour. The area is on Gumbaynggirr country, between Bongil Bongil National Park on the coast and Bindarri National Park to the west. Both parks have been recognised by the New South Wales Government as assets of international significance for koalas. This missing connection is a relatively small area of public forest, but it is essential to the movement of wildlife between the coast and the hinterland towards the Dorrigo National Park and the New England National Park.

The original Forest Bridge proposal covers approximately 1,650 hectares. Its proponents deliberately designed the boundary around the corridor and allowed for productive plantations along some external edges to remain outside the reserve. This is a considered conservation proposal developed by people who know these forests and have watched the consequences of logging them. In 1996, ecologist Dr Andrew Smith identified Pine Creek as the most important State forest around Coffs Harbour for koala conservation based on its koala records, habitat and connection between coastal and hinterland populations. The forest also supports gliders, spotted-tailed quolls and other animals that need large, connected areas of habitat to survive.

The coastal forest around Bongil Bongil National Park escaped the Black Summer fires, making the protection of this connection particularly important as the climate changes. Some of the land is native forest and some is classified as hardwood plantation. There are genuine planted timber crops in this landscape, but the plantation classification also covers original vegetation and naturally regenerated forests with significant ecological value. We should assess and protect those values rather than allow Forestry Corporation's timber classifications to determine the boundaries of a national park. The Government has already included parts of this landscape in the bill, and the Legislative Assembly agreed to strengthen the protection of Bongil Bongil National Park by reserving land as national park rather than regional park. I welcome that outcome.

The bill also contemplates the reservation of additional State forest land by order. Parliament therefore now has the opportunity to complete the Forest Bridge while it is legislating for the larger park. Leaving this gap available for clear-fell logging threatens the very connection that makes these protected areas so important. The Greens ask the Committee to reserve the remaining State forest land within the mapped Forest Bridge area and give that part of the Great Koala National Park the permanent protection it warrants.

Ultimately, the amendments seek to reserve the whole of the Forest Bridge area. But, if that were not to happen, the amendments seek to place a moratorium over the Forest Bridge area now and have it assessed for its inevitable inclusion in the Great Koala National Park. There is no doubt in my mind that, as we get more connected and more awake to the realities of what it would take to make the very best Great Koala National Park we can have, the areas that connect some of the most important parts of the GKNP are essential for koalas. These amendments seek to have the whole of the Forest Bridge area included, but, if not included now, then set aside. Stop logging, assess them and then include them in time.

The other amendments seek to go piece by piece. If all this Parliament does tonight is reserve that one small area that connects the north and the south components from Pine Creek to the northern parts, we should do it now. We should not leave them out. We know those areas are absolutely essential for the safe passage and movement of the wildlife that relies on what, after tonight, will be the Great Koala National Park. The Forestry Corporation maintains that its logging operations in Pine Creek State Forest are conducted entirely within authorised hardwood plantations. But that is a classification that has been challenged by conservation scientists and the National Parks Association, who have documented natural forest vegetation within the compartments.

The idea that it is legitimate plantation is not completely true. The desperate call to protect those areas tonight and include them—if not as part of the park, then set them aside—is because the management practice adopted is one of the worst for those areas at this time. It is a clear-fell operation. Forestry Corporation has this year already resumed clear-felling in Pine Creek. Friends of Pine Creek reported in October that logging was underway in compartment 32 and that subsequent planned operations would enter the proposed Forest Bridge corridor. The plantation regulator has also recognised unique or special wildlife values within the authorised plantation in both Pine Creek and Tuckers Nob, imposing additional conditions on Forestry Corporation.

Those determinations do not settle which compartment should be permanently protected, but they absolutely demonstrate that the conservation concerns warrant proper examination. There are genuine hardwood plantations in this landscape—nobody doubts that—alongside naturally regenerated native forests, the areas containing original vegetation. An independent assessment should establish the present ecological condition of each compartment, its significance for threatened species, the integrity of the plantation classifications and its contribution to the surrounding national parks. If we set aside those areas now, stop the logging, protect them and assess them, the Government would retain responsibility for determining the appropriate long-term reservation of the forests.

There is no reasonable conservation justification for allowing further clear-felling while the evidence required to make the decision about their ultimate fate is being gathered. The compartments adjoining Bongil Bongil National Park, compartments 14, 16, 15 and 17 of Pine Creek, contain some of the most extensively researched koala habitat on the North Coast. There are important differences in the condition and history of each compartment, but the scientific evidence demonstrates the extraordinary conservation value of these forests. Compartment 14 was a mapped koala hub. According to research published by Wilderness Australia and the National Parks Association, the forest that the Forestry Corporation clear‑felled in October and November 2023 contained mature tallowwood and grey gum occupied by multiple koalas. Adjoining areas of northern grey ironbark, brush box and forest oak were also destroyed, and substantial areas of the logged compartment subsequently became heavily infested with lantana. That is what logging does. It trashes the joint, lets in invasive species and degrades the entire ecosystem.

In September 2023, Friends of Pine Creek recorded a koala in compartment 15, together with koala scat inside the plantation boundary and the adjoining Bongil Bongil National Park. The National Parks Association has photographed the forest either side of that boundary, where the vegetation continues across the line that separates land protected for conservation from land available for logging. In compartment 16, the National Parks Association documented mixed species native forest classified as plantation and, in compartment 17, it documented rainforest vegetation within the plantation classification. Those forests have ecological values that require and deserve permanent protection.

The importance of Pine Creek extends well beyond koalas. A government-commissioned ecological assessment associated with the Pacific Highway upgrade recorded giant barred frogs along Pine Creek, little bent‑wing bat calls within the State forest and 13 vulnerable rusty plum plants in or near the road corridor through the forest. My dear friends the yellow-bellied gliders had also previously been recorded in the wider study area. Those records are from the broader Pine Creek landscape, but they demonstrate the significance of the forest ecosystems adjoining the national park.

The research of Andrew Smith and John Pile also provides compelling evidence about breeding koalas. Their studies found that females depend on mature, structurally complex forests containing preferred food trees, particularly tallowwood and grey gum. Their dietary research identified more than 16 tree species consumed by koalas in Pine Creek, with tallowwood accounting for 39 per cent of the leaf fragments identified in scat samples, while blackbutt was consumed substantially less than its availability would suggest. Those forests provide habitat for breeding, feeding and movement through an important coastal koala population. Their values cannot be maintained through repeated clear-felling and replacement with less diverse timber crops.

The alternative to immediately adding compartments 14, 15, 16 and 17 into the Great Koala National Park would be, as suggested with the entire Forest Bridge, to put a moratorium on them, set them aside, assess them and then determine their future. I have no doubt that any proper assessment would recommend their inclusion into the park. Andrew Smith and John Pile's 2023 research into koalas in Pine Creek identified just how restricted the opportunities for movement from those coastal forests have become. The population is largely isolated by the Bellinger River to the south, the Pacific Highway and coastline to the east, and extensive clearing to the north and west.

The researchers identified just two narrow forest corridors remaining connecting Pine Creek to the forests of the Great Dividing Range through Tuckers Nob State Forest and private land. I cannot impart enough to all members that it cannot be underestimated how important it is to protect that little connection of compartments 22 and 23 so that the Great Koala National Park will completely achieve the objective we are seeking—that is, to allow the free, safe, proper movement from areas that are currently protected to other areas that will be protected tonight. We also need to remember that, in the past couple of months, a koala was killed in broad daylight during a logging operation. It is not necessary to operate like this.

We also know that the logging threat continues right now. Earlier this month, reports emerged of new logging plans for Tuckers Nob, prompting renewed community protests and concerns from Gumbaynggirr Elders about the protection of cultural and environmental values. In Pine Creek, Forestry Corporation has already resumed clear-fell logging in plantation compartments that were excluded from the Great Koala National Park assessment area. The assessment of the four compartments—compartments 22 and 23 and Tuckers Nob compartments 5 and 6—needs to establish what originally and naturally regenerated native forest remains, the habitat available for koalas and other threatened wildlife, and whether the existing connections can survive further clearing. I seriously doubt that they can. The assessment should examine the opportunities to restore degraded sections of the corridor, rather than treating their previous logging as a reason to exclude them from conservation.

The assessment should be undertaken independently, with Gumbaynggirr traditional owners properly involved in decisions affecting their country. The Greens beg the Parliament and the Government to take note of the amendments. I have worked very hard to canvass members. I do not think that I will get the necessary support tonight, notwithstanding our efforts and the clear-cut case before us. If we were doing the right thing, we would be supporting the amendments. My intention in moving the amendments is to place on public record the work that now needs to be done. Tonight we will create the Great Koala National Park. I have no doubt in my mind or in my heart that we will soon add these small but vital and significant areas to the Great Koala National Park. I commend the amendments to the Committee.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 21:31 :24 ): I am not surprised by the amendments and thank the member for moving them. There has been an ongoing discussion about what is and is not included in the Great Koala National Park. Tuckers Knob and Pine Creek State Forest have been at the pointy end of that discussion. I understand the passion of the local community and those who wish to add those areas to the park, but I have to be very up-front, as the Government has been throughout the process, that the Government supports plantation forestry. Those are plantation forests, and we believe it is very important to continue harvesting them. I understand the passion of the member and the locals whom I have met, but the Government supports plantation hardwood forestry, and those are plantation forests. Therefore the Government cannot support the amendments.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 21:32 :42 ): Although my colleague the Hon. Jacqui Munro may also make a contribution, I indicate that the Opposition also opposes the amendments. My understanding is that the amendments are quite similar to those moved by the member for Pittwater in the other place, which the Opposition also opposed. Opposition members have been clear throughout the debate that we cannot support incorporating additional land into the Great Koala National Park. Expanding the national park estate should not come at the cost of further forestry land and the industry jobs that depend on it. I understand why people in the community are sometimes a bit cynical. When he spoke to similar amendments moved in the other place, my colleague the member for Coffs Harbour pointed out that every time native hardwood harvesting has been raised, communities get the same message from the left, "Come out of native forest. Move into plantations." As the Minister said, the amendments add plantation lands to the park.

I can count. I understand that the bill will pass eventually, whether it is tonight or tomorrow. But The Greens, of course, want to go further and include plantations. Communities have been told for a long time that plantations are the answer in terms of having sustainable wood products, but they are now being asked to give those up too. As I said, this is why there is a deep lack of trust among timber communities in what The Greens put forward. It does feel like death by a thousand cuts. An inch is given; then a mile is taken. We do not support any of The Greens amendments. We did not do so in the other place and we do not support them in this place tonight either.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 21:34 :45 ): I contribute to debate to ensure clarity—because obviously The Nationals and the Liberals will be voting separately on some amendments—that we are voting together on these amendments. The Liberals support the position of the Government and as outlined by my colleague the Hon. Sarah Mitchell.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 21:35 :07 ): The Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party vehemently opposes the amendments. They are just another veiled ambit land grab. I distinctly remember the evidence that we took during the parliamentary inquiry into the sustainable timber industry. We heard quite clearly from the people in Coffs Harbour that they were quite frustrated with the hypocrisy and lack of good faith from The Greens, who tried to push the industry into plantations and then, in the next breath, when there were plantations in the area wanted to take them too. The lack of good-faith discussions around this issue has continued. Even after the announcement of the Great Koala National Park, some Greens members jumped on the bandwagon straightaway and said, "We want to take private native forestry as well."

We cannot support the amendments. As I said, they are just a blatant land grab. I also seek a procedural clarification from you, Mr Chair. Ms Sue Higginson moved her amendments in globo. But then, when explaining the amendments from different sheets, she seemed to indicate that one set of amendments would include the land as part of the proposal while another set of amendments—what I would probably call a contingency or backup set of amendments—would create a moratorium on harvesting in those areas should the first set of amendments not pass. Even if the numbers are not there to support any of the amendments, would it be wise procedurally for the two sets of amendments to be put separately as one set of amendments is potentially contingent on the other passing or not passing? T he CHAIR ( The Hon. Rod Roberts ): Before I seek advice from the learned Clerks, it appears to me from glancing around the Chamber that the amendments will not succeed in any form. Therefore, I do not think the Hon. Mark Banasiak's concerns, although valid, will hold.
The Hon. Mark Banasiak: I am just concerned about the good order of the House, Mr Chair.

The CHAIR ( The Hon. Rod Roberts ): I am sure you are, and I appreciate your concern. But I think the amendments will be defeated and there will be no contingency because they will all be wiped out. I think Ms Sue Higginson wishes to make a contribution.

Ms SUE HIGGINSON ( 21:38 :01 ): Yes. I thank all members who made a contribution. I am sad that they are not coming on the good journey with me to support the amendments. I will deal with this idea that there is bad faith somehow or that The Greens are shifting the goalposts again or doing this or that. It does not work like that, and members need to wake up to what we are trying to do here. It is not a land grab. I am not grabbing land—and I am certainly not grabbing it for myself or Ms Cate Faehrmann or the Hon. Stephen Lawrence or the Hon. Sarah Mitchell. This is about sustaining ecosystems and their functions, which sustain us all. It is about clean water, carbon sequestration, the living planet and koalas surviving into the future. Going forward, it is the reality of what we are all going to do together to protect the forests from fire and invasive species. This is how it goes. If members think we are trying to go after plantations for plantations' sake, they have not listened to a word I have said.
The Hon. Robert Borsak: And neither should we listen to a bloody word you say.
Ms SUE HIGGINSON: The interjections are disorderly.
The CHAIR ( The Hon. Rod Roberts ): We have a long night in front of us. I am not calling the Hon. Robert Borsak to order but ask him to stop interjecting.

Ms SUE HIGGINSON: Members are struggling because they think The Greens are going after plantations and we never made a deal to go after plantations. A lot of landholders, conservationists, scientists, mums and dads, nurses and teachers who live around these forests are saying, "Hang on. I am seeing that these forests are used regularly and persistently by some of the world's most iconic, wondrous and globally significant threatened species. I really don't think we should just be cutting them down and turning them into woodchips, toilet paper, fence posts, tomato stakes and firewood." In the case of the forests I am talking about, the timber is actually sent to the sugar mill, burnt and sold by Cape Byron Power as green power, which is a lie. They have got to be kidding.

Members should not talk to me about the incredible, noble timber industry, as though that is somehow what is taking place. It is not like that anymore. It is actually a really sad state of affairs. The highest and best use of those forests is to take pride in world-class land management, where we do it together and where children and young people are involved. We could have well-managed forests, regeneration, recovery and forests alive with wonderful, globally significant animals and clean water running through them rather than nuking them. Have members been to a plantation up north? It is literally clear-felled and then nuked with chemicals as far as the eye can see. People cannot breathe or let their kids go there. Not long ago the Coffs Harbour water supply literally went on red alert because of plantation chemical application.

Ms SUE HIGGINSON: The plantations we are talking about today—which I have been to and stood in—that I seek to include in the park through the amendments are much more akin to beautiful native forests. The truth is that they should be managed to regenerate back into the native forest that they were and are becoming, because they have come from a gene pool that is thousands of years old. The fact is, if we clear-fell them again, we will lose the biodiversity they contain.

With that, I absolutely reject the idea that this was done in bad faith or that it is about a land grab. That is preposterous. I have my own land; I do not need to grab any more land. This is about the best interests of conservation—clean water and carbon sequestration—and the mental and physical wellbeing of the communities who rely on and live around those areas. Of course, it is also about the better integrity of the Great Koala National Park, which members of Parliament are doing brilliant work right now to create.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 21:46 :59 ): I will not speak for long, and I genuinely mean that, but I raise one issue with the amendments. (ii)the number of relevant ACCUs subject to the option or contract,
(f)the number of relevant ACCUs held by the State at the end of the financial year to which the report relates,
(g)the allocation of money under section 37B.

The amendments are about the sale of carbon credits. The Opposition intends to make sure that there is a clear and transparent commitment to regional communities that those who will be affected by the introduction of the park will receive a fair share of the benefits, and also that there is transparency through the Parliament so that the community knows how any revenue generated from the sale of carbon credits is used. These four amendments create a new part 4A of the bill, dealing with the Australian carbon credit units generated through the Great Koala National Park. As I said, the amendments are about ensuring transparency and the right accountability measures for the carbon credits generated. Through these amendments, we would also like the Minister to table a report in both Houses of Parliament each year about the State's dealings with the relevant Australian carbon credit units in the previous financial year. These amendments are really all about accountability.

The proposed sections in amendment No. 7 go to making sure that the revenue from this carbon credit dealing is directed back to the local community. In particular, there are three areas we would like to see that revenue focused on. We want to make sure the funding is directed towards the local communities and the workers of the timber industry affected by this legislation, particularly on the Mid North Coast. We also want to make sure there is investment by the Government in local tourism, community infrastructure and the management of the national park estate reserved under the legislation, including for biosecurity and fire risk mitigation. The residents and communities on the Mid North Coast will shoulder the burden of the Great Koala National Park. We strongly believe they should get any benefits that come as a result, which is exactly what these amendments do. They are about ensuring that the money goes back into those communities.

Without these amendments to the bill—which would make it crystal clear in the legislation that this money will go back to those communities—we are concerned that the revenue from some of these credits will just end up protecting the Government's bottom line and not actually supporting the communities that are most impacted. A guarantee of support for the workers in the timber industry who are affected and will be affected by Labor's decision to close that industry on the Mid North Coast—which is what this bill will do—is a big issue that we have raised in other debates in this Chamber. We think these are sensible amendments that will make sure the Government looks after those whom it is tearing the industry away from.

We also want to make sure that we have recreational facilities for tourists. Again, in putting this bill forward the Government has said the park will bring all these people to the community. We want an ironclad guarantee in the legislation that funding will be available in order to do that. We think these amendments will make that pretty clear. They are sensible amendments. They will give those communities comfort that any sort of revenue generated does not fill a budget black hole for Labor but comes back into regional communities, which is where we think that money should be spent. We hope the Committee will support the amendments.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 22:06 :56 ): The Government does not support the amendments. They were moved during consideration in the lower House and debated there, so I am not going to go into it in detail. But the point is that the Government has already committed $6 million out of consolidated revenue to tourism and work in this area. The transition package in relation to impacted workers is already funded. The creation of the park and the issues the member raised are not being funded through carbon credits. What this Government has committed to is that any money from carbon credits will be used for management of the park. These amendments are unnecessary and we do not support them.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 22:07 :36 ): I indicate that the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party will support the Opposition amendments. We think they are sensible amendments that go to the concerns raised during the second reading debate around the carbon credit accounting scheme. In other schemes we have seen money supposedly set aside for certain projects or certain uses—such as with the regional development fund, where it went to pools in The Rocks.
The Hon. Penny Sharpe: That wasn't us.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK: I acknowledge the interjection, although I know I should not. That was not done by this Government. But these amendments would give the community the surety that the money is going to the right place. I think reporting to Parliament and keeping it informed in terms of how this money is spent and what it is going towards is an excellent provision. Parliament is better when it is properly informed. We can make better decisions based on that information. With those remarks, I support the amendments.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 22:08 :53 ): I respond briefly to the Minister, who said that money has already been set aside. That may be true. However, the concern comes from the local community. It was also raised by my colleagues during debate in the other place. Those North Coast communities find it hard to take the Government at its word on some of the issues surrounding the national park. The amendments put those guarantees in black and white. Before the previous election, when the Government committed to the park, it said, "No, we will still be able to have a viable timber industry after the creation of this park." We now know that is not the case, so there is not a lot of faith in the Government among those communities.

To be frank, the Government tends to say one thing and do another. That is why The Nationals want to protect that money and make sure that the right amount is invested back into community facilities and support for the timber industry. My response to the Minister is that if the Government will do those things anyway and ensure that everyone in the community is looked after, why not support the amendments and put that commitment in black and white, with no confusion? That would provide certainty for the local community. If the Government does not support the amendments, it is no wonder there is deep mistrust and concern about Labor's intentions, when it is not prepared to put its money where its mouth is.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 22:17 :43 ): I move Opposition amendment No. 4 on sheet c2026‑314A:
No. 4Continued perpetual leases
Page 13. Insert after line 16—
33AContinued perpetual leases
Despite another provision of this Act, land subject to a continued perpetual lease must not be reserved by or under this Act without the written consent of the lessee.

This amendment requires landholders with perpetual leases to agree to any land being reserved under the provisions of the bill for the purpose of the State forest. We think it is important that we protect the rights of existing perpetual leaseholders by ensuring that the land cannot be brought into the reservation process without their consent. Again, these points were mentioned in the lower House, so I will not speak for too long. The reality is that people have entered into perpetual leases on land in this area, and they have done so in good faith. Those landholders have made improvements to the land, and they cannot be ignored in the passage of this legislation. I understand that the Government is undertaking just terms compensation negotiations with perpetual leaseholders, whose leases are generally family assets. Some of the leases have been held for more than a century. Some residents may have lawfully built a cottage on their perpetual lease. Those structures would be acquired by the State Government through the compulsory acquisition process, effectively kicking people out of their home.

This amendment makes it clear that the leaseholders need to be consulted and need to agree to their leases being extinguished. This is about making sure that the Government consults with people who entered into a perpetual lease in good faith and who made improvements to the land. I conclude by aligning myself with the comments of the member for Coffs Harbour, who made some very good points on this issue in the other place. We are not talking about big pieces of land or people who are harvesting timber or clear-felling land. These families and groups hold perpetual leases and might have a cottage. Until this bill came into play, they had expected to hold the land forever. This amendment will give them a bit of respect and a proper process. We urge the Committee to support our amendment.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 22:20 :33 ): The member is right to raise the issue of people who will be impacted by this bill. To be clear, the bill does not extinguish existing perpetual lease interests without compensation. We are working through this process in accordance with the Land Acquisition (Just Terms Compensation) Act, which is a fair and transparent compensation framework. The Government does not support this amendment.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 22:21 :00 ): We support this sensible Opposition amendment, which provides some certainty for people who have signed up to a perpetual lease. I turn now to the Leader of the Government's comments. The compulsory acquisition process in the Act has a lot of flaws, which several governments have tried to fix, to no avail. There is no political will to fix this, because it benefits both sides of politics. Members should not rely on the Act as a smokescreen to not support this amendment.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 22:21 :45 ): I speak in support of this amendment. I note that when the Minister spoke about the just terms Act, she did not use the word "fair". I do not think that any member in this place would say that the just terms Act will provide fair compensation to these people, which is why we have moved this amendment. These leaseholders signed perpetual leases in good faith. Some of them may have had only a short‑term connection with the area, but I suspect that the majority of them have quite a long-term connection with the area. Many of these perpetual leaseholders have invested so much into their lease areas. I do not use the word "investment" in its financial sense alone. There are emotional, physical and financial investments. These leaseholders have dedicated themselves to their leases, and it is not unreasonable to expect the Government to adopt a certain level of consideration when it seeks to compulsorily acquire their leases.

Members need to put themselves in the shoes of someone who holds a perpetual lease in one of these areas and consider how this process has been rolled out. The Labor Party obviously made an election commitment, but I do not think that the boundaries that were published prior to the election would have necessarily provided every single one of the leaseholders with fair warning that this process was going to be considered at the end of a parliamentary term, right before an election. It has been just under four years since the Labor Party won government. At the time of the election, the leaseholders would not necessarily have realised that their lease would be captured by the Great Koala National Park.

The Coalition has discussed the impacts of the issues with those stakeholders, which is why we bring this amendment to the Committee. There is a lack of transparency about how those leases are going to be progressed. Those landholders made physical, emotional and financial investments, in good faith, in leases that they thought were going to be for much longer terms. The amendment seeks to provide them with the ability to have their voice heard in a way that is captured not just by the Land Acquisition (Just Terms Compensation) Act because, as the Hon. Mark Banasiak indicated, there is an understanding amongst a lot of members of this House, if not all members, that the Act does not necessarily provide for fair and reasonable compensation for compulsory acquisition of those leases. While the Minister sought to allay some of the fears communicated by the Hon. Sarah Mitchell by saying that there is a process, the amendment will ensure that process is providing a greater level of consultation with the leaseholders. Dialogue will then arise from that consultation, and that may provide the perpetual leaseholders with a feeling that they are being heard in circumstances where they may not necessarily have realised less than four years ago that their leases would be captured by the Great Koala National Park.

The Opposition has engaged with a number of the stakeholders impacted by the decisions of this Government and its bill. Our amendment is informed by those consultations and will ensure that the Government better consults with those leaseholders. It may be the case that the consultation process does not result in an agreement on all sides for an appropriate and just compensation package. By passing this amendment, at least those conversations will be had. Some stakeholders have articulated to us that they feel there has not necessarily been the consultation process that the Government indicated may be on the table when it announced the Great Koala National Park. The Opposition wants to make sure that the stakeholders who were not captured initially but whose perpetual leases are being extinguished and who are being offered fair and just compensation packages for those investments are also captured by this amendment.

For those leaseholders who are perhaps anxious and concerned about the process, this amendment will provide them with a level of certainty and clarity. I do not think any member in this place would begrudge or deny perpetual leaseholders the opportunity to have their voices heard, and nobody would expect them to forgo those perpetual leases and the investments that they have made—in many cases, long‑term investments—in places that are home to their family and that they hold dear. On this side of the Chamber, we recognise that value. We understand that some perpetual leaseholders are concerned that their leases may be compulsorily acquired without appropriate and well‑considered compensation. With those few words, I suggest that the amendment is supportable.
The Hon. Chris Rath: More! We want more.
The Hon. WES FANG: I never leave my fans disappointed.
The Hon. Sarah Mitchell: Wes always leaves them wanting more.

The Hon. WES FANG: It sounds like I am being called to give an encore. I have got my second wind. However, I did say that I would keep my contribution brief, and my word is my bond. I conclude by encouraging members to support the amendment. Nobody should be dispossessed of the place that they hold dear without fair and adequate compensation.
The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 22:32 :30 ): Very briefly, Chair, I want to address—
The Hon. Wes Fang: My "briefly" or your "briefly"?

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL: My briefly. In her contribution, the Hon. Penny Sharpe made a point about compensation. I put on record in this Chamber, as it was in the other place, that some of our lower House colleagues who have constituents who are caught up in this issue have said that the compensation amounts that have been offered to those people are nowhere near adequate. They are very concerned about it. That was said in the lower House and I just wanted it on record in this Chamber also, in response to the Minister.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 22:40 :39 ): By leave: I move Opposition amendments Nos 5 and 6 on sheet c2026-314A in globo:
No. 5Motor sport events
Page 14, clause 35(1), lines 7–10. Omit "on the" from line 7 and all words on lines 8–10. Insert instead "on land reserved by this Act.".
No. 6Motor sports
Page 14, clause 35(4), lines 23 and 24. Omit all words on the lines.

These amendments go to the issue of motor sports and the trails within the proposed Great Koala National Park. The Opposition knows that throughout the footprint of the proposed park there are existing trails and roads that are already used for motor sport activities. As my colleagues in the lower House covered this extensively, I will not speak for long on these particular amendments. But local communities are concerned about what happens to some of these events that have a long history. The amendments try to give certainty to local communities, clubs and event organisations.

The Coalition believes strongly that the creation of new park reservations should not unnecessarily jeopardise activities that have a long history on the park's land. The amendments make clear that motor sport events can continue to be conducted on land reserved by the bill and give the Minister greater flexibility when considering motor sport proposals. The Minister will have the decision-making power, but the Opposition believes these amendments are important to give that clarity in the bill. Again, I acknowledge the Leader of The Nationals, and member for Coffs Harbour who spoke in the other place about the World Rally Championship, which is held in much of the area that is to become the Great Koala National Park. That event brings tourists to the region. There is concern, if we do not get a guarantee through these amendments, about what that will mean for future events.

The amendments are about giving the Minister the discretion to make decisions. They do not force the Minister to do anything. We are not saying that rallies must occur or that the Minister must approve them, but the amendments will give the Minister discretion to approve them, if the conditions are appropriate and if they line up. We think it is important to have that in the bill. I hope the Committee supports the amendments.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 22:43 :25 ): The Government does not support the amendments. This matter was well canvassed in the lower House. The Opposition proposes that motor sports events be allowed on all lands reserved under the bill, including national parks, regional parks and nature reserves in Aboriginal areas. That is inappropriate. The Government supports continued racing in the areas where that has occurred historically. That is reflected in the categories set out in the bill. The Government does not support the amendments.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 22:44 :03 ): The Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party supports both amendments. I will deal with them individually. We support amendment No. 5 because the bill gives the Minister responsible for administering the National Parks and Wildlife Act a power to approve motor races and ancillary activities. As drafted, that power is tied to specified regional park land and access roads on or adjoining a regional park. This amendment replaces that description with land reserved by this Act. That broadens the land on which the approval power can operate. That matters because a change in the legal category attached to a piece of land can otherwise determine whether an event is even capable of being considered under this provision.

Motorsport organisers need a workable process. Clubs cannot plan an event, engage suppliers or give participants certainty if the legislation rules out consideration simply because a route crosses a different reservation category. The Government should be prepared to assess a proposal on its circumstances and the requirements of the approval process. The amendment retains that assessment. The Minister must still consider natural and cultural values, participant and public safety, environmental risks, and the relevant guidelines. Conditions can still be imposed. Supporting a broader approval power does not require us to pretend that every proposal will be suitable.

We should also state clearly what this amendment leaves unresolved. It does not remove the five named regional park exclusions in clause 35 (5), does not guarantee approval and, by replacing the existing wording, does not expressly retain the separate reference to access roads on or adjoining a regional park where those roads fall outside land reserved by this Act. Organisers with routes using those roads will still need clarity about the applicable authorisation. Those limits should be acknowledged. They do not change the fact that expanding the power beyond the present regional park description is a useful improvement for motorsport proposals on reserved land. Regional events depend on practical access arrangements. They involve volunteers, local suppliers, accommodation providers and families who deserve a clear answer about what the law allows to be considered. We support this amendment because it creates a broader opportunity for that consideration. We will continue to press for reliable access and workable approvals, but I think we should take this improvement when it is before us.

Amendment No. 6 removes clause 35 (4), which prevents the Minister from approving motor vehicle use anywhere other than a road that existed immediately before this part commenced. That is a rigid restriction on the approval power, and removing it makes the provision more workable. An event route may need to change over time. Safety considerations, storm damage, maintenance or the practical management of an event can require organisers to propose a different alignment. The law should allow the Minister to examine such a proposal rather than make the date on which a road existed the decisive barrier.

That distinction matters for clubs trying to plan responsibly. An organiser who identifies a safer or more suitable route should be able to have that proposal assessed. A statutory rule tied to the commencement date can prevent the approval process from considering whether the alternative would produce a better result. Removing this subsection does not compel the Minister to approve a race. The other considerations remain, including natural and cultural values, public and participant safety, environmental risks, and relevant guidelines. The Minister can still impose conditions or refuse a proposal. As with amendment No. 5, the five named regional park exclusions also remain. Members should not describe this amendment as removing every restriction on motorsport or guaranteeing unrestricted vehicle access. It removes one particular prohibition within the motor race approval scheme. It also does not itself authorise someone to build a road or start driving through reserved land. What it does is remove the rule that an approval under this section can only permit vehicle use on a road that predates commencement. That allows the approval decision to address the proposal actually put forward.

The Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party wants legislation that can deal with practical circumstances on the ground. Clubs should be accountable for safety and responsible conduct, and the Government should be accountable for providing a process capable of assessing their applications fairly. This amendment moves the bill in that direction. It preserves the ministerial assessment while removing the inflexible restriction that can rule out consideration before the merits are examined. For those reasons, I support amendment No. 6 and encourage other members to do the same.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 22:48 :21 ): I support these amendments, and I note the words of the Hon. Mark Banasiak encouraging members to do the same. A World Rally Championship race was held on the roads that are now captured in the area prescribed by the legislation. For those who have never seen the World Rally Championship, that race has some of the best drivers using some of the fastest machinery on some of the most challenging courses in the world. The Minister, in her contribution about why it is important to create this new national park, indicated that increased tourism is one of the outcomes the Government is seeking to encourage by prescribing this area as a national park. I assure members that this motorsport event is a huge driver of tourism, and nothing would showcase Australia—and certainly the Great Koala National Park—better than broadcasting it to the world. Motorsport events held all across the world are broadcast all across the world, and that is why so many locations fight for them.

It would be shortsighted for members not to adopt the Opposition amendments. If the goal of the Government really is to drive tourism in regional areas, these amendments will aid that goal by ensuring that we do not unnecessarily put a handbrake on what could be a fantastic event that showcases a beautiful part of New South Wales. Many members in their contributions to the second reading debate mentioned the natural beauty of the area, so why not share it with the world by hosting an event, as we have done previously, on the very roads now part of the Great Koala National Park? If the Government considered these amendments in detail, I cannot see why it would not support them.

To be honest, I am not sure that a motor vehicle poses much of a risk to the koalas or the park. The hosting of a motorsport event in a national park would be so noisy and so busy with spectators that it would preclude the risk of a vehicle injuring any koalas. But the event would certainly boost tourism in the area. It really is a win‑win. It is a win for the local economy. It is a win for the workers who have been thrown by the wayside by a Labor government that pretends to support them but has shut down an entire industry with very little warning and expects those same workers, who worked with their hands for so long, to become baristas, tour guides or Uber drivers. The motorsport event that these amendments propose will provide opportunities for those workers to engage in a tourism event in a meaningful way.

If I am honest, I do not know anybody who does not like motorsport. If a person does not like motorsport, there is perhaps something wrong. Motorsport brings out the best in people. It brings joy, happiness and elation to the people. The community has been decimated by job cuts and the death of an industry, and they are disappointed in the Government. We want to try to bring them a bit of joy. Everybody loves motorsport. Everybody loves fast cars. Everybody loves the sound of a turbocharged four-cylinder engine. A V8 or a flat six would be better, but a turbocharged four cylinder—one takes what one can get.

People get a rush from hearing and seeing a vehicle being piloted or driven—or whichever word one wants to use to articulate the skill that those world-class drivers bring to motorsport events—particularly in places like the Great Koala National Park. There is an opportunity to lift a community up—lift their spirits and provide them some joy. This Committee could be considered somewhat miserly and Grinch-like if it were to deny that community that level of joy. The community is in need of boosting, and this may be an opportunity to do that. We bring these amendments in good faith. The Opposition moved very similar amendments, if not exactly the same, in the other place.
The Hon. Sarah Mitchell: Pretty much exactly the same.

The Hon. WES FANG: Pretty close. I do not know what it is about members of the other place. Maybe there are too many metropolitan members who do not like motorsport much, but there is a great affinity for motorsport in rural and regional New South Wales. There is a great history of participation in motorsport, as competitors, as marshals or even on organising committees. The level of joy and excitement that people get from motorsport permeates through a community when an event comes. The Opposition is strong in its conviction that we need to make sure, in the same way we have previously, that we do not provide a disincentive for world-class events to come to areas like the Great Koala National Park in the future.

As I said, any disincentive that may provide a commercial or competitive advantage to our opposition—that is, other locations that want to hold those motorsport events—would be a terrible impediment to the economy of New South Wales. It would also be a second punishment from a decision that was made by a Sydney-centric government for a rural and regional community. I have consulted with that community and spoken to them about their love of motorsport. The Leader of The Nationals, the member for Coffs Harbour, has been a strong advocate for the motorsport community in his area. Indeed, the member for Coffs Harbour before him, Andrew Fraser, was heavily involved in motorsport as well. Those members have seen the value of motorsport because their communities sees its value.

Their communities are strong advocates for the ability to continue to host motorsport events. It is on the back of their advocacy and desire to see motorsport return to the Mid North Coast that they have asked us to move amendments in the Legislative Council, as we did in the lower House. I am not sure that the Labor Party is particularly fond of motorsports, so its failure to consider that the legislation may be an impediment to hosting future motorsport events on the Mid North Coast might have been an oversight. In keeping with the old adage "Help me help you", the Opposition is trying to help the Government to help our community by moving the amendments.

My friend and colleague the Hon. Sarah Mitchell moved amendments Nos 5 and 6 in globo. By moving them in globo, the Opposition has shown in good faith that it is not filibustering or trying to hold up the bill. The Opposition simply seeks to provide clarity to our communities and an opportunity for members to repent for not adopting the amendments in the other place. The amendments are a second chance to make things right and say that the Government does not hate motorsport or want to impede the motorsport community on the Mid North Coast, but that it wants to see the mid North Coast move ahead.

To conclude, motorsport is important. A number of Opposition members, both in this place and the other place, have made quite clear that the community has asked us to move the amendments. While it is unfortunate that they were not adopted in the other place, members now have an opportunity to look at them again and perhaps provide a little comfort and clarity to the communities that may seek to hold a motorsport event. I cannot be sure but I hope that, through the advocacy for the amendments, we could soon have another motorsport event in that area. If we do not pass the amendments tonight, we may pose a risk to any of the good work to encourage motorsport events on the Mid North Coast. On balance, the benefit of passing the amendments certainly outweighs the risks. I commend the amendments to the Committee.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 23:10 :46 ): I move Opposition amendment No. 8 on sheet c2026-314A:
Page 15. Insert after line 29—
39AFire trails
Despite anything in this Act or the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974, fire trails, on land reserved by this Act, may—
(a)following consultation with the Commissioner of the NSW Rural Fire Service—be developed, and
(b)be maintained.

The amendment is about fire trails. Concern about what might happen should there be bushfires in the newly created national park was a pretty consistent theme in some of the second reading debate contributions. Amendments more broadly about fire management were moved in the other place. I understand that those were accepted by the Government, but the part about fire trails was not accepted. Therefore, we place the amendment on record in this place and ask the Committee to support it. If we want to be able to safely and quickly respond to bushfires, we need to make sure that access is available to firefighters. They cannot protect communities if they cannot safely and efficiently reach the fires. One concern with the new national park is whether access for firefighting could become more difficult.

In the past when State forests have transitioned into national parks, the fire risk has increased, given the different ways of managing those forests. That is very likely to be the case here. A significant amount of State forest land will be transferred into the national park estate. That brings with it higher bushfire risk. The amendment gives the Government the capacity to build fire trails in the park if needed. We have been in government, and we know fire trails are expensive. We know that they are not something that a government creates unless it needs to. But if it needs to do that, we do not want the legislation to be an impediment. Just to be very clear, the amendment does not say that the fire trails must be built or that they are compulsory. It simply says that they may be built. We do not want a bushfire getting out of control and there being no allowance within the Act to develop and maintain fire trails if the need arises. We ask the Committee to support it.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister f or Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 23:13 :22 ): The amendment fundamentally misunderstands the way in which fire is managed in national parks. I place on record that a lot of rubbish has been spoken in relation to fire management in this State. There is already a rigorous, well-developed process for fire trail management in place across all national parks that will continue to be followed in the Great Koala National Park. In New South Wales, bushfire management trails are governed under the Rural Fires Act and managed through fire access and fire trail plans. Local bushfire management committees develop those plans with the input of all land managers, including Forestry Corporation, the National Parks and Wildlife Service and the Rural Fire Service.

All trails identified in the current fire access and fire trail management plans within State forests identified in the bill will be automatically transferred to the National Parks and Wildlife Service. That is the first reason that the amendment is unnecessary. Secondly, the National Parks and Wildlife Service has more firefighters than Forestry Corporation. It does most of the fire management that occurs in this State, and it does it well. The furphy that I am tired of hearing is that somehow fire risk is worse as a result of that land being a national park. More people will be available to fight fires and there will be more staff on the ground than ever before. To suggest otherwise is, frankly, misleading at best. Thirdly, regarding carbon credit units, if members want any more incentive to keep fires under control—aside from the fact that we are already doing that as much as we can—we would get less carbon credits and earn less income to look after the park if it is burnt down in a fire and we lose carbon.

Those are three very good reasons why fire is a top priority. I have tried to be very polite in this debate, and it is right that members raise those issues, but I am tired of the misinformation, particularly from the National Party, about the way in which fires are managed and the care with which that work is undertaken. I am also very tired of that insult to the over 1,000 professional firefighters in the National Parks and Wildlife Service, who put their lives on the line every single fire season. They manage the vast majority of hazard reduction burns and they look after that land very carefully.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 23:15 :56 ): The Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party supports the amendment, which makes clear that fire trails on land reserved by this bill may be developed following consultation with the Commissioner of the NSW Rural Fire Service and may be maintained despite provisions in this bill or the National Parks and Wildlife Act. That is a practical provision. A fire management strategy must be supported by useable access on the ground. People responding to fires need routes that they can travel on, and the location and condition of those routes must be considered before an emergency develops. The Minister said the Rural Fire Service Association is largely responsible for the management of fire trails in this State. I put on record some of the concerns provided by the Rural Fire Service Association to the inquiry that I chaired into—
The Hon. Penny Sharpe: The Rural Fire Service. You're talking about the Rural Fire Service Association.

The Hon . MARK BANASIAK: Yes. At the inquiry into access restrictions to public lands, the Rural Fire Service Association raised serious concerns about a reduction in dedicated fire trail funding and tenure‑blind prioritisation. Because of those issues, the association was very concerned about the ability to safely fight fires in national parks. The association specifically identified national parks as being problematic in terms of knowing whether a fire trail will be safely accessible when its members go to fight fires. It specifically identified national parks as being of concern. To be frank, I have been sent lots of photos of national parks in my time where it was quite obvious that people were deliberately dropping trees across trails to stop vehicle access. Those photos cannot be interpreted in any other way.

Ultimately, trees were deliberately dropped across tracks to prohibit access. That practice should not be used by any government agency because it puts at risk another government agency when those workers go to fight fires. We support the amendment. We think it is sensible. I urge the Government to address more broadly the funding shortfall for fire trails in this State. The evidence from the agency that fights those fires shows quite clearly that it has serious concerns about being able to do that work safely during the next bushfire season.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 23:19 :09 ): I speak in support my colleague the Hon. Sarah Mitchell, and I congratulate her on bringing this amendment to the Committee and providing the Government an opportunity to once again repent and correct an error that occurred in the other place, where the amendment was not supported. The Hon. Mark Banasiak has been quite clear as to the importance of the amendment. That is not to say that the Hon. Sarah Mitchell did not clearly articulate why it was important, but I think the Hon. Mark Banasiak provided an additional level of clarity by articulating what he has seen. There certainly have to be some questions asked about how the trees that he mentioned came to be across those roads. It may be that there are left‑wing activists who seek to destroy, disrupt or impede access to areas of the park.

There have certainly been some lunatic left‑wing activists who seek to engage in that sort of conduct to frustrate access to some areas, but this amendment will not create a great impediment for the Minister or the Government in finally gazetting and delivering on their commitment to deliver this park. It provides an additional level of comfort for the community to know that those fire trails may have been made in consultation with the Commissioner of the NSW Rural Fire Service. The Minister was quite strident in her contribution to debate on this amendment. In doing so, she articulated a number of criticisms of my colleagues. My interpretation is that she was saying that the Coalition was unfairly critical of our national parks firefighting teams, but nothing could be further from the truth.

The Opposition moved the amendment in good faith. We respect and acknowledge the vast experience and enormous level of professionalism of the firefighters in the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service. In no way do we seek to undermine that. We want to ensure that they have at their disposal the best tools and the ability to do the job they love and have dedicated so much time and training towards. This amendment puts a further feather in the cap of those firefighters by ensuring they have every opportunity to make those fire trails the best they can be. It provides for the coordination that will almost certainly be needed in the unlikely event of a bushfire in that area, with the Rural Fire Service commissioner providing a level of consultation to the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service firefighting and maintenance teams. It is so important that we do not forget that the maintenance team is also involved in ensuring that the fire trails are maintained.

The Minister was quick to single out the work of the National Parks and Wildlife Service firefighting team, but I think she was a bit too quick and left out the great work of those other members of the National Parks and Wildlife Service who actually do the enabling work that allows the firefighters to be successful in the work they do. The amendment makes sure not only that the firefighters the Minister referred to in her contribution are provided every opportunity for success in fighting fires in the Great Koala National Park area but also that those other workers who are tasked with their fantastic work—often done without accolades—are too. They do the work that ensures that those firefighters have the tools they need for success.

The amendment itself effectively says that, despite anything in the Act or the National Parks and Wildlife Service Act 1974, fire trails on the land reserved by the Act may follow consultation with the Commissioner of the Rural Fire Service. That is such a sensible and supportable amendment because, as much as the Minister was strident in her support for the professionalism of the National Parks and Wildlife Service firefighters, there is no harm or issue with seeking external guidance from or consultation with other relevant experts. This amendment effectively provides a level of guidance, but it also enshrines in the legislation a clear provision saying that this Chamber and the other House—should it be the case that this Committee adopts the amendment and the bill returns to the other place—can effectively articulate that they have a level of agreement that the commissioner is somebody who should provide the National Parks and Wildlife Service a level of consultation in developing those fire trails.

This amendment not only does that but also ensures that they may be maintained. The Minister touched on something in the contribution she made about this amendment. She was critical of some of the contributions in the second reading speech about the observed fires that have occurred in national parks previously. This amendment will effectively say that the fire trails may be maintained. I know I have used this line previously, but this is one of those times when Government members should help us to help them. We do not want to see any criticism of how a fire may have been fought coloured or tainted through the prism of a lack of maintenance of those fire trails.

Whilst the Minister was strong in her support for the professionalism of the National Parks and Wildlife Service team, it would be unfair of the Committee to not provide every single tool that is possible to those firefighters so that they can demonstrate that professionalism. If it is the case that the Minister calls any criticism unfair, that criticism should be minimised as much as possible. As the Hon. Sarah Mitchell articulated in her contribution to debate on the amendment, it says "it may". There is nothing in the amendment that will create a burden or enforce aspects of firefighting or consultation or maintenance on the Government. But it does provide a level of certainty and clarity for this Government—and I certainly have some views about the clarity and advice that this Government needs, and it probably needs more than what the amendment before the Committee provides.

It will also provide future governments and others that read the legislation as passed and the Acts that may or may not flow from the passing of the bill with very clear instructions and guidance as to what it is that the Parliament, when passing the bill, thought was best practice and was something that should occur in terms of these fire trails. It is clear that the Minister also indicated in her contribution that there is no doubt that the National Parks and Wildlife Service—and, indeed, the Government—is reliant on those carbon credits to ensure that it minimises the risk of fire as much as possible. Ultimately, the loss of those carbon credits is detrimental to the financials of the maintenance of this Great Koala National Park. If it is so tenuous that it will put a lot of the house of cards at risk if there is a fire—and we have articulated our views about what we think is a Ponzi scheme of carbon credits that the Government has dodged up to try to justify a lot of this—and the Government does need to have this Ponzi scheme uninterrupted so that it can try to con its way through funding this work, then it should be walking towards us on bended knee and thanking us for moving the amendment.

It is unfortunate that the Government does not necessarily want to do that. Maybe that is because, ultimately, the Government is aware that it is a Ponzi scheme and maybe it is not so worried if there is a fire because it knows that it is all, as I said, a house of cards and could collapse at any minute. But the burning of the timber that exists now in the boundaries that will border the Great Koala National Park, as articulated by the Minister in her second reading speech, will perhaps risk, again, damaging the fragile ecosystem that exists there.
I seek an extension of time.
Leave not granted.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 23:41 :41 ): I move Opposition amendment No. 9 on sheet c2026-314A:
No. 9Plan of management
Page 15. Insert after line 29—
39BPlan of management
(1)A plan of management required to be prepared under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974, section 72 for reserved land must be prepared within 12 months after the commencement of section 11.
(2)A plan of management for reserved land must include a recreation strategy for the land that deals with the following—
(a)the road, track and trail network available for public recreational use,
(b)camping areas, including dispersed camping areas,
(c)areas in which dogs and horses may be permitted,
(d)proposed recreation infrastructure and a timetable for delivering the infrastructure.
(3)The NPW Minister must table a plan of management for reserved land in each House of Parliament within 5 sitting days of the House after the plan is adopted.
(4)In this section—
reserved land means land listed in Schedule 1, sections 1–5.

The amendment goes to a plan of management. Any national park requires a plan, but, by requiring a plan of management to be adopted within 12 months, we will give the public clarity on where they can undertake activities. The absence of a legislated requirement for a plan means that the Government can simply gazette the park and have no plan of management. This is a commonsense amendment that should have been considered as part of the original bill. I move this amendment for the reasons outlined in the debate in the other place. It is about providing certainty for the community, because we are still hearing a lot of concerns about what will happen to access once the land becomes part of the national park estate. People want certainty about whether tracks will remain open, camping will continue or horseriding will be permitted, and about how recreational facilities will be improved and the land will be managed over the long term.

I briefly place on record in this place the concerns of some lower House members about the feedback they have received from their communities. There have been stakeholder meetings. Members—including the member for Coffs Harbour, the member for Clarence, the member for Oxley and the member for Myall Lakes—have told me that people are curious, including representatives from four-wheel drive clubs, mountain bike clubs, motorbike clubs and other groups that will want to use the new national park. The consistent and common feedback is that people have not yet been told where they will be allowed to do various activities. There is uncertainty around that. There have been no maps, trails or anything else provided to identify the locations where people will be able to do those activities. This amendment is important for the bill, and that is why we hope that members will support it.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 23:43 :57 ): The Government prefers the bill as it is and does not support the amendment.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 23:44 :02 ): The Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party supports the amendment. It requires relevant management plans to be prepared within 12 months of the commencement of section 11. It also requires a recreation strategy addressing the public road; track and rail network; camping, including dispersed camping areas, where dogs and horses may be permitted; and proposed recreation infrastructure with a delivery timetable. Those are practical questions that people who use these forests will want answered. They need to know where they can travel, where they can jump, where they can camp and what facilities are actually proposed. General statements about recreation do not give a family or a local club enough information to plan an activity.

The requirement to address dispersed camping is particularly useful. Recreation should not be discussed only in terms of a handful of developed visitor sites. The planning process should expressly consider different ways people use the landscape and explain how those uses will be managed. The same applies to dogs and horses. This amendment requires a strategy to deal with areas where they may be permitted. It does not make those activities lawful everywhere, and it requires these questions to be addressed in the plan rather than granting blanket permission. The timetable for proposed infrastructure also improves accountability. People should be able to distinguish a proposal with an identified delivery schedule from an aspiration that could be repeated for years without progress.

Once a plan is adopted, it must be tabled within five sitting days of each House of Parliament. That gives Parliament access to the document and an opportunity to question whether the recreation commitments have been properly addressed. The 12-month deadline concerns preparation. This amendment does not expressly require adoption within that same period. It does not guarantee that existing routes will remain open, and we will continue to press those issues in the broader protection of existing access. Even with those limits—requiring a timely plan, express recreation strategy and parliamentary tabling—it is a worthwhile improvement. The Government should be willing to put its recreation promise into documents that people can read and Parliament can examine.

This issue was brought up extensively in the inquiry into access to public lands and waterways by a broad range of recreational users. They are calling out for a comprehensive understanding of what can and cannot be done across not just national parks but all public land in New South Wales so they can freely engage in recreation and cross-tenures as part of that recreation. Many people love traversing through our public lands and experiencing all different types of public land, but they struggle to do that because there is no clear map or indication of what can be done where. Perhaps starting slowly with the Great Koala National Park is a good way of gradually introducing such a proposal and implementing a map or scheme. With those remarks, I commend the amendment to the Committee.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 23:47 :25 ): Despite the invitation from the Hon. Stephen Lawrence to filibuster this bill, clearly we have not been filibustering, and I expect that we will vote on this amendment tonight. I will keep my remarks very brief to indicate that members can thank the Hon. Stephen Lawrence for the fact that we are still discussing these amendments. I put that on record.
The Hon. Stephen Lawrence: You shouldn't let other people control you, Wes.
The Hon. WES FANG: Let us see just how much control there is tomorrow.
The Hon. Stephen Lawrence: It is all about control.
The Hon. WES FANG: Yes, it is. I am sure the 41 other members in this place are loving your contribution, my friend.
The CHAIR ( The Hon. Rod Roberts ): I draw the Hon. Wes Fang back to the amendment before the Committee.

The Hon. WES FANG: This is an incredibly sensible amendment. My colleagues the Hon. Sarah Mitchell and the Hon. Mark Banasiak have outlined quite clearly why the amendment should be adopted by the Committee. If those two arguments were not enough to persuade the minds of the Legislative Council, then I simply point members to the fantastic contribution of the Leader of The Nationals, the member for Coffs Harbour, in the other place. He so clearly articulated in his contribution the way that this amendment will benefit the community and also the Government by ensuring that the plan of management that could be developed, submitted and adopted actually aids us in so many ways. Road trails, track networks and camping areas where dogs and horses may be permitted are all things that the Government says it wants to bring to the area by way of increasing tourism. Developing this park as a tourist attraction can be further aided and enhanced by adopting this amendment. It is almost impossible to comprehend why the Government, in reading this amendment, does not actually value or recognise what the amendment will bring it.

The work that has gone on behind the scenes of this amendment has been done with a level of consideration, forethought and consultation—which I think is the most important aspect of this. Members have seen that this Government is very poor on consultation in a number of bills that have come before them this week. The Opposition has already articulated quite clearly the concerns we have about the consultation on this bill. This small amendment might be minor in stature, but it is so important and major in terms of its ability to guide and shape the park and to make it better. We often say that this Government needs to be better. It has the opportunity to make this bill better with this small amendment that has such a mighty heart. I note that there will be a five‑minute division and a count of the vote before we hit midnight. I take the opportunity to again encourage members to support this amendment. I tell members who are perhaps being guided by a caucus decision to not necessarily let that bind them. This is about the park. This is about making sure—
The Hon. Mark Banasiak: He's right, Steve. Don't let anyone control you.

The Hon. WES FANG: You knew exactly where I was going! Members should not let a decision of the caucus bind them, because they are their own people. I know that there are Government members who perhaps feel curtailed by the decisions of a left-wing Minister who does not necessarily value a lot of the things that we are trying to bring forward with this amendment. They should not let that stop them. I ask them to look into their heart and look at the amendment that is before them, and allow themselves to be the park and to be the amendment. In circumstances where an amendment speaks such volumes, I ask members to let its voice be heard. I commend the amendment to the Committee.
