The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 09:01 :02 ): By leave: I move Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments Nos 1, 2, 4 and 8 on sheet c2026‑309B in globo:
No. 1Pre-implementation report
Page 2, clause 2, lines 7–10. Omit all words on the lines. Insert instead—
(1)This Act commences as follows—
(a)for Part 1—on the date of assent to this Act,
(b)otherwise—on a day or days to be appointed by proclamation.
(2)A day appointed under subsection (1)(b) must not be earlier than—
(a)the day on which a relevant project declaration is made, and
(b)the day that is 30 days after the pre-implementation report is tabled in both Houses of Parliament.
No. 2Pre-implementation report
Page 2, clause 3. Insert after line 31—
pre-implementation report—see section 7A(1).
No. 4Pre-implementation report
Page 2, clause 3. Insert after line 36—
relevant project declaration means a declaration made under the Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative) Act 2011 of the Commonwealth, section 27 that includes land specified in Schedule 1.
No. 8Pre-implementation report
Page 3. Insert after line 29—
7APre-implementation report
(1)The NPW Minister must prepare and table in both Houses of Parliament a pre-implementation report that sets out the way the government proposes to implement this Act.
(2)Without limiting subsection (1), the pre-implementation report must include the following—
(a)the details of eligible offsets projects included in a relevant project declaration, including the following—
(i)the name of the project,
(ii)the name of the project proponent,
(iii)the land covered by the project,
(iv)the carbon credit methodology used for the project,
(v)the status of the project with the Clean Energy Regulator of the Commonwealth, including—
(A)outstanding approvals, and
(B)conditions attaching to an approval,
(vi)the names of persons with an interest in Australian carbon credit units created for the project,
(vii)when the Australian carbon credit units are expected to be registered,
(viii)when the Government expects to start generating revenue from Australian carbon credit units,
(b)the financial estimates and assumptions underpinning implementation, including the following—
(i)the number of Australian carbon credit units forecast to be created and when the credits will be issued,
(ii)when the Australian carbon credit units are expected to be sold and the anticipated sale price,
(iii)forecast gross and net revenue from the sale of Australian carbon credit units,
(iv)the forecast cost associated with establishing and managing the Great Koala National Park,
(v)whether there is expected to be a shortfall in revenue and if so, how implementation costs will be met,
(vi)material risks associated with financial modelling and assumptions,
(c)the ongoing obligations to the State from the project, including—
(i)restrictions on future land use,
(ii)monitoring, reporting and verification,
(iii)obligations arising from bushfire, drought, illegal clearing or another event that reduces carbon storage,
(iv)circumstances in which Australian carbon credit units may be required to be relinquished, replaced or otherwise accounted for,
(v)the government agency or other party with legal and financial responsibility for eligible offsets projects,
(vi)arrangements to manage or mitigate risk, including insurance or contingency funding,
(d)the actual and forecast impact of land transfers and forestry operations on the following—
(i)forestry corporation employees,
(ii)harvesting and haulage contracts, timber mills and other businesses dependent on timber supply,
(iii)other businesses relying on access to State forests,
(iv)employment and economic activity in affected regional communities,
(e)the details of each assistance, compensation, retraining, redeployment or business transition program associated with the establishment of the Great Koala National Park, including—
(i)the government agency administering the program,
(ii)the funding allocation and whether funding is capped,
(iii)eligibility criteria for participation,
(iv)exclusions and application deadlines,
(v)how assistance under the program is assessed,
(vi)the expected timeframes for determining eligibility and making payments,
(vii)review and complaint mechanisms,
(f)the arrangements for maintaining access—
(i)to private property and leased land, and
(ii)for maintaining public utilities, and
(iii)for recreational and other lawful activities,
(g)the allocation of responsibilities for road maintenance and emergency access.
(3)The pre-implementation report must also include details about the following, include staffing allocations and implementation timetables—
(a)strategies for bushfire prevention and management, including hazard reduction,
(b)pest animal and weed control.
(4)In this section—
Aus tralian carbon credit unit has the same meaning as in the Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative) Act 2011 of the Commonwealth.

This package of amendments requires the Government to explain its implementation plan before the main provisions start. Parliaments should not be asked to accept costs, carbon liabilities and access consequences on trust and then receive the details after the decision has taken effect. The sequence should be disclosure first, followed by the time to examine it. Amendment No. 1 starts at part 1 on assent and leaves the remaining provisions to proclamation, subject to proposed conditions. A relevant carbon project declaration must have been made and at least 30 days must have passed since the implementation report was tabled in both Houses. Amendments Nos 2 and 4 supply the definitions linking that condition to the report and the formal Commonwealth project declaration covering schedule 1 land.

Amendment No. 8 sets out the regulatory substance of the report. It must identify the project proponent, land methodology, regulatory status, credit interest and expected timing of credits and revenue. The financial information includes forecast credits, prices, gross and net receipts, establishment and management costs, funding shortfalls and material risks. It must also explain the continuing obligations, land use restrictions, monitoring and verification, consequences of fire and other reversals, possible credit replacement or relinquishment, responsible parties and risk mitigation.

The report extends beyond carbon. It covers employment, business effects, assistance programs, funding caps, eligibility, exclusions, deadlines, decision payment times, review arrangements, and it must explain access for holdings, utilities, lawful recreation, road and emergency responsibilities, and staffing and timetables for fire, pests and weeds. This package does not guarantee the forecasts or approve carbon project merits. It requires the Government to state its case in a document that the Parliament can examine before the main changes proceed. We believe that is a reasonable condition on implementation. I ask the Committee to support the amendments.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 09:03 :30 ): On behalf of the Government, I indicate that we oppose these amendments. Rather than repeating myself, I flag to the Committee that there is a whole range of amendments being put forward by the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party, essentially trying to set up a bespoke system for the Great Koala National Park when those matters are dealt with through the plans of management and various advisory committees that already exist for national parks. They are well known and well understood, and there are a bunch of those.

In terms of the implementation, the National Parks and Wildlife Act is quite comprehensive. It has a whole range of rules that already set out the existing arrangements. Rather than repeating myself, I will note the issues now. They are around a pre‑implementation report, access roads, maps, existing interests, the way vested land operates, easements and rights of way, motorsports, annual reporting and a whole range of other matters. I flag that the Government will not support all those amendments, on the basis that they are covered in the existing way in which parks operate across the State. We do not believe that it is wise to set up a bespoke system just for this park. Long term, the member wants to talk to us about the reforms to the way in which parks are done overall—I am sure he probably does. Our door is always open, but I just flag to the Committee that we will oppose all of those amendments.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 09:05 :23 ): I offer a contribution to debate on behalf of The Nationals and indicate that we support these amendments. In debate yesterday—although technically, in Hansard, it will be earlier today—
The Hon. Penny Sharpe: It's still my birthday.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL: It is still Penny's birthday. It is the festival of Penny, a gift that keeps giving. We raised our concerns on community consultation, or lack thereof. Many questions still come about how the park would operate and where access would be available, so we think that the suggestion in these amendments to put in place a pre-implementation plan and a report back to Parliament is sound. The Minister commented that the National Parks and Wildlife Act already covers a lot of those issues and that it does not make sense to set up bespoke arrangements for this park. However, Government members have spent a lot of time out in the community saying that the park being set up is special and wonderful. It would be akin to visiting the Great Barrier Reef and all of those other places.

On the one hand, they are happy to put it out there as the gold standard mega national park that will do all those things. Yet when we want another layer of protection, scrutiny and transparency for the community, the argument is that is not necessary. It does not hurt to have more plans in place for pre-implementation. The Nats have always pushed for certainty for the community. We know that the Government will do this park and that the legislation will pass this place eventually, but we are happy to support any measures like these amendments that will put in more stringent processes in place to make sure that it is done in a proper way.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 09:07 :10 ): On behalf of the Liberal Party, I indicate that we do not support these amendments. While we are sympathetic to the aims of the member for greater scrutiny, we believe enough provisions exist in the bill that go to the member's intention. Therefore, we do not support the amendments.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 09:07 :37 ): I support my colleague the Hon. Sarah Mitchell in her confirmation that the National Party supports the amendments moved by the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party. I also support the member who moved the amendments, the Hon. Mark Banasiak and note that he did it in good faith. The first thing I want to say about the amendments probably covers off part of the contribution of the Leader of the Government. For the Leader of the Government to stand up in this place and effectively say that she is going to make one contribution for the amendments that are before us and that will be it to save time is disrespectful to the process of the Parliament and actually disrespectful to the member moving the amendments. With each amendment that is moved, whether they were moved after leave was sought to move those amendments as a group or they are moved singularly, there is a need to look at, examine and vote on each as they are moved. Making a blanket statement that effectively covers all of the amendments is problematic and disingenuous of the Government.

I suggest to the Leader of the Government that there should be a little bit more meat on the bone, shall I say, in terms of contributions, because ultimately this bill will have a dramatic impact on rural and regional New South Wales, particularly on the Mid North Coast. In those circumstances, the community is owed at least a detailed and thorough explanation if the Government seeks to oppose the amendment. I encourage the Leader of the Government to make a further contribution in relation to this set of amendments. It is quite clear that the amendment moved by the Hon. Mark Banasiak is easily supported, because it provides an opportunity for the Government to further examine and provide a pre‑implementation report, in particular, not only to the Parliament, which is the nexus where the issues will be managed, but also for our communities.

Ultimately our communities will be bearing the brunt of these decisions. In circumstances in which the Government seeks to make sweeping and wideranging changes, it is incumbent on the Government to provide clarity to the community. This pre‑implementation report that the amendment seeks to have included is quite clear. For the benefit of the Committee, let me outline in greater detail some of that pre‑implementation report for members who may not have looked at the amendment. Amendment No. 8, Pre-implementation report, states:
Page 3. Insert after line 29—
7APre-implementation report
(1)The NPW Minister must prepare and table in both Houses of Parliament a pre-implementation report that sets out the way the government proposes to implement this Act.

That is important. It is not an unreasonable suggestion to adopt as an amendment to the bill. It is quite sensible that, prior to implementation, the Government outlines how, why and the impacts et cetera that are almost expected. Because of the breadth of the changes moved by the Government, and because the requirement for that report was not part of the bill in the first instance, the Hon. Mark Banasiak had to move this amendment. The amendment continues:
(2)Without limiting subsection (1), the pre-implementation report must include the following—
(a)the details of eligible offsets projects included in a relevant project declaration, including the following—
(i)the name of the project,
(ii)the name of the project proponent,
(iii)the land covered by the project,
(iv)the carbon credit methodology used for the project,
(v)the status of the project with the Clean Energy Regulator of the Commonwealth, including—
(A)outstanding approvals, and
(B)conditions attaching to an approval,

The Opposition has outlined clearly in the second reading stage and during consideration of amendments that there are a number of questions about the manner in which the carbon credit scheme will be rolled out in the park. The pre‑implementation report would provide further clarity for communities that are screaming out for more information about carbon credits. It is clear that there are questions about the carbon credit program that will fund the park. I need only refer to the contribution yesterday of Ms Abigail Boyd to know the questions that even The Greens have about the scheme and whether it will actually reduce carbon as a carbon credit scheme. Amendment No. 8, which includes a requirement for a pre‑implementation report, will provide clarity to the community about the carbon credit scheme. I will continue on. Subparagraphs (vi), (vii) and (viii) state:
(vi)the names of persons with an interest in Australian carbon credit units created for the project,
(vii)when the Australian carbon credit units are expected to be registered,
(viii)when the Government expects to start generating revenue from Australian carbon credit units,

That is, I think, incredibly important for the Parliament. I am sure the Treasurer in particular is interested in these figures, but it is also clear that the community and the Parliament should be made aware of these at the time. By adopting a pre-implementation report, as is proposed by this amendment, a lot of these matters will be able to be ventilated and clarity provided to the Parliament and to the wider community, the same community that is impacted by these changes. I will move on, because I know I am fast running out of time and there is a lot to say. Paragraph (b) (i) states:
(b)the financial estimates and assumptions underpinning implementation, including the following—
(i)the number of Australian carbon credit units forecast to be created and when the credits will be issued,

This aspect of the pre-implementation report is incredibly important for the Parliament to understand what the forecasting is. Obviously, I suspect there has been modelling in terms of what has been proposed by the Government in terms of the carbon credit scheme, but also I think the modelling is incredibly important because we know that the Leader of the Government in particular has indicated that it is a government policy in relation to these carbon credits that they will not be sold to any industry that is involved in fossil fuel. They are going to be sold, indeed, to manufacturing industries, but they are not actually going to be sold to any fossil fuel industries.

There clearly has to be a question about how they are going to delineate a lot of these things, because I suspect a lot of manufacturing industries will, in some way, involve a level of fossil fuel. The Government has not quite articulated that policy in granular detail, and that granular detail may well impact the way that these forecasts are modelled. The pre-implementation report seeking to have that forecasting published prior to implementation will provide the community with some better understanding about how these matters are going to be progressed by the Government.

It is notable that in the second reading debate yesterday, one voice was completely missing. The forestry Minister was not heard at all. I wonder why the Minister responsible for forestry in this State did not speak on the second reading of this bill. That is a matter for her and a matter for the Government, but it did not provide clarity about what the Government is going to do in terms of these matters. That is disappointing because our communities did not get a chance to hear from the forestry Minister about effectively shutting down forestry in this area.

The TEMPORARY CHAIR ( The Hon. Taylor Martin ): It is early in this second half of Thursday, according to Hansard. I draw the Hon. Wes Fang back to the amendment and we will go on from there. The member had a good point, so I will allow the Hon. Wes Fang to redress.
The Hon. WES FANG: Roger that. Moving on into further detail of the amendment, paragraph (b) (ii) states:
(ii)when the Australian carbon credit units are expected to be sold and the anticipated sale price,

This clearly is something that is absolutely required as part of the pre-implementation report. We, as a Parliament, need to know exactly what revenue is going to be generated, because there has not been any clarity around the modelling that underpins a lot of the assumptions about the park. In fact, I would encourage the mover of the amendment to clarify whether the sale price he is referring to is a global price or an Australia-only price. Once I have completed my contribution, it would be good if he could clarify what he was anticipating—whether it was a global market price or an Australian market price only—given that the Minister has indicated there will be restrictions around the part of the market these credits can be sold on. I seek clarity because that I think the Committee needs to know that now.
Paragraph (b) (iii) states:
(iii)forecast gross and net revenue from the sale of Australian carbon credit units …

Again, this is vitally important because the Minister has articulated the policy of the Government's that these carbon credits effectively have a big asterisk next to them. That big asterisk means that they cannot be used in fossil fuel industries. That raises a number of questions about the way that the Government is seeking to take these carbon credits to the market. The idea of having a market-based scheme is that the market will dictate a price and then an equilibrium will be found where the seller and the buyer will effectively work out a price that the exchange can occur at. If it is the case that that we are seeking to artificially limit the market by saying that there will be no fossil fuel industries that are able to purchase these credits, I think it is pretty clear that the general market where these carbon credits are being traded is not applicable to the carbon credits that apply to this park.

Ultimately, you would expect that industries that use fossil fuel are typically the ones that are required to purchase carbon credits, so when the Government says, "We will not sell those carbon credits to certain industries," it is effectively limiting the base to which those credits can be sold. In effect, that limits the price that can be achieved. It is not as if the Government can go to the Parliament and say, "This is the price that carbon credits can be sold at," because the market is being artificially controlled by the Government when it says that fossil fuel organisations cannot be part of the scheme. I am running out of time. I will ask the member to clarify those points that I asked about.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 09:22 :43 ): The Hon. Wes Fang asked me about the report and whether it would be a domestic price or a global price. I think the will of the Committee would be that it would want to see both. I think that is how it should be interpreted. That is my reply.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 09:23 :14 ): Continuing on, I think paragraph (b) (iii) is important because we know that the carbon credits that are in the market need to be understood. I have made it pretty clear that I expect that there will be a price impact from limiting the market. By a pre-implementation report being provided to the Parliament about that forecasting, the Parliament and the community will be able to better understand the revenue that will be generated from the park. That is incredibly important. I reiterate that it is not just members of this place who are seeking to better understand the changes of this Government through the pre-implementation report; it is also our communities, because our communities have been the most impacted by the changes. It is not an unreasonable thing. For the Leader of the Government to stand up and effectively dismiss the amendment by saying it is covered under the national parks and wildlife legislation that currently exists is disingenuous.

This park, in particular, is special. The Hon. Sarah Mitchell was clear in her contribution that there are perhaps a number of special provisions with this park. I do not know of any other park that is so reliant on the sale of carbon credits. We know the Government sought a change to the way that carbon credit accrual could be measured and sold. The Federal Government has clearly adopted those changes. I know there were issues in the Federal Parliament about that. That is not a matter for us. As a State Parliament, we have these amendments that will provide some clarity about those credits. The Hon. Sarah Mitchell was right to say that the park is special because of those carbon credits.

Part of the reason why the pre-implementation report is so important to adopt as an amendment is because the Government could seek to do this time and time again, maybe with other national parks or other areas. Other amendments have been moved in this place and have been tailored to looking at that issue. That is why the pre‑implementation report is important. Moving to (b) (iv), it says "the forecast cost associated with establishing and managing the Great Koala National Park". Whilst that is buried down in proposed section 7A (2) (b) (iv), it should have perhaps been moved right to the top because it is really the nub of the issue. There has been a lack of clarity from this Government about the cost associated with the establishment and management of the Great Koala National Park.

The pre-implementation report will provide to the community, the Parliament and the Treasurer—because I'm not sure the Treasurer even knows what this is going to cost—greater clarity around the cost of having the Great Koala National Park rolled out and gazetted. That is incredibly important for the Parliament to understand. It is incredibly important for our communities to understand. They have had a lot of upheaval in terms of industry, jobs and, indeed, the social fabric of those communities. A pre-implementation report providing clarity about how the costs are going to be measured and adopted by the Parliament and the Government, even if they are forecasts, will force the Government to put on the table what the forecasts are. At this stage, I am not sure that has been provided with a level of certainty.

There are guidelines, estimates and guesses. The pre-implementation report requiring the publishing of the forecasts means that the community will have greater clarity and there will be an opportunity for the Parliament and those members to understand the costs. I ask the Hon. Mark Banasiak if he could clarify, in a further contribution, whether it is just the forecast as a sum total figure, or whether it also includes the modelling, as that is not clear. Proposed section 7A (1) (b) states:
(iv)the forecast cost associated with establishing and managing the Great Koala National Park,
I ask the member to provide some more clarity to the Committee in a later contribution. Moving on, the subsection further states:
(v)whether there is expected to be a shortfall in revenue and if so, how implementation costs will be met,

I said that the other amendment should be moved straight to the top—number two with a freight train. I was going to say something else with another vernacular but, given the current circumstances, it is probably not appropriate. Knowing "whether there is expected to be a shortfall in revenue and if so, how implementation costs will be met" is so important for our communities. The carbon credit scheme—the Ponzi scheme, as I like to call it—that the Government is rolling out, which even Ms Abigail Boyd has said will not do anything to reduce a single tonne of carbon, is literally an accounting trick to try to get extra money from the Federal Government by way of carbon credits. If we curtail the number of entities that can purchase those carbon credits, it is important that the community and the Parliament know what the shortfall is and how it will be met.

I can see why the Government is so quick to dismiss this amendment. I can see why the Leader of the Government seeks to pull the wool over everyone's eyes by saying that we do not need a pre-implementation report because it is all there and it will all happen. It is quite clear why the Government does not want this amendment passed: because the amendment would effectively require the Government to provide clarity about the funding that it will receive from the carbon credits, the total cost of the park and, most importantly, how the cost of any shortfall in revenue will be met. The Government does not want to admit that the park may have a dramatic impact on the finances of the State Government. Creating the park is a "do it at all costs" matter for the Government. That is why the pre-implementation report is so important.

Whilst the Minister was very quick to dismiss the amendment, if people take the time to read it, as I have done, it is clear that some of what the member seeks to move is entirely reasonable. I am surprised there are not more parties supporting the amendment. Any party that pretends to be fiscally responsible and that claims to support transparency and accountability in how things are rolled out should support the amendment, because it requires the Government to clearly outline a lot of those matters prior to implementation. The Leader of the Government was reasonably clear in her contribution about what she viewed as a significant piece of legislation that would outline those matters, but I do not think the bill outlines these particular points. These particular points are incredibly important for the Committee to adopt because, at the moment, there are a lot of questions about the cost and any shortfall. Ultimately, the pre-implementation report, if adopted, will provide clarity prior to adoption. That is the key aspect of this amendment: "prior to the adoption".

The TEMPORARY CHAIR ( The Hon. Taylor Martin ): For the benefit of members, it was suggested previously that Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments Nos 3, 12, 13 and 15 on sheet c2026-309B would be moved in globo. The Hon. Mark Banasiak has also moved amendment No. 6 on the same sheet.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK: The amendments protect necessary access to lawful holdings and make clear that that protection extends to specified leasehold land as well as private ownership. A person can depend on a single road regardless of whether their tenure is freehold or a continuing Crown lease. The legislation should recognise that practical dependence. Amendment No. 3 changes the definition reference to "protected holding". Amendment No. 12 supplies the detailed scope of land, including land held by an owner under national parks legislation, a holding under Crown land legislation and land under a continued relevant lease. The wording identifies the category as protected. It does not turn every informal use of land into a protected holding.

Amendment No. 13 prevents the Minister from closing an access road where it is the only practical means of reaching that protected holding. That is a focused safeguard. It does not give a person a general right to select any route through reserve land for any purpose. Amendment No. 15 addresses what happens later, when an access road becomes reserved. It permits continued use where the road is the only practical means of access to a protected holding despite the reservation. That includes the bill's mechanism under which a road may become reserved after 10 years. That latter point matters. Protecting access at the beginning is insufficient if the protection disappears when the road status changes. The person may still occupy the same holding and depend on the same road years afterwards.

Taken together, the amendments align the definition, the closure protection and the post‑reservation protection, and give lawful holders a clearer basis for continued access while leaving the protection within its defined scope. Amendment No. 6 goes to Roads Act consent requirements. It removes the bill's special exemption from section 138 of the Roads Act. The usual consent requirements would therefore apply where that section requires them for things done on or to a road. The legislation would not provide a blanket exemption from that process. A road can serve people and activities beyond the immediate park proposal. The normal legal process for consent to work on or affect the road should not be displaced by a broad exemption without good reason. The amendment removes that special exemption and leaves the ordinary section 138 requirements to operate where applicable. With those words, I commend the amendments to the Committee.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 10:13 :24 ): By leave: I move Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments Nos 5, 9, 22 and 27 on sheet c2026-309B in globo:
No. 5Henry VIII provisions
Page 2, clause 3, lines 38–42. Omit all words on the lines.
No. 9Henry VIII provisions
Pages 5–7, line 5 on page 5 to line 15 on page 7. Omit all words on the lines.

These amendments remove the Henry VIII clauses. This place has had a chequered history with Henry VIII clauses, and quite a few members have raised individual concerns about Henry VIII clauses in legislation. I personally think they diminish the power of this House to review and make legislation. We should remove clauses that essentially overrule and ultimately undermine the legislation that is passed in both Houses of Parliament. If changes are needed to the park in any shape or fashion, we should have a full and wholesome debate about it, like we are having today. With those remarks, I commend the amendments to the Committee.

The Hon. EMILY SUVAAL ( 10:14 :46 ): The Government does not support the amendments. The bill includes targeted implementation powers to amend certain schedules making minor boundary adjustments and to reserve additional land following the commencement. This was canvassed extensively in the other place. As the member for Coffs Harbour explained in the Legislative Assembly, when the boundary is surveyed, it might be two-thirds of the way onto the road rather than on the edge of the road. From speaking to my colleagues, I am advised that the Henry VIII provisions are usually for 10 years. These amendments will make it four years. We recognise the level of interest in this matter, but it is important that these provisions are retained. We oppose deleting them.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 10:15 :36 ): On behalf of The Nationals, I indicate that we support these amendments moved by the Hon. Mark Banasiak. We moved amendments in the other place relating to the Henry VIII provisions in the bill, which were not successful. The fact is we already have concerns about the way that the Government is setting up this park. As I canvassed in my second reading debate contribution, we are concerned about the lack of community consultation and we are deeply concerned about the impact on the timber industry. When we go through the legislation, it is particularly jarring to note that the bill contains clauses that will allow the Minister—whoever that may be—to make unchecked changes, through regulation, to increase the boundaries of the park.

Much like what the Hon. Mark Banasiak said in his contribution, if there is a need—for whatever reason—to make changes to the size of this park, and the government or the Minister of the day may well have legitimate reasons at any given point to do that, then we should be a required to discuss those changes in this place. There should be a provision that legislation is needed to increase the size of the park. We should not cede sovereignty to the Executive on this, because any unchecked government could increase the size of the park across all manner of land under this bill. It is important that there is proper parliamentary scrutiny relating to any proposed additions of land to the park. The fact that this bill sets up a national park estate for the Great Koala National Park is proof that the Government thinks that it should be done this through the Parliament.

We are debating legislation to set new boundaries for a new park right now. Yet, in the same legislation, the Government basically wants a green light to add as much as it wants and whenever it wants. What does that mean for the future? We think it allows too much unchecked potential for the Government to exploit this legislation and add things without consultation and consideration of the impact on local industry. As I said, my colleagues in the lower House had particularly strong views on this. We tried to make some changes to the Henry VIII clauses in the other House. We were not successful, but we think it is worth reconsidering them here. The amendments moved by the Hon. Mark Banasiak are sound, and we think they make a lot of sense.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 10:18 :24 ): I indicate that the Liberals support these amendments for the reasons that the Hon. Sarah Mitchell has outlined. I raised this issue in my contribution to the second reading debate and it has been canvassed widely in the other place. We are comfortable supporting these amendments, given the simple principle of unchecked power. We want to ensure that proper scrutiny is applied to any further changes.

The Hon. SCOTT BARRETT ( 10:18 :59 ): I will not go into too much of the detail around these amendments, as I think they have been very well covered by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition and also by members in the other place. The concerning point for me is the unchecked power, which the Hon. Jacqui Munro just spoke about, where the Minister or the secretary can decide to expand the national park. The Government recently released its NSW National Parks Establishment Plan, which was out for consultation until 12 October and is now closed. This process even skips over the consultation that the Government was supposedly doing on the establishment plan. I think the plan itself is slightly flawed. In the whole document, which is 100‑plus pages, the only reference to the impact that national parks have on communities states:

In some areas, particularly more remote parts of NSW, expansion of the national park estate is sometimes associated with community concerns about impacts on agricultural land use, employment, local services, and regional economies.

This park is going to have a massive impact on all of those things but, for the sake of time, I will not rehash them all in this contribution. Another part of the establishment plan covers the assessment themes that need to be considered before expanding or establishing a national park, which include threat urgency, social and economic considerations, cost effectiveness, long-term management capacity and resourcing needs. The Henry VIII clause in the bill skips all of that. I support these amendments because they will remove that clause.

Amendment No. 7 requires the maps referred to in the schedules to be published online, with notice in the gazette. They must clearly show boundaries, existing access roads and the land's reservation or ownership status. Reservation or vesting cannot take effect until at least 30 days after notice of the relevant map is published. People should be able to see which land is changing status before the change takes legal effect. I think that is quite sensible. A map held inside the department is not enough for a neighbour or operator trying to understand the boundary and access consequences. Publication must be public, identifiable and sufficiently clear to be useful, and this amendment allows that to occur. Amendments Nos 14 and 16 to 21 deal with easements, rights of way and safeguards before road narrowing. These amendments change the treatment of existing easements and rights of way from automatic loss to preservation, with safeguards around road changes. A legal access right can be central to the use of a holding. It should not disappear simply because the Government makes an order changing the road's status. These amendments provide certainty around those easements and rights of way.

Amendment No. 10 relates to protecting continuing leases and permits during renewal. It gives holders of existing interests a clearer renewal process, with a decision within 90 days of applying and written reasons for refusal. Renewal cannot be refused simply because the land has become reserved land or vested in the Minister. The interest continues on its existing terms until written notice of the decision is given. Renewal itself is not guaranteed. Amendment No. 11 goes to protections for road access to vested land. It limits when the secretary can refuse an authorisation under clause 22. Authorisation cannot be withheld unless another relevant road can lawfully and reasonably provide access to the vested land. These are very sensible amendments that provide certainty for landholders affected by the proposed park, which is important if it is to be successful and accepted by the community. With those remarks, I commend the amendments to the Committee.

The Hon. EMILY SUVAAL ( 10 :48 :04 ): The Government opposes the amendments. Regarding amendment No. 7, the Great Koala National Park boundary map is already online. Regarding amendment No. 10, the bill and the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974 already set out provisions that recognise existing interests. These provisions work in national parks across the State. The bill also preserves existing lawful rights, such as recreation clubs operating under permit, apiary sites, utilities and access roads to neighbouring lands. Regarding amendment No. 11, which relates to activities on vested land and existing access roads, the bill and the National Parks and Wildlife Act already set out provisions that recognise access roads and easements as existing interests. These provisions work in national parks across the State. The Government also opposes the remainder of the amendments. The bill and the National Parks and Wildlife Act set out provisions that recognise access roads and easements as existing interests. These provisions work in national parks across the State. Bespoke arrangements are not needed in the Great Koala National Park.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 10:49 :01 ): On behalf of The Nationals, I indicate that we support all the amendments moved in globo by the honourable member. I address a couple of them individually, the first being amendment No. 7, in relation to maps. We think it is a sensible amendment. As I have said many times both in the second reading debate and in debate on some of the amendments considered so far, there is nothing wrong with having more transparency about the park for the benefit of the community. All this amendment seeks to do is to make sure that every map must be published on a publicly available government website, that notice of the publication be given in the Government Gazette and that the vesting of the land does not take effect before the day that is 30 days after the date of notice of the publication.

We just tried to pass an amendment to ensure that the Government could not add new parts to the park willy-nilly. The majority of the Committee decided not to accept those amendments, so the boundaries of the park could change. We think a clause in the bill that provides that maps that clearly identify the boundaries and access roads are made publicly available within a reasonable time frame is important, because those maps could change due to how the bill has been drafted. Given that the Henry VIII clauses persist in the bill, it is necessary to have maps updated more regularly. All this amendment does is put in black and white what the Government says it intends to do anyway, so I do not understand why it would not support it.

I also briefly speak to the amendments in relation to easements, right of way and access roads, particularly amendment No. 18. It seeks to make sure that before there is an exclusion order to narrow an existing access road, the Minister must give all persons known to have benefit of that road not less than 30 days written notice, invite them to make a submission and consider all submissions. In essence, if someone is already using an access road and that road is going to be narrowed, that person has a right not only to be notified but also to put their concerns in a submission and receive a written response that includes the decisions and the reasons for those decisions. This amendment is just enhancing good governance. It is what should happen. It is about showing respect to people who might be using an access road. We are happy to support these amendments. As I said, the rest of the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments make sense, so The Nationals are happy to support them all.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 10:52 : 04 ): I indicate that the Liberals do not support these amendments. While we appreciate the intention of the mover and our Nationals colleagues, we believe that the provisions that already exist within the scope of national parks and existing legislation are sufficient to allay the concerns of the mover. As the Hon. Emily Suvaal said, maps are already online and there are already arrangements in place that relate to easements and use of land in national parks.

Ensuring that the consistency exists is obviously important for anybody who reads legislation after it has passed this House, because, ultimately, whilst the corporate knowledge may exist at the moment in the Government and certainly in the Opposition in terms of what we are debating, these sorts of clarifying insertions are helpful for future members to consider.

The member has also moved a number of other amendments as part of his in globo sets of amendments addressing the existing roads. They are amendments Nos 12, 13 and 15. I think amendment No. 14 was one as well. I want to speak on one of the substantive ones, which is important for this House to consider. Certainly when I indicated that I was seeking to encourage some of my Liberal Party colleagues to adopt these amendments, I was in part referring to amendment No. 18, which is around the narrowing of existing road access. Just for clarity and just so people understand which amendment I am speaking about, it is on sheet c2026‑309B and it is found on page 5. It is about one-third of the way down from the top:
No. 18Narrowing existing access road
Page 12, clause 27. Insert after line 9—
(5)Before making an exclusion order to narrow an existing access road, the NPW Minister must—

That is why it is important. It outlines the steps that the Minister must take. We have certainly consulted in terms of the amendments that our community is expecting. It is clear that the Hon. Mark Banasiak has done the same thing. These are concerns that have been articulated to us by people who, whilst they may disagree with the legislation, are seeking to ensure that there are protections in it. The amendment lists a number of things which the Minister must do, one of which is to:

(a)give all persons known to have the benefit of an easement or right of way affected by the proposed narrowing (affected persons) not less than 30 days written notice of the proposed narrowing and invite the persons to make a submission on the proposed narrowing, and

That is entirely sensible. When the Government is seeking to narrow access to a road, it is not unreasonable that a bill such as this would include provisions that would seek to provide a person or persons the ability to know that it is happening and make a submission. That is an entirely reasonable thing, but also it should have already been included in the bill. For a lot of the aspects around the Great Koala National Park, stakeholders have not felt heard. If the Government was to adopt the amendment, it would prove, at least in some small way, that the Government has taken some of those concerns on board. There is no question that there will be concerns about previous consultations, but at least the bill itself, if the amendment is passed, will contain a requirement for notification and consultation beforehand. It also states:
(b)consider all submissions made by affected persons, and

That goes to the heart of what we have been saying about this Government for quite a while, which is that it treats consultation as a tick-a-box exercise. It does not genuinely consult. There are any number of pieces of legislation that have recently been before this House where we have clearly articulated that stakeholders have not felt consulted. The inclusion of the amendment is appropriate so that those stakeholders will better understand and know that there is a requirement that they are consulted and that those consultations are actually considered. I think that is where there has been a real lacking in this Government. Whilst we do not necessarily legislate because of the conduct of the government of the day, it is clear that the current Government has been lacking in its consultation. That is certainly the feedback we are getting from stakeholders. That is why the amendment is important. It then states:

(c)not make the proposed exclusion order unless satisfied that affected persons will continue to be able to use the road for the lawful purposes for which the affected persons used the road before the proposed narrowing, and

That is obviously sensible. I am surprised that the Government has not jumped at it. Perhaps when the Parliamentary Secretary gave her contribution, she was not given appropriate notes to actually understand that those were the amendments being moved and the impact that they would have. I note I am about to run out of time so maybe another member might want to make another contribution so I can continue.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 11:30 :56 ): By leave: I move The Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments Nos 23 and 24 on sheet c2026-309B, and amendments Nos 34 and 35 on sheet c2026-309AA in globo:
No. 23Motor sport events
Page 14, clause 35. Insert after line 10—
(1A)An application for approval must be made in the form approved by the NPW Minister.
(1B)The NPW Minister must decide an application for approval within 90 days after the application, and all reasonably required supporting information, is given to the NPW Minister.
No. 24Motor sport events
Page 14, clause 35. Insert after line 24—
(4A)The NPW Minister must—
(a)give the applicant for an approval written notice of the decision, including reasons for and the conditions imposed on the approval, and

(b)publish the notice on an appropriate government website and in the other ways the NPW Minister is reasonably satisfied will bring the notice to the attention of the public in the area to which the approval applies.
No. 34Equivalent insurance for motor sport events
Page 15. Insert after line 40—
42AG Equivalent insurance for motor sport events

(1)In determining an application under section 35, the NPW Minister must assess the scope and adequacy of the insurance proposed and must not reject insurance solely because the applicant is not affiliated with, or the insurance is not arranged through, a motor sport organisation preferred by the NPW Minister.

(2)If the NPW Minister requires different or additional insurance, the applicant must be given written reasons identifying the material deficiency and a reasonable opportunity to provide equivalent cover.
(3)This section does not require acceptance of inadequate cover or insurance provided contrary to law or confer a power to impose an insurance requirement.
No. 35Approvals for recurring motor sport events
Page 15. Insert after line 40—
42AH Approvals for recurring motor sport events

(1)Subject to section 35, including subsections (4) and (5), an approval under that section may authorise a recurring motor race for no more than 5 years if it identifies the locations, maximum number of events and arrangements for annual notification and compliance checking.
(2)The NPW Minister must consider a request for such an approval on its merits and give reasons for requiring separate applications for each year.

(3)The NPW Minister may impose conditions for variation, suspension or revocation where necessary to address a material safety or environmental risk. Such action must follow reasonable notice and an opportunity to respond unless urgent action is necessary.
(4)This section does not authorise a race in a park excluded by section 35(5) or use of a road contrary to section 35(4).

Amendment No. 23 sets a time frame for motorsport applications. The amendment requires a motor race approval application to use the approved form and sets a 90-day decision period. That period starts once the application and all reasonably required reporting information have been supplied. It creates a decision deadline but does not guarantee approval or expand places where races can be approved. Amendment 24 makes those motorsport decisions public. Transparency is always good and is what this House supports. The amendment requires a written notice of the Minister's decision on a motor race application, including reasons and any approval conditions. The notice must also be published online and brought to the attention of the local community. The amendment makes those decision processes more transparent without removing anything to do with existing access restrictions.

Amendments 34 and 35 go to motorsport insurance and recurring approvals. Those two amendments make the administration of motorsport approvals fairer and more workable where the bill already allows approval. One amendment deals with insurance and the other deals with recurring events. They should be judged on those improvements without claiming that they remove separate geographic restrictions that remain in the bill. The insurance amendment requires the Minister to assess the actual scope and adequacy of the cover. Insurance cannot be rejected solely because an applicant is unaffiliated with a preferred motorsport organisation or has obtained the cover through another channel. If the Minister requires a different or additional insurance, the organiser must receive reasons identifying the material deficiency and a reasonable opportunity to provide equivalent cover.

The recurring approval amendment allows an approval to cover a defined recurring race for up to five years. Locations, maximum event numbers, annual notification and compliance checks must be specified, and the Minister must consider a request on its merits and explain a requirement for separate yearly applications. Conditions can address variations, suspension or revocation for material safety or environmental risks, with notice and an opportunity to respond unless urgent action is necessary, and organisers can gain a more predictable process without a loss of accountability. I indicate that I do not intend to ask for division on these amendments.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 11:34 :29 ): For the reasons outlined to the Committee before, the Government does not believe that these are necessary. We support motor rallying in the areas it has been, and we believe that the arrangements that exist under the National Parks and Wildlife Act are sufficient.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHEL L ( 11:34 :39 ): On behalf of The Nationals, I indicate that we support the four amendments that have been moved by the Hon. Mark Banasiak in relation to motorsport events and the equivalent insurance. During the second reading debate I spoke at length about the importance of having motorsports available to continue in this area, and I think some amendments about that were moved earlier. There is a long history of motorsports taking place, and we think that these amendments embed some of that in the legislation. Amendment No. 34 means that the Minister must assess cover for particular motorsport events on their merits, not on which body arranged it. That is a commonsense amendment.

Amendment No. 35 is about having multi-year approvals, up to five years, for established rallies and races. That is a sensible amendment because established rallies and races bring a lot of tourism to many towns. I think the Hon. Wes Fang spoke about the joy of motorsports in a contribution to debate on an earlier amendment. I am not a big motorsport aficionado, but all power to those who are. In all seriousness, in some of these communities, these events are big drivers of the tourism economy for their areas. We would like to see that continue. What we like about this amendment is that it means less red tape for these clubs and organisers for established rallies and races and being able to bring visitors to regional communities. These amendments make sense, and that is why we are happy to support them.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 11:36 :49 ): The Liberals will be voting against these amendments, for the reasons the Government has outlined. We believe that there are sufficient provisions and support to achieve what the Hon. Mark Banasiak is trying to achieve.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 11:37 :12 ): I encourage those members who have indicated they may not support these amendments. I believe, actually, they are entirely sensible and supportable amendments. Obviously, they are over two pages, but I will address amendments Nos 34 and 35 first, on sheet c2026-309AA, which are about equivalent insurance for motorsport events. This is very reasonable. As much as I have spoken about the joy of motorsport—and I think that has been clear through my contribution and others who have participated in and enjoy observing motorsport—it is somewhat of a dangerous activity at times. There are, of course, ways with which we can ameliorate some of those dangers, but insurance is, obviously, an important aspect.

It is also important that, when a person seeks to bring a motorsport event to an area, the relevant insurances have been considered by the Minister or the body overseeing an area where they wish to undertake that motorsport event. In bringing this amendment, the member, I think, has done so with an eye to ensuring the Minister's stated aim of the park being a wonderful tourist hotspot attended by a large number of people.

I cannot think of a better way to showcase what is a beautiful part of the Mid North Coast than with coverage of a motorsport event. Anybody who follows motorsport will understand that there is often not only the event itself that is covered but also much of the area in the filler or padding that is required for TV coverage. These events can showcase an area to the world. When the World Rally Championship was held in that area, it would have provided an opportunity for the local area to be showcased to the world. If it is the case that the Minister does want to see increased tourism and the Great Koala National Park frequented by a number of visitors, this is a perfect opportunity to extract, and have the natural beauty and terrain of the area exploited for motorsport, which is not necessarily going to have a detrimental impact on what it is that the organisers will seek to do. It will provide coverage all around the world. That may be the case, but we need to ensure that the i's are dotted and the t's are crossed in terms of these issues before an organiser is really prepared to bring an event to these areas.

Amendments Nos 34 and 35 will enshrine in the bill the important first step in encouraging any organiser to consider this area as one that is suitable and appropriate for hosting a motorsport event. Insurances, as I have already outlined, are one of those key matters, but so are approvals. Amendment No. 35 is clear that the approval issue is a live one. If I reflect back on the second reading contributions of Ministers, in this place and the other place, in terms of how it is that the Government is approaching this park, there are competing narratives around whether the Government wishes this to be, effectively, land that is locked away or land that will be accessible and available for people to utilise, not only for certain activities but also for a wider range of activities, including things like motorsport.

Because there has been that dual narrative and because there is a lack of clarity around what the Government intends for this park by way of activities outside of koala spotting and those sorts of tourist opportunities, the member brings the amendments to the Committee in good faith to ensure that the bill enshrines the protection of motorsport in that area. I have spoken about this in my contributions to both the second reading debate and amendments. Those other uses are so important, at a time when the community is fragile from all of the jobs losses and feels betrayed by the Government because the boundaries that were published prior to the election are now certainly a lot more different, like the Government's rhetoric around supporting local jobs and supporting the industry.

The Minister responsible for forestry did not even make a contribution to the second reading debate. That speaks volumes about the actual priorities of the Government. Adopting the amendments will provide the community with a level of clarity that the Government does listen to it and is prepared to adopt sensible and reasonable amendments that will see motorsport enshrined in the legislation. It is something that brings joy to those communities. It is an economic driver for those communities. I have spoken about those timber workers who have lost their jobs. The Labor Government has effectively put them on the scrapheap, which is surprising given that the Timber, Forestry and Textiles Union is so enshrined in what the Labor Party does. The opportunity to participate, observe or even volunteer in some of these activities from time to time might give those workers a little bit of solace and a little bit of comfort.

I have already articulated how motorsport brings a lot of joy. Not only that, it also brings economic benefit to the region. At this time there is a question about what those workers are going to do and what industries are available to them on the Mid North Coast to retrain in as a vocation post-forestry. For many of those workers, forestry has been a multigenerational endeavour. Their grandfathers worked in that industry, their fathers worked there and, indeed, their children expected to work there. I note that the Hon. Sarah Mitchell has already mentioned the Parkers, to whom we have both had an opportunity to speak. They are a multigenerational forestry family. What is it that this Government expects them to do? By adopting this amendment, we will give them knowledge that it may be motorsport that gives them a future in their area. Amendment No. 35, which is at the bottom of page 11 of sheet c2026-309AA, for those who are following, states:
Page 15. Insert after line 40—
42AH—
Approvals for recurring motor sport events

(1)Subject to section 35, including subsections (4) and (5), an approval under that section may authorise a recurring motor race for no more than 5 years if it identifies the locations, maximum number of events and arrangements for annual notification and compliance checking.

That provides clarity to an organiser that they are not going to see an approval they receive for an event stripped away without some certainty. This is not something that is usually a one-off. Usually a promoter or an event organiser will want a level of certainty and clarity because these are multi-year investments. The member has moved this amendment with recognition that, particularly for these motorsport events, there is a high level of investment. That is exactly what we want to see. We want to see the investment into these regions. Ultimately, if we do not see that investment, what do we have in the region? This Government has already stripped away so much of the identity of those communities by ripping out those forestry jobs, betraying those workers and selling a green dream to try to pick up metropolitan votes at the expense of our regional communities.

This amendment recognises that there is a level of investment required for motorsport events. It also recognises that the investment needs to be certain. The actions of the Government and the way it has conducted itself in bringing this legislation to the Parliament have demonstrated that currently this Government cannot necessarily be trusted by those on the Mid North Coast for the things it says. There is a clear acknowledgement that the government of the day is on the nose up on the Mid North Coast for decisions like this. That is unfortunate for them. But by moving this amendment with the provisions it contains, the member seeks to ensure that those provisions have locked into them some certainty for those promoters who seek or at least attempt to conduct motorsport events. I suspect that there will be other roadblocks along the way, as there are with this Government on everything else it seems to do. But at the very least this amendment will provide some protection and clarity for a member who wants to move those or seek to bring an event. It goes further and states at paragraph (2):
The NPW Minister must consider a request for such an approval on its merits and give reasons for requiring separate applications for each year.

That is clearly aimed at ensuring that the Minister considers requests in an appropriate way. I suspect, without it being clearly articulated in this amendment, that it is drafted and written with an eye to the fact that there is a belief that this Minister may not actually consider all applications on merit, and so knowing that there may be a need to enshrine it in the bill. But also, we do not necessarily know what other Ministers may do. This could be the worst Minister we have ever had for the National Parks and Wildlife Service, but we may actually see a worse one. Who knows what is going to happen in the future? By ensuring this is part of the legislation, we will protect ourselves against an even worse Minister than the one we have currently got. Paragraph (3) states:

The NPW Minister may impose conditions for variation, suspension or revocation where necessary to address a material safety or environmental risk. Such action must follow reasonable notice and an opportunity to respond unless urgent action is necessary.

I am reading between the lines in the way that these amendments are drafted, but I think that the member acknowledges that there is a material risk to any event that is held, because it may be the case that there is a lack of trust in the Minister. Now, I am not at all suggesting that this is written with an eye to the current Minister. I suspect it may be, but I cannot speak for the member in making that suggestion. All I can say is that if we were to have a Minister who does not appropriately respond to material safety or environmental risks, and perhaps uses any delegated power they have to derail or upend these motorsport events, that these things are considered. Unfortunately, I note that I am almost out of time. There is so much more to say. Maybe if another member makes a contribution, I can add further.

The TEMPORARY CHAIR ( The Hon. Taylor Martin ): The Hon. Mark Banasiak has moved Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments Nos 23 and 24 on sheet c2026-309B and amendments Nos 34 and 35 on sheet c2026-309AA. The question is that the amendments be agreed to.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 11:52 :37 ): By leave: I move Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments Nos 25 and 26 on sheet c2026-309B and amendment No. 1 on sheet c2026-309AA in globo:
