These are fantastic procedural amendments of the kind that we often see in bills. Amendments Nos 25 and 26 deal with annual reporting to Parliament on the implementation of the bill. Amendment No. 26 deals with an independent review. We have statutory reviews of that kind in Acts all the time. The amendment simply inserts provision for that independent review particularly in relation to landholders, employment, business impacts, compensation and carbon projects. That is eminently sensible. Amendment No. 1 on sheet c206-309AA deals with the commencement date and brings any additional safeguards into force as soon as the bill receives assent. That is a sensible approach. Before land is transferred or any status is changed, any additional safeguards will therefore be in force and active on assent. People will not be left waiting for those safeguards to come into effect. Because these amendments are so great, I do not think I will need to divide on them.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 11:54 :24 ): The Government does not support these amendments. Amendment No. 1 on sheet c2026-309AA deals with the safeguard mechanism. In some ways, the Government believes that is redundant at this point, given the project was listed and registered yesterday.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 11:54 :41 ): On behalf of The Nationals, I indicate that we support these three amendments. We obviously agree with the intention of amendment No. 1 on sheet c2026-309AA. It makes sense that the protections should apply from day one. Amendments Nos 25 and 26 on sheet c2026-309B are sensible. They will ensure that each year we get a report to the Parliament about how things are operating under this Act, what changes there might have been and, in particular, what revenue has been raised by the State for dealing with the relevant Australian carbon credit units [ACCUs].

I spoke about this at length in my contribution to the second reading debate, and I do not intend to rehash the points I made. As National Party MPs, we want to see any of the revenue raised from dealing with the ACCUs invested back into the Mid North Coast and areas of the park. If there is a requirement in the legislation for the government of the day to report annually to Parliament, it puts transparency in place. It will make it clear exactly where that money has gone, how much has been raised and, as paragraph (2) (c) talks about, what support has been given to communities and workers affected by the transition away from forestry industries. That is incredibly important.

We spoke a lot in this place about the impact on the timber industry on the Mid North Coast. Hundreds of people will lose their jobs as a result of the creation of this park. The Government has tried to say in this place, in the other place and to the local community that it will look at transition programs for affected workers. Members have debated the merits of that, or lack thereof. The thought that someone who might have been working in the timber industry for decades can suddenly work as a barista or a tourism operator is far-fetched. It is far removed from their skill set but also from what they want to do for work.

Every timber worker I have met loves their job and is quite devastated at the thought of losing it. However, it will be a good thing to have a report to Parliament to make it clear and apparent how that is all tracking. We know that this Government shies away from transparency and accountability—we have seen it time and time again. We support amendment No. 25 on sheet c2026-309B. The Hon. Mark Banasiak has indicated he does not want to divide on it, but I disagree—I think it is worth making the point.

In the same way, amendment No. 26 is a commonsense amendment. It is about the independent review of the Act and its implementation to determine whether the policy objectives of the Act remain valid. If this fabulous park is going to be the best thing since sliced bread and will bring in all those tourists and be wonderful for everybody, why is the Government so afraid of an independent review of the Act to consider its implementation, its impact on landholder interest and on employment and business interests as well as the compensation paid to those affected industries and displaced workers?

All that amendment No. 26 does is that it requires the Government to do what it says it will do, but with the provision and capacity for an independent review of that Act to be in place. I do not think there should be anything to hide. The Government should support the amendment. The Nats actually considered it but did not move it when we saw the Shooters' amendment. We support it wholeheartedly and may potentially vote on it in order to make that point when the time comes.
The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 11:58 :42 ): I indicate that the Liberals do not support these amendments.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 11:58 :52 ): I briefly speak on these amendments before the Committee and back in what my colleague the Hon. Sarah Mitchell said. When members look at these three amendments as a group, they will see they are entirely sensible. They seek to provide transparency to this House and the wider public, which is required for this bill. People have a number of questions about the bill, the way the legislation has been brought to the House, and the methodology and assumptions that underpin the Great Koala National Park.

I now turn to the detail of the amendments. Amendment No. 25 is about the annual reporting to Parliament. I do not understand why the Government will not adopt this amendment which requires that a report be provided to Parliament every year in relation to the matters that the Hon. Mark Banasiak has listed. For the sake of clarity, I will make sure that members understand exactly what the Government has said it is not supporting. Amendment No. 25 on page 6 of sheet c2026‑309B, states:
Page 15. Insert after line 32—
40AReport to Parliament
(1)The NPW Minister must, by 31 December in each year, table a report in each House of Parliament about activities under this Act in the previous financial year.

That requirement is not too onerous for the Minister, who should have that information to hand. It would be a real problem if the Minister did not have that information to hand, because it is information that should clearly be available to the Minister. The department should soon be providing that information up the chain. I note that the amendment provides the Minister with the ability to get it done by 31 December, which is within six months of the end of the financial year. The amendment gives the Minister six months to provide, by the end of the calendar year, the previous financial year's activities, which is not unreasonable. Amendment No. 25 goes on to state:
(2)The report must include information about the following—
(a)land reserved or vested in the NPW Minister under the Act,
(b)the revenue raised by the State for dealings with relevant ACCUs,
(c)support given to communities and workers affected by the transition away from forestry industries as a consequence of the reservation of land by this Act,

I stop there to discuss that part of the amendment for a moment. Is that the reason why the Government does not want to adopt this amendment? Does the Government not want to provide information to the Parliament and the community about the support it is prepared to give to those workers who have lost their jobs as a result of its decisions? It is an absolute disgrace if that is the reason why the Minister does not want to support the amendment. It is an absolute disgrace that the Minister is refusing to provide any of that information or any of the other information that I have already outlined.

People in our communities have had their livelihood stripped out from where they live. Local communities have been part of the responsible and sustainable renewable forestry activities that have occurred in the area for many decades. Our city-centric Minister lives in the middle of Sydney and travels out to these places every once in a while. The Minister has never understood in great detail what these communities do, nor have they understood the actual impact of losing these jobs or the mental toll and stress created by their decisions. The Government is not prepared to outline what supports it has provided in a financial year, which makes me wonder what the Government is hiding. I encourage my Liberal Party colleagues, who do not support this amendment, to look at this matter again and perhaps reconsider. It is clear that this would not be too onerous for the Minister. In fact, one would think that any government worth its salt would say, or volunteer, this information readily without the requirement to report it to Parliament.

In circumstances where we would expect that a government would be prepared or even promote this level of information, the fact that the Government comes into this place and says it is not prepared to support reporting to Parliament on an annual basis clearly demonstrates the lack of transparency of this Government. It is incumbent on all members of this House to look at these amendments in detail and consider what it is the Government is seeking to shut down by not supporting these amendments. The community has a right to know. The community deserves to know what it is that the Government is not telling them. In circumstances where the member has moved an extraordinarily reasonable amendment to provide that information and clarity to the community, we have to ask why the Government has not elected to support that. The amendment goes further and states:
(d)the number of displaced forestry staff employed by the Department in accordance with section 38,

Once again I highlight that the Government should, one would expect, be promoting that it wants to see these matters told to the public because the Government's decision to shut down these forestry jobs should mean that there is a will from within the Government to ensure that those workers have an opportunity to have those jobs that may come up and that that be reported to the Parliament. That the Government is not prepared to support that either makes me think that there is something quite clear about the fact that the Government perhaps does not have the will to see those things done and does not have the drive to see those displaced workers employed back in industries that the department is responsible for.

It is a real shame when a member moves amendments such as this that the Government simply dismisses them. I cannot even find the words to articulate what the Minister's dismissive attitude was in terms of this amendment. But this is an amendment that I think is important for those workers because they need to know that they are being supported by this Government. At the moment, there is a clear understanding that they are not being supported, and that is why this is important. The reporting details that the member is asking be provided to the Parliament are reasonably short, but the amendment does include one other section, which is:
(e)expenditure by the State for the following—
(i)maintenance of the Great Koala National Park,
(ii)road and access maintenance,
(iii)fire management,
(iv)pest animal and weed control.

Anybody who has watched question time or followed debates in this place in particular—and I have no doubt it would happen in the other place, although I suspect their debates are less interesting and less articulate—would know that the question around maintenance of national parks, including road maintenance, fire management and pest and weed control, is an issue that keeps recurring, and it recurs for very good reasons. There is a narrative in our communities that national parks can be poor neighbours. Some landholders feel as if the burden of managing those matters tends to fall to the landholder, as opposed to the National Parks and Wildlife Service carrying its fair share.

I do not think that is an unreasonable contribution to make. I am looking over at the Hon. Mark Banasiak to see if he is frowning. He is not frowning, so I think he potentially agrees with me that National Parks could do better in terms of those things. By moving this amendment, he is seeking to understand exactly what contributions are being made in terms of those matters. What does maintenance of the Great Koala National Park cost? I do not understand why that is an unreasonable thing for the Committee to ask. It would be entirely sensible for the Committee to understand the maintenance costs, how the Great Koala National Park is being maintained and the Government's investment in that. They are entirely sensible requirements.

We have already discussed the issue of road access and road maintenance, in part. It has sort of been covered in previous amendments. But there is great concern amongst many in the community—and I am included in that group—that expenditure on maintenance of roads in the Great Koala National Park may not be sufficient or appropriate to ensure that fire and emergency services have continued access. That access is incredibly important, given that the Government itself has suggested that this is going to be somewhere where we see an increased level of tourism. We know that tourists, especially people who have perhaps travelled there, may face any number of medical issues, and so access for emergency services is very important. Road maintenance to ensure continued road access needs to be kept up in a national park, especially in one the Government wants more people to attend. Understanding what the Government is doing by way of maintenance expenditure is entirely relevant and important for the Committee to understand.

On the issue of fire management, the Government belled the cat on this one. Again, members should ask themselves why the Government is not prepared to support an amendment like this. This whole park is, in effect, one big carbon credit for the Government. Those opposite are treating the whole park as a carbon credit. Yesterday the Minister made a very relevant point that should there be a fire in the Great Koala National Park, all of those carbon credits would be gone. They would burn.
The Hon. Jacqui Munro: Up in smoke.

The Hon. WES FANG: They would go up in smoke—much like the Hon. Jeremy Buckingham, if he was here. In that circumstance, the Government has a real motivation to ensure that fire management is maintained and, where required, upgraded. One would think that the Government would be prepared to support this amendment, because it does very much outline why fire management is important in a national park that is, effectively, being treated like one big carbon credit. The issue of pest animal and weed control is, again, one that we keep talking about. It is curious that, noting all of the members who have contributed to debate on the bill so far, there is one Minister that we have not heard from, and that is the Minister for Agriculture, who is responsible for forestry and for pest animal and weed control.

Maybe that is deliberate. Maybe there is a very good reason as to why we have not heard from the agriculture Minister on this bill. But it may be a very good indicator of why it is that the Government is not prepared to support this amendment. Ensuring good pest animal and weed control in a national park is vitally important to not only the national park itself, but also to surrounding landholders. Locking up that much land creates a haven for those issues. I know I am about to run out of time. I have so much more to say. Hopefully, another member will make a contribution and I can continue on.

I will be quite brief in my contribution to debate. These amendments seek to reverse the amendments passed in the lower House. Those amendments were moved by The Greens to include additional lands to the park estate. Ever since the announcement that the State would get a Great Koala National Park, there has been a lot of argy‑bargy in relation to what will be the park's final size and boundaries. A lot of that has been bouncing backwards and forwards in different consultation groups—the community, industry, environmental groups and other community groups. It is not really good faith that a decision is made with those groups and then we come to Parliament and differ from the decision greatly by moving amendments that include additional lands. I do not think that instils confidence in government consultation processes.

I do not think it does anything to improve what the community feels about how consultation generally is done. We should not be arbitrarily moving the goalposts in relation to what has been decided, particularly in the mind of the community, as to what the national park boundaries would be. I think that sets a dangerous precedent that we can arbitrarily change things, despite what the community thinks. I do not think that is good representation and I do not think we should make a habit of doing that. I commend the amendments to the Committee.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 12 :23 :30 ): The Government does not support the amendments. These matters were dealt with in the lower House.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 12:23 :34 ): On behalf of The Nationals, I indicate that we support the amendments. We opposed The Greens' amendments when they were put in the other place, so we certainly support the amendments here to effectively repeal the amendments that were made in the other place, if that makes sense to those playing at home. I will make a couple of points in relation to this set of amendments because what these amendments really do is ask the Government to go back to standing by the bill that the Government brought to Parliament originally and the deal the Government made with the people on the Mid North Coast. The Hon. Mark Banasiak was spot on in his contribution. Supposedly, there was consultation with the community. The boundaries were meant to be clear. Then we come to Parliament and suddenly, when The Greens in the other place move amendments to change those boundaries, it is all fine to do it on a whim. This bill was supposed to be the product of months of consultation with local communities, recreation groups and industry—and work was done on how that was supposed to happen—but a boundary was literally redrawn and a new map was inserted. In practice, that means that land has been incorporated into the national park with no consultation with the people who actually live there. That is not how land use decisions in this State should be made. This is a house of review, and that is exactly what the Opposition is doing by supporting these amendments of the Shooters.

The other thing I say in support of these amendments—and part of this goes also to earlier amendments that we have discussed—is the constant theme of boundaries having been drawn, then suddenly the Legislative Assembly adding a new bit of land, and the bill still providing that the Government can add more on a whim at the request of the Minister of the day. Consider what that means for the local community, but also for the timber industry in the region. They get told where the lines are going to be, only for them to get changed the next minute and then again changed by The Greens in the lower House, who, with respect, might be very sincere in their intentions. But when a Sydney-based Greens MP, whose electorate is nowhere near the impacted area, does that, it makes people who live in these communities cranky. They feel that city-based parliamentarians are telling them how things should operate without any consideration of what the impact might be on them in their local community. Moving boundary lines at the last minute again and again at the whim of The Greens or the Minister of the day adds uncertainty. That is not good governance and it is not how this Parliament should work.

The Opposition supports the amendments moved by the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers to pull that provision out of the bill. If the Government were happy with the bill as it was, it should not have supported those changes either. These amendments respect the process and the community by returning the bill to the form that the Government designed and consulted on. I commend the amendments to the House.
The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 12:26 :36 ): I indicate that the Liberals will be supporting the amendments. I refer members to the comments of my colleague the Hon. Sarah Mitchell.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 12:26 :49 ): I rise to make a contribution in relation to the amendments that have been moved on sheet c2026-313A. I reflect on the contributions to this point in relation to these amendments, which have been moved in globo, to encourage other members also to reflect on them and consider the fact that the Government, in good faith, brought to the House, in the initial sense, a bill that prescribed the boundaries of the Great Koala National Park. Not only did it do that through the legislation but, as the Hon. Sarah Mitchell quite clearly articulated in her very sensible contribution, this was something that was reflected in the consultation with the communities that have been impacted by the legislation that has been moved.

In terms of that consultation, I have spoken with a number of affected stakeholders. I have also spoken with a number of the communities that are impacted by these decisions. Again, there is a level of betrayal felt because the Government, in supporting this in the other place, has effectively said to our communities that the consultation was worthless. That may not have been the intention of the Government. I do not know. I suspect it was, but that is only my personal suspicion. By extension, the Government does not really care about the fact that it consulted on the original legislated boundaries. By adopting the amendments of The Greens in the other place, which the Shooters are now seeking to reverse, the Ministers in the Cabinet would have known that they effectively trashed the whole consultation process that occurred in our communities.

The fact that the Government does not seem to care about that and has indicated that it was prepared to support the amendments in the other place but is not prepared to support the reversal in the Legislative Council is interpreted by our communities as not only a betrayal but also an active choice to ignore their voices. It was based on the original boundaries that our communities' voices were heard. That betrayal that is felt in our communities is not something that is readily going to go away. In her brief contribution, the Minister did not take the opportunity to try to correct those matters or allay the fears that the community clearly has around the Government's support of this in the other place. I am sure the Minister has received correspondence or feedback that the Government's adoption of these amendments in the other place has left our community feeling betrayed.

The Government cannot go to the community with a set of boundaries and then adopt in the other place these amendments that effectively rule any consultation null and void. The Minister can, at the drop of a hat, effectively, change those boundaries. That is of concern. The community does not feel as if their voices have been heard. That is a betrayal. It is also of concern because the level of uncertainty that will exist if we do not adopt these amendments in this House is too high. The anger about these amendments in our communities is palpable. That the Government does not see that, has not acknowledged it and is prepared to ignore it is extraordinarily disappointing for our communities.

I urge the Minister to take this opportunity in Committee of the Whole to look at these amendments again and either seek to adopt them and go back to our communities with another round of consultation to listen to them and let them know this is a proposal that the Government is prepared to support, or clearly articulate now why the Government is prepared to ignore the consultation that occurred and not reverse these amendments. I encourage the Minister to consider that. Perhaps my contribution will persuade the Minister that she should clarify the Government's intention. I also speak on behalf of my Nationals friend and colleague in this place the Hon. Nichole Overall, who has unfortunately had to leave because of appointments that could not be altered. She asked me to put on record that she also has great concerns about the amendments adopted in the other place and that she, in consultations with the same communities, has had very similar, if not identical, feedback to the feedback that I have had.

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 12:45 :44 ): I indicate that I do not think it will be 20 at all, but there may be the potential for a short bell division if members keep their contributions concise on this amendment. I move Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendment No. 2 on sheet c2026-309AA:
No. 2Regulated hunting in gazetted areas
Page 15. Insert after line 40—
42ARegulated hunting in gazetted areas
(1)In this section—

eligible land means land reserved by this Act as national park or regional park that is public land within the meaning of the Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002, but does not include land declared as wilderness or included in a World Heritage property.
hunting area means eligible land designated under subsection (2).
hunting permission means a permission given under subsection (6).
introduced animal means a feral pig, feral goat, feral deer, fox, rabbit or feral cat living in the wild, but does not include a domestic animal or an animal of a native species.
Regulatory Authority has the same meaning as in the Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002.
(2)The NPW Minister may, by notice published in the Gazette, designate eligible land as an area in which introduced animals specified in the notice may be hunted in accordance with this section.
(3)Before designating land, the NPW Minister must—
(a)obtain the written concurrence of the Minister administering the Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002, and
(b)comply with the public notice and consultation requirements applicable to a declaration under that Act, section 20, and
(c)consider the objectives of the relevant plan of management, existing lawful uses, public safety, native wildlife and cultural heritage.

(4)Despite the Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002, section 20A, a designation under subsection (2) is taken to be a declaration under that Act, section 20. The public notice requirements for the designation are additional to publication in the Gazette.

(5)A prohibition on hunting in a plan of management under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974 does not prevent designation of eligible land or hunting expressly permitted under this section. Apart from that prohibition, a designation or permission does not override an otherwise lawful exclusion or closure. The Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002, section 6B does not displace such an exclusion or closure in connection with hunting under this section.

(6)The Secretary may, with the written concurrence of the Regulatory Authority, give a person aged at least 18 years who holds a current restricted game hunting licence under the Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002 written permission to hunt specified introduced animals in a hunting area.

(7)A permission must specify the land, period, animals, permitted methods and conditions. It must not authorise entry onto land excluded from the designation, an activity contrary to the person's licence, or possession or use of equipment contrary to another law.

(8)Before giving a permission, the Secretary must approve arrangements for visitor safety, protection of native wildlife and cultural heritage, animal welfare, clear maps, entry notices, booking limits and coordination with other park and pest control operations. The Secretary must consult adjoining occupiers and relevant Aboriginal organisations about those arrangements.

(9)A hunting permission is taken to be the written permission of the land manager and the Regulatory Authority for the purposes of the Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002. The requirements of that Act and its regulations applicable to hunting on declared public hunting land apply, including licence conditions and reporting requirements, subject to this section.

(10)The Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002, section 6A does not apply to hunting under this section. Instead, a person acting in accordance with a hunting permission does not commit an offence under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974 or its regulations merely by—
(a)hunting an introduced animal specified in the permission, or
(b)possessing, carrying or using a firearm, ammunition or other hunting equipment expressly permitted for that hunting, or
(c)possessing or removing, otherwise than for sale, the carcass of an introduced animal lawfully killed under the permission, to the extent expressly permitted by the permission.

(11)This section does not authorise harm to native wildlife, Aboriginal objects or vegetation, entry onto private land without lawful authority, or conduct contrary to the Firearms Act 1996, Weapons Prohibition Act 1998, Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1979, Biosecurity Act 2015 or food safety law. It does not affect native title rights.

(12)The NPW Minister may vary or revoke a designation by a further notice published in the Gazette. The Secretary may vary, suspend or cancel a permission for breach of a condition or a material risk to safety, animal welfare, native wildlife or cultural heritage.

(13)Before taking action under subsection (12), the decision-maker must give an affected permission holder notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond, unless immediate action is necessary to address a serious risk. Written reasons must be given, including as soon as practicable after urgent action.

(14)This section does not change a reservation category, a statutory land boundary or a schedule to this Act. It does not authorise the Secretary to exercise the Regulatory Authority's functions under the Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002 other than as expressly provided by this section.

This amendment allows licensed adults to hunt specified introduced animals in eligible areas that the Minister formally opens for hunting. It requires ministerial agreement, public consultation and written permissions, with safety and wildlife protections. It excludes wilderness and World Heritage land, and preserves other lawful closures and adherence to firearms laws. Licensed hunters should have a lawful, carefully managed opportunity to contribute to controlling introduced animals where the land is suitable. A change in the sign at the forest entrance should not end the discussion about practical pest management. Suitability, safety and the conditions of access should be examined, rather than ruled out without that assessment.

This is a permission system, not a general right to arrive in the Great Koala National Park with a firearm. An adult would still need to have the appropriate current licence and a written permission covering the area, species, methods and period. The two ministerial portfolios and the hunting regulator have defined roles. Visitors, neighbours and Aboriginal organisations would have to be considered, and native animals would remain protected. This is a serious proposal for a regulated access scheme. Our position is that responsible hunting should be considered a legitimate activity within a properly controlled system where the land and circumstances are suitable. There is no need to pretend that every area is going to be appropriate or that every method should be permitted.

The amendment provides a way to make those distinctions. It also gives the land manager tools to set conditions and respond to breaches or serious risks. Members can disagree about the merits of opening a particular area while still supporting a legal framework in which that proposal can be examined seriously and decided through defined responsibilities. For those reasons, I endorse the amendment. It is a cause our party has been pushing, and will continue to push, for a very long time. I ask other members to support it. The safeguard should be judged on its practical purpose and the specific obligation set out in the text of the amendment.
The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 12:48 :14 ): The Government does not support the amendment.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 12:48 :18 ): The Nationals support the amendment. I will not go too much over what the honourable member has said in moving it. But the reality is that some feral animals are amongst the biggest threats to koalas and native wildlife. We have also seen some of the issues we can have when there are massive numbers of feral pigs, goats or deer, and the incredible destruction that they can cause. This is a sensible amendment. It is clear that it only applies to certain areas that will be regulated. It is only for introduced pest species, and native animals are expressly excluded. It also makes clear that there can be no harm to native wildlife, vegetation or Aboriginal objects.

I also make the point that there are a lot of safeguards within the amendment. It makes it clear there has to be a Gazette notice; concurrence of the hunting Minister; public notice and consultation; and consideration of public safety, native wildlife and cultural heritage. As the member mentioned in moving the amendment, only adults with a current restricted licence and with written permission specifying the land, the period, the species, the methods and the conditions will be able to take part. Before any permission is granted, the secretary must approve visitor safety, animal welfare, maps et cetera. All firearms and weapons, animal cruelty and biosecurity laws will still apply in full if the amendment is passed, and permissions can be suspended or cancelled for breach of a condition or material risk. The Minister will have the power to revoke any area at any time. We are happy to support the amendment.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 12:50 :05 ): The Liberals do not support the amendment. We believe that the bill as it stands is sufficient to achieve the Liberal Party's aims in relation to the creation of the Great Koala National Park.

The Hon. SCOTT BARRETT ( 12:50 :22 ): I strongly support the amendment and urge others to do the same. I think the mover put it really well. This is a permission system, not a general right. All it would do is permit the Minister to allow people to go in and hunt as needed under very strict conditions that are working well within State forests. I urge members to support the amendment.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 12:50 :54 ): I also support the amendment, and I do so for a number of reasons. As outlined by the member, hunting in the national park may actually help the Government achieve an outcome for the issues that it is likely to see when that amount of land is locked up. A number of contributions have already discussed a level of concern in the community about the issue of pests and wild animals. The Government is calling the park the Great Koala National Park. Wild dogs, in particular, are such a risk to koalas. The hunting community, where it is granted permission—and permission is a really key aspect of the amendment that is being moved by the member—could go into the national park and seek to manage some of the pests that will likely thrive in a national park where the current management practices may not continue.

We know that Forestry Corporation is typically a good neighbour. It does a good job of managing pests, feral animals and weeds. The community fears that we may see an explosion of those things, but I suspect that the Government has a level of concern as well, because we know that those circumstances are ripe for an explosion of things like wild dogs. There is no doubt that those wild dogs may cause an increase in injuries to the koala population within the park. It is the case that amendment No. 2, as moved by the member, will ensure that regulated hunting is permitted in gazetted areas. The amendment is quite specific in terms of the eligible land, because there is a definition that is provided which states:

eligible land means land reserved by this Act as national park or regional park that is public land within the meaning of the Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002, but does not include land declared as wilderness or included in a World Heritage property.

That clearly articulates to any person seeking to understand or interpret the legislation—if this amendment is passed—what eligible lands the hunting amendment would be attached to. It goes on further to actually indicate that the "hunting area" definition means "eligible land designated under subsection (2)". I will come to that in a moment. It talks about the "hunting permission", which is defined as a "permission given under subsection (6)". These things are not a free-for-all. There is a clear outline, within the amendment that provides an opportunity for any person seeking to make an application to the National Parks and Wildlife Service to hunt in those areas, of what eligible lands are covered, what hunting areas are covered and how the permission is granted.

What is also very important in terms of the issues we are talking about now is that the amendment also has a definition in it for "introduced animal", which includes a feral pig, feral goat, feral deer, fox, rabbit or feral cat living in the wild, but does not include a domestic animal or an animal of a native species. The definition is quite clear about what animals may be targeted in terms of the application of the amendment. In moving this amendment, the member has done a lot of detailed work to ensure that it is an amendment that can be supported by the whole Committee. What it does is it actually provides the framework, so members of the Committee can rest assured that it is not effectively a free-for-all.

The national parks and wildlife Minister may, by notice published in the Gazette, designate eligible land as an area in which introduced animals specified in the notice may be hunted in accordance with this section. Again, we come back to the issue around the transparency of the Government in terms of ensuring that its decisions are communicated to the public. I think the Government Gazette, in particular, is an appropriate place for the Minister or the secretary to make known that there is going to be a designation of those areas. That will provide the community with an opportunity to participate, where a designation is communicated in the Gazette.

I think that is something that, again, clearly outlines what the member is seeking to do in terms of this total amendment, but it provides the specifics, which means that the Committee can actually support it with confidence. What is quite appropriate in terms of the amendment is subsection (3), which says, "Before designating land, the national parks and wildlife Minister must"—this is important because it outlines to people who are following any designation in the Gazette by the Minister what the Minister must do prior to that. I think that is really important for the Committee to consider. It states that the Minister must—
(a)obtain the written concurrence of the Minister administering the Game and Feral Animal Control Act 2002, and—
it is not "and/or"; it is clearly "and"—
(b)comply with the public notice and consultation requirements applicable to a declaration under that Act—

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 13:40 :02 ): By leave: I move Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments Nos 3 to 12, 96, 97 and 98 on sheet c2026-309AA in globo:
No. 3Public consultation on carbon project registration
Page 15. Insert after line 40—
42B Public consultation on carbon project registration

(1)Before the NPW Minister, or a person acting on behalf of the Crown in right of New South Wales in connection with establishment of the Great Koala National Park, applies, or gives the State's consent to an application, for registration of a carbon abatement project involving land reserved or vested, or specified for reservation or vesting, by this Act, or for a material variation of the project area or permanence obligations, the Secretary must publish a description of the proposal, the land, proposed duration and expected management obligations.

(2)The Secretary must invite submissions for at least 30 days, consider the submissions and publish a response to material issues before the State application is made or the State's consent is given, as the case requires.

(3)This section applies only to an application made by the State or consent given by the State after commencement of this section. It does not invalidate a registration or variation under Commonwealth law or require disclosure of legally privileged information.
No. 4Independent valuation before disposing of carbon credits
Page 15. Insert after line 40—
42C Independent valuation before disposing of carbon credits

(1)Before the NPW Minister, or a person acting on behalf of the Crown in right of New South Wales in connection with establishment of the Great Koala National Park, enters an arrangement to sell, assign or grant an option over Australian carbon credit units attributable to land reserved or vested, or specified for reservation or vesting, by this Act, the NPW Minister must obtain an independent valuation of the consideration and material contractual risks.
(2)A valuation is required for the first arrangement and for a later arrangement materially different in price structure or risk allocation.

(3)The valuer must have relevant expertise and no financial interest in the transaction. A summary of the valuation and reasons for a material departure must be published within 30 days after the arrangement is entered into. Information that would prejudice continuing negotiations may be withheld until that risk ceases, with published reasons.
(4)In this section, Australian carbon credit unit has the same meaning as in the Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative) Act 2011 of the Commonwealth.

(a)Without a financial cap or other objectively ascertainable maximum exposure, or
(b)for loss to the extent caused by the indemnified party's fraud, wilful misconduct or negligence.
(2)Before agreeing to another indemnity for the project, the NPW Minister must obtain the Treasurer's written concurrence and publish the maximum exposure or the method by which it is limited.
(3)This section does not confer power to give an indemnity, appropriate money or affect an agreement except to the extent it is renewed or materially varied after commencement of this section.

42F Conflicts in carbon credit transactions

42CQ Public inventory of carbon project agreements

These amendments deal with transparency around the carbon credit scheme. Amendment No. 3 provides for at least 30 days of public consultation before the State applies for, cancels or consents to the registration of a carbon project. Amendment No. 4 requires an independent valuation around disposal of carbon credits. Amendment No. 5 places a limit on carbon project indemnities. Amendment No. 6 deals with parliamentary approval for long carbon commitments extending beyond 25 years. Amendment No. 7 deals with conflicts in carbon credit transactions, requiring people negotiating and selecting parties for carbon credit deals to disclose personal interests.

Amendment No. 8 deals with the annual testing of financial risks around the carbon credit scheme. A summary must be published within six months of the financial year ending, showing the assumptions, possible liabilities and ways to manage them. Amendment No. 9 deals with compliance action regarding a carbon project, requiring notification publicly within 14 days. Amendment No. 10 deals with evidence for public carbon claims. It requires public carbon claims to distinguish estimates from verified results and credits issued when credits sold are already used. That prevents claims that the same abatement remains available for another offset after the entitlement has been transferred or used.

Amendment No. 11 deals with the traceability of carbon project receipts, requiring clear records of carbon income, transaction costs and the amount left for the State. An annual summary must be published and the supporting records kept available for a lawful audit. Amendment No. 12 deals with contractual secrecy over aggregate carbon costs. Amendments Nos 96, 97 and 98 all deal with the assessment of carbon‑related management restrictions and having a public inventory of carbon project agreements. Amendment No. 98 specifically concerns there being no contractual override of statutory duties with regards to the scheme. With those brief remarks, I commend the amendments to the Committee.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 13:42 :50 ): These issues have been well canvassed. The Government does not support these amendments.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 13:42 :54 ): I put on record that The Nationals will be supporting all of these amendments. Amendment No. 3 is about ensuring 30 days of public submissions before the State registers or materially varies a project. We think this is important because communities should hear about any changes before they are locked in, not after. Amendment No. 4 is about independent valuation before selling credits, which would apply in any other transaction we make. You would not sell your farm without a valuation. This amendment just puts in place an independent valuer with no financial interest and a published summary within 30 days. We think whatever should apply in other cases should be the same for the selling of carbon credits.

We support what amendment No. 5 seeks to do, which is to ensure there are no uncapped indemnities and there is no indemnifying a counterparty for its own fraud or negligence, and that the Treasurer must sign off on any other indemnity. Amendment No. 6 requires Parliament to approve commitments over 25 years. We are happy to support this amendment, because we have concerns that any sort of permanence can bind the State for a very long time. We do not think a decision that binds governments that have not yet been elected to Parliament is a good idea.

Amendment No. 7 concerns conflicts of interest. It makes sense to ensure that officials negotiating carbon deals declare personal interests and step aside unless those are managed properly and published annually. That will lead to basic integrity, which we should all want. The annual stress test will test exposure against bushfire, drought, credit price falls and noncompliance. The Nationals also agree with amendment No. 9, requiring the regulator to disclose action within 14 days. Again, we think that is good public process, ensuring that the public is told if there are any breaches or cancellations of credits. Amendments Nos 10, 11 and 12 ensure that there is no greenwashing. Public claims must be very clear about estimated and verified abatement, credits issued, sold or retired, and no double counting of carbon already sold. We think transparency is important.

Amendment No. 12 ensures no secrecy clauses on the aggregate cost. Commercial pricing can stay confidential, but total cost, duration and maximum exposure cannot be hidden by contract. We agree with that in terms of transparency. Finally, amendments Nos 96 to 98 are also about transparency, making sure that the public register of carbon agreements is published within 30 days, that there is a table of the carbon restrictions on fire, pest and access, and, if there is a carbon contract that limits hazard reduction, pest control or access, Parliament is the body that sees it first. It makes sense to have a clause that contracts cannot override statutory duties. Therefore, The Nationals support the amendments.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 13:46 :01 ): The Liberals will vote against the amendments. Like the Government, we believe that the existing processes need to be scrutinised. I raised those matters in my second reading debate contribution. We have questions about how the Australian carbon credit units will be operational in the scheme. This will be the first test of the improved native forest management method, and proper scrutiny should be applied, but we do not believe that this is the appropriate way to do that.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 13:46 :43 ): I indicate that I support the amendments moved by the Hon. Mark Banasiak and outlined in detail by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, my colleague and friend the Hon. Sarah Mitchell. From the outset, in rejecting the amendments, in the contributions of the Leader of the Government and the member leading in debate for the Liberal Party, the Hon. Jacqui Munro—she is also my friend, but on this issue I might perhaps disagree with her a little bit—effectively rejecting the amendments, they did not necessarily go into detail as to why that rejection is the case. If we were to look at these amendments—and there are a number of amendments moved in globo—they provide a level of transparency.

Even the Hon. Jacqui Munro, in her contribution, whilst indicating that the Liberal Party would not support the amendments, indicated that there is a level of concern about the carbon credits scheme being rolled out. Given the only very recent Federal Parliament adoption of the new method, there is a level of concern about the way that these matters will be scrutinised by the State Parliament, given that the Government is also so reliant on the funding from the scheme to effectively bankroll the Great Koala National Park. Just looking at the amendments that have been moved, the public consultation on carbon project registration is entirely reasonable. I think that the community deserves the right to be consulted on these matters.

We have already outlined in previous contributions that the Government has effectively treated consultation as a tick‑box exercise. Given that the Government does that so readily, it is unusual that it would not actually be prepared to support these reasonable amendments that would require consultation on the matters.

Amendment No. 4, "Independent valuation before disposing of carbon credits", again provides some clarity about the value of those carbon credits. I have already raised my personal concerns that we have a potential here that the carbon credits will be limited in their value, specifically because the Government has said a class of purchaser is excluded from being able to access those carbon credits. Any time that you limit that market for the carbon credits, you create a circumstance where you are perhaps curtailing the price that you can achieve.

Ultimately, governments have to make decisions, and I think that the public is right to be informed about the cost of those decisions. If it is the case that the Government seeks to artificially curtail the market that exists around the carbon credits, then they should be made aware of the costs of that. By insisting that an independent valuation occur, the public will be able to be better informed about what those carbon credits may be valued at and what they may be valued at in terms of a limited market, given the constraints that the Government has put around those carbon credits. Amendment No. 5 effectively has a limit on the carbon project indemnities. I think that is extraordinarily reasonable in terms of the contributions that have been made previously. I do not need to labour on that point.

Amendment No. 6 relates to parliamentary approval for long carbon commitments. I do not think it is unreasonable that Parliament be considered the appropriate place to consider these issues. Whilst some of those reasons have been perhaps articulated in other debates, I note that we are talking about periods of 25 years. There has already been, I think, some concern about what was, say, a plantation being enveloped as part of this Great Koala National Park and it being drawn into the carbon credit scheme. I think those long-tail commitments need to be a question for the Parliament. The Parliament is the appropriate place to bring those.

Amendment No. 7 relates to conflicts in carbon credit transactions and is entirely appropriate. There is—amongst the community, at least—concern that what I have called the Ponzi scheme, but what other people call the carbon credit scheme, creates a circumstance where people are trading pieces of paper. I keep reflecting on this—Ms Abigail Boyd articulated concerns around how this new methodology may or may not remove carbon. The other issue that it points to, in terms of the trading of carbon credits, is that there are, in effect, potentials for conflicts of interest where we know that there are bodies that trade in carbon credits. These are a newly adopted carbon credit that did not exist previously.

It is my contention that they are not even really carbon credits because I am unsure as to exactly how much carbon they are removing from the system, given that we are effectively not chopping down a tree, but it is not as if that tree was necessarily always going to be burnt. It may have been turned into floorboards; it may have been turned into furniture. That carbon remains captured. This method of valuing the carbon credit that exists within those forests is, I think, perhaps questionable. Those conflicts that may exist in those circumstances should be declared. Again, that is why the amendment is entirely reasonable.

It is interesting that both the Liberal Party and the Government have sought to not adopt this amendment. The testing of financial risks to the carbon credit scheme is quite sensible. As the Minister outlined quite correctly, bushfires create an incredible risk to the carbon credit scheme. If you burn down a forest where you have effectively not cut down any trees, you are releasing all of that carbon. The carbon credit exists because the trees have not been cut down, but members can imagine what would happen if a fire went through that area. If a carbon credit has been granted for not cutting down a tree and a fire goes through the area and burns the tree down, then that carbon is released. If that tree had been cut down and turned into furniture or floorboards, like some hardwoods are, it would release less carbon than if it had burned in a bushfire.

The circumstance I just highlighted points to how ridiculous this carbon credit scheme is, because there is not really any additionality. Members have always made the point that there has to be a level of additionality with carbon capture. It is also the case that there are so many risks to the carbon credit scheme, given bushfires and the like, that it is appropriate for members to look at this amendment. It is also appropriate to have compliance for carbon projects and to require evidence for public carbon claims. I have already outlined why traceability and having no contractual secrecy are so important. We have vast concerns. A number of other amendments were moved by the Hon. Mark Banasiak, but I think I have covered the main ones. I conclude my remarks by saying that these amendments are sensible. It is interesting that the other parties in this place are not prepared to adopt the small level of transparency that these amendments provide.

(3)In this section, existing interest means a lease, licence, permit, authority, authorisation or occupancy held immediately before reservation or vesting under this Act and continuing in force, including a renewal or extension, other than a forestry right extinguished under section 31.

Amendments Nos 13 to 15 are largely to do with access to the national park. Amendment No. 13 deals with an open process for exclusive commercial visitor rights. An open expression of interest process is required before any new, exclusive visitor rights are granted. That is a sensible approach given the conversations we have had in this place around potentially offering campsites to commercial companies to run. Amendment No. 14 sets out published criteria for commercial filming and photography applications. A lot of constituents have asked for a clearer process to apply for filming and photography. Amendment No. 15 deals with fee relief for school field studies. We want young people to visit the park and engage in our environment. Providing fee relief options for schools, particularly schools from low socio-economic backgrounds or schools that might have to travel great distances to visit the park, is a worthwhile cause to pursue.

Amendment No. 16 is about maintaining a local advisory group on the park for at least three years while the park is in its infancy. Amendment No. 17 deals with an independent review for any complaints around land handover, requiring a written response within 30 days, or an explanation if longer time is needed. Amendment No. 18 says that there should be no second processing fee for any transfers or applications. Only one fee should be charged, unless the application is substantially different. Amendment No. 19 says there should be no rent increase solely because of a transfer as the land status changes.

Amendment No. 20 protects lawful buildings and improvements from being ordered removed simply because the land changes hands. If infrastructure is in good order, we do not see why it should be removed because of the land status changing. Amendments Nos 27 and 28 are around protecting Aboriginal cultural heritage. They require applicable Aboriginal heritage checks and consultation before any new ground disturbing works. That is a sensible amendment. Amendment No. 28 applies something similar for the assessment of historic forest heritage. A lot of forestry infrastructure within our State forests has heritage value and significance to people who have worked in the industry for generations. That is worthwhile conserving as part of any park.

Amendments Nos 78 to 86 are around existing interest holders. Amendment No. 78 requires one departmental contact point for holders of continuing leases, permits and licences. People dealing with one person and not getting the runaround makes the transition smoother. That causes distress for people in other areas. That is a sensible amendment. Amendment No. 79 is around issues with missing applications and information about them being provided earlier. Being able to respond to that within 14 days is a sensible amendment. We think there should be a timeline for status updates of outstanding applications. That would be a key performance indicator for agencies to be held to. Existing interest holders should not be waiting for more than 60 days and should be afforded an explanation if that is the case.

Amendment No. 81 deals with the recognition of existing compliance records. Lawfully available compliance records from Forestry Corporation of NSW or other State agency are to be considered when assessing an application concerning an existing interest. Applicants should not have to supply the same evidence again if it has already been provided a first time. Amendment No. 82 deals with the time to respond before adverse permit decisions, giving the permit holder at least 21 days to respond before a discretionary decision ends or substantially restricts an interest. Amendment No. 83 is around proportionate permit conditions. The amendment requires new discretionary conditions on continuing leases, permits and other existing interests to serve a lawful management purpose and be no more restrictive than reasonably necessary for that purpose. Conditions required by another Act would still apply.

Amendment No. 84 is about disclosure. Before requiring a new bond, deposit or insurance amount from an existing interest holder, reasons identifying the risk and an explanation of how the amount was set must be given. That makes the demand accountable without creating a new power to impose it. Amendment No. 85 provides for an independent internal review of any new conditions on existing interest holders. An interest holder can seek, within 28 days, an internal review of any new discretionary condition. The 28‑day period is pretty standard for departmental internal reviews. Amendment No. 86 deals with the retention of interest holder records, requiring that they be held for the duration of the interest and at least seven years afterwards, regardless of the interest continuing or not.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 14:06 :13 ): I appreciate the member grouping these amendments together. The Government does not support them. Again, we have had this conversation. There are already existing mechanisms in place to cover those matters through plans of management and a range of other aspects of the National Parks and Wildlife Act and the Contaminated Land Management Act. The Government does not believe they need to be put into the legislation.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 14:06 :34 ): I indicate that The Nationals will be supporting all of these amendments. I make a couple of comments about a few of them, particularly amendments Nos 13 to 15. We support making sure that local businesses and school students—particularly those on the North Coast—get fair access to the Great Koala National Park. As a former education Minister, I think it is really important that any land reserved under the Act be available to school students. The Shooters amendment ensures that an application by a school to conduct a non‑commercial field study will not be subject to a processing fee. We think it is important for students to have access to learning experiences outside of the classroom, so amendment No. 15 in particular makes a lot of sense.

The Nationals think amendments Nos 16 to 20 are a good block of amendments. They ensure that the people who know this country best have a seat at the table and are not worse off because of the changes made here, by implementing a local advisory group and good complaints processes, and avoiding double fees and rent hikes. They are commonsense amendments. In relation to amendments Nos 27 and 28, about Aboriginal forestry, we think it is important that Aboriginal cultural heritage assessment and consultation requirements are satisfied before any new works, so that culturally sensitive information will stay protected. The same applies to historic forestry heritage.

Lastly, amendments Nos 78 to 86 are sensible in terms of ensuring that there is good administration in place for local communities, and not just further bureaucracy. Having a one-door approach means that people will not have to repeat the same information to different agencies. It is good governance to have a one‑stop shop, answer phone calls, not lose people's files and be there to support the community. They are sensible amendments to limit administration and bureaucracy.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 14:09 :03 ): The Liberals do not support the amendments. Again, we are sympathetic to the Hon. Mark Banasiak's aims and intentions, and the National Party's support for the amendments. But we, like the Government, believe there are existing and sufficient provisions within the bill and existing regulatory structures.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 14:09 :28 ): I make a brief contribution to debate on the amendments. From the outset, I say that it is unfortunate that some of these amendments cannot be supported by the Government or the Liberal Party, particularly amendment No. 15, which I think is incredibly important for us to consider. I am not sure that a lot of consideration has been given to that one, which is about permit fee relief for school field studies. The Government has said, effectively, that this is going to be a koala sanctuary, it is going a national park, it is going to be tourist hotspot and it is going to be a number of things. But that should not be at the expense of schools, students and their learning.

By moving this amendment, the member has made a reasonable and supportable proposal. I know a lot of parents who send their kids to school are already under cost‑of‑living pressures. If schools were exempt from any fees to enter or study the Great Koala National Park, that would provide schools with an ability to consider sending students to attend there and providing opportunities for students to learn in that environment, because that cost would not be imposed on the school—although it is probably more likely the case, let's be honest, that the cost would be to the parents of the children who attend the national park to study.

I do not know what the cost of that policy would be. I cannot imagine that it would be a huge cost. Again, that it was not already written into the bill is a problem, particularly for the education Minister in this Government. I know that my colleague the Hon. Sarah Mitchell, as a former education Minister, would have been quite strident in her support.
The Hon. Sarah Mitchell: We wouldn't have done this bill, to be fair.

The Hon. WES FANG: I acknowledge that interjection. We would not have done something like this. In circumstances where there were impact on other portfolios, I am sure the Hon. Sarah Mitchell, as an education Minister, would have been strident in her support for an amendment like this. It is interesting that the member in the other place, the education Minister, has not pulled the Minister for the Environment aside and demanded that something like this be supported. That is a failure of the education Minister, but I probably do not need to labour that point too much.

The member has moved a number of sensible amendments, and he has moved them in globo. I accept that there is perhaps a circumstance where members who have indicated that they are not prepared to support all the amendments that were moved may be reluctant to support the grouping of amendments because they were moved in globo. I submit to all those members that this is, in fact, a sensible group of amendments that effectively can be adopted with very little cost to the Government. For example, amendment No. 16 is about local advice on park establishment. There is very little pushback in terms of adopting this. But it just seems to me that we are currently debating a bill with a government that is reluctant to listen and learn from the errors of the past—errors that they made in the seeking and understanding of local advice.

I appreciate that the Hon. Mark Banasiak has moved these amendments to try to help the Government to help itself. I know I used that phrase a lot yesterday, but that is also what is happening here: With the experience that we all bring to this Committee, we are trying to provide the Government with an opportunity to do better and be better. We are trying to help the Government do that. You can lead a horse to water but, unfortunately you cannot make it drink. That is certainly the case with these amendments. The Hon. Mark Banasiak has led the Government to the water, but the Government is too stubborn to take a drink. Ultimately, with that analogy what we will see is a government that is going to go thirsty. It will go thirsty for the consultation of local communities.

Looking at the amendments that have been moved, as I said previously they are all supportable. I do not know why the Government has failed to adopt them. I am not sure why our Coalition partner is not adopting them, either. Certainly the National Party will support them. I encourage members to reconsider their positions.

The TEMPORARY CHAIR ( The Hon. Taylor Martin ): The Hon. Mark Banasiak has moved Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments Nos 13 to 15, 16 to 20, 27 and 28, and 78 to 86 on sheet c2026-309AA. The question is that the amendments be agreed to.
Amendments negatived.
The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 14:15 :30 ): By leave: I move Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments Nos 21, 22, 29, 32, 33, 36 to 40, 45, 87 to 89 on sheet c2026-309AA in globo:
