I will deal first with amendments Nos 21 and 22, which deal with legacy contamination and particularly asbestos in assets. Having hunted in State forests quite avidly around the State, I know there is naturally occurring asbestos in some of those State forests as well as asbestos that has been dumped, not necessarily by hunters, of course, but by other people who use the forest. There may also be asbestos in old buildings that were in use before the area became Forestry land. Those contaminations are mapped. These amendments seek to make sure that those legacy contaminations, or that presence of asbestos, continue to be mapped and continue to be assessed and managed when the areas are transferred. We think that is sensible. We want people to use the forests without any adverse impacts from stumbling into contaminated areas without prior knowledge.

Amendment No. 29 deals with access road load restrictions and requires engineering evidence about road weight limits, particularly with respect to access to private or occupied lands. I cast no aspersions on National Parks, but there have been shenanigans with some local councils on the mid North Coast, whereby local landholders who apply for private native forestry permits have had load restrictions on bridges and roads reduced, and trucks could not get in to do the work. But then, magically, when the Local Land Services private native forestry application fails or is abandoned, the load restrictions return. If road load restrictions are to be changed, evidence should be provided to the public.

Amendment No. 32 is around the restoration of essential access after bushfires. After the 2019 bushfires, it has taken an inordinate amount of time for locals to get essential access back to their properties. In some cases on the South Coast, some people still have not had that access restored to the degree that they had it before the fires. This amendment provides a requirement that there is a prompt assessment of roads after a bushfire so that we get in, get it done and restore access. The Shooters think that is sensible.

Amendment No. 33 speaks to the issue I raised in the second reading debate—I think it might have been last night—where the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, in some cases, it would seem, has wilfully dropped trees across roads to restrict or hinder access. I have photos of that. I am not just making stuff up. Evidence of that has been sent to me on several occasions. This amendment allows for the removal of fallen obstructions on sole access roads. We know the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service has concerns around not wanting downed trees moved. But the Shooters think that if a tree is blocking a sole access road, it is sensible that it be removed, at least off to the side of the road. People who use those roads to get to their properties should be able to do that. They should not have to apply to move a log to the side of the road. We think that is sensible.

Amendments Nos 36 to 40 and amendment No. 45 deal with what happens to infrastructure when it is transferred to a new land tenure. The Shooters are saying that any record of transferred infrastructure should be published within 90 days of any parcel of land coming under that provision. Amendment No. 37 requires an incoming department to seek a joint record of each infrastructure asset's condition and known defects before taking responsibility. We think that is sensible. In the past couple of years, a huge amount of Crown land has been transferred to NSW Maritime. We are talking about billions of dollars of Crown land, and I am still struggling to find a publicly accessible register of what was transferred, the condition it is in and its value.

When land tenures are moved around, that goes to the issue that was encountered in the access restrictions inquiry about confusion over who owns what land and what can be done with it. These amendments will help clear a lot of that up. Amendment No. 38 deals with a similar inspection of transferred bridges, making sure they are in good condition and that other agencies are not inheriting assets that perhaps should have been brought up to standard before they were transferred. The same applies to drainage. We know that drainage in our forests often suffers wear and tear from traffic, so that needs to be properly maintained to ensure access and deal with any erosion or downstream water quality issues.

Amendment No. 40 goes to the issue of fence responsibilities. Something I have come across when hunting in State forests that border private properties is disputes over who is responsible for fences. Sometimes fences are moved or liberties are taken with where they are located, and then all this argy‑bargy happens. Users might think they are on public land, but they run into a private property owner who says, "Well, no. You're actually on my land." That makes it clear around fence responsibilities. We know that maintenance of fences and cost-sharing arrangements is a huge bugbear for neighbouring properties in regional communities. Amendment No. 45 seeks to provide for the maintenance of a public record of existing and known tracks and trails and what their status is. That goes to my comments last night around the management of fire trails and their conditions and making sure that we provide an adequate record and advice for the people who use those tracks, particularly our RFS people.

I now turn to amendments Nos 87 to 89. Regarding No. 87, another bugbear that surfaced during the access inquiry is about access to apiaries. A lot of apiarists have contacted many members about having access to be able to maintain their sites. We know how important bees are for food production and our environment. The apiarists have been crying out for improvements to access arrangements on our public land, but they particularly identified the National Parks and Wildlife Service as problematic and as an agency they struggle to deal with. This amendment seeks to address those access issues for apiarists.

Amendment No. 88 deals with emergency utility repair procedures in terms of infrastructure. Amendment No. 89 deals with plantation access coordination and requires the Forestry Corporation to coordinate with lawful operators where departmental works or closures substantially affect access to an adjoining plantation. Those are likely to occur given The Greens amendments did not get up last night. There will still be plantations near this park, and we want those interactions to be managed smoothly for the benefit of everybody, so we think this amendment is eminently sensible. With those remarks, I commend the amendments to the Committee.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 14:26 :27 ): The issues for the Government remain the same, in that these are dealt with through the plan of management. However, I note that the member made a number of speculations and/or assertions around the motivations of National Parks and Wildlife Service staff, which I reject. I understand that these matters are being worked through, so I place on record that I do not necessarily agree with some of the assertions made. However, that does not change the fact that the Government does not support the amendments.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 14:27 :04 ): I indicate that The Nationals will support all these amendments. Amendments Nos 21 and 22 provide sensible ways to deal with issues of legacy contamination and asbestos. That obviously goes to the issue of basic worker safety, but it also makes sense to have these areas mapped and assessed. Amendments Nos 29, 32 and 33 ensure that people are able to access their property. Particularly if there is a new weight limit on someone's only access road, it must be backed by an engineer's assessment, with reasons given. It is important, particularly for local landholders who might need to get trucks or stocks in and out. We think it is also important that there is prompt damage assessment in order to restore access after any bushfire events that may occur. We have all seen how devastating it can be when bushfires go through these areas. We think this amendment makes sense. Likewise, we think amendment No. 33, which provides for the ability to clear fallen trees from sole access roads, is also sensible.

Moving to amendments Nos 36 to 40, what has been inherited, making sure there is an infrastructure inventory within 90 days, doing the bridge inspections and doing drainage maintenance and the like we think are important. Focusing on amendment No. 40, as the honourable member said, who is responsible for boundary fences is something that gets raised a lot. It is a bugbear for a lot of people. I think it is important to have this amendment inserted into the bill, which is why we support it. Turning to amendment No. 45, we think having a register of existing tracks and their status is important.

Lastly, on amendments Nos 87 to 89, similarly to the comments I made regarding the previous set of amendments, it is good governance to make sure there is good administration in place. I concur with the comments made by the Hon. Mark Banasiak about apiarists. A lot of them have contacted my colleagues in the lower House about this. We know how important it is to have them there. Honey producers rely very much on these forests, so we certainly support amendments Nos 87 to 89. They are just about having good processes in place. That is why we are happy to support the amendments.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 14:29 :50 ): I indicate that the Liberals do not support these amendments. Again, we have sympathy for the intention of the amendments but believe that once the bill passed, with scrutiny and a reliance on existing arrangements, we can achieve the aims of these amendments.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 14:30 :15 ): I briefly speak in support of the amendments. I note the Temporary Chair's previous comments and rulings. In terms of the asbestos issue, I start by indicating that the Hon. Nichole Overall is very supportive of the amendments around asbestos. She has historically been a warrior in terms of registers of asbestos. She asked me to pass on to the Committee her support of these amendments. I do so without having commented on them myself so that I do not breach the ruling around repetition. A number of other amendments have been moved. A number of sensible and reasonable amendments have been moved in terms of ensuring that any access roads that have been blocked by fallen trees are cleared and that members who come across fallen trees are able to do that. Changes to the engineering basis for access road load restrictions are clearly articulated. Restoration of the central access after bushfire is crucial. These amendments are sensible and practical. They have the support of The Nationals. I commend them to the Committee.

Ms SUE HIGGINSON ( 14:31 :43 ): The Greens do not support these amendments. I place on record that The Greens have not supported any of the Opposition or Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party amendments that have been moved last night or today. The amendments before us are beyond unnecessary. It is where we get into attempting to generate a legislative scheme that is not only entirely unworkable and unfeasible but also dictates a regime as if members of this place somehow know better than the people on the ground doing the actual work and management. Frankly, that is entirely preposterous. As it stands, the bill is pretty spectacular and has been worked on for some time. We have waited a long time for it. The Greens do not support these amendments.

The first few amendments deal with the termination of timber supply agreements and the transition of our forestry workforce, including our contract workers, who often feel like they are the last to be considered in a lot of those processes. They feel like, even though they are in the forest and have done the harvesting for generations, they have been the last ones consulted on a lot of this. Amendment No. 23 deals with the termination of timber supply agreements. It requires written reasons if a State body ends a timber supply agreement or substantially reduces supply as a direct result of the bill. The explanation must distinguish what the legislation requires from what the body has chosen under the contract, and identify available claim or review processes. Amendment No. 24 requires recruitment under the bill to give proper consideration to forestry experience and practical skills relevant to the job. Applicants must have a reasonable chance to demonstrate those skills, but it does not remove required qualifications or guarantee an appointment.

Amendment No. 25 is a consideration of contract workers in transition assistance. It requires the Minister to consider contractor and timber processing workers when designing or changing relevant worker assistance programs. The Minister must publish the eligibility decision and explain any treatment that differs from that of Forestry Corporation employees. However, it does not itself create a right to payment, if members are concerned about that. Amendment No. 26 deals with notice before closure of retraining applications. It requires 60 days public notice before applications for a relevant retraining program close, with reasonable efforts to contact eligible workers. People who apply in time must have a reasonable chance to finish supplying evidence. If fixed funding runs out, the department must explain what that means for pending applications.

Amendment No. 90 is the publication of transition procurement opportunities. It requires significant purchasing and contracting opportunities arising from the park's establishment to be publicly advertised, with information for regional suppliers on how to participate. Lawful, direct or emergency procurement remains possible, but the reasons for using an exception must be recorded and summarised publicly. Amendment No. 91 concerns local workforce skills assessment. It requires a published assessment of the skills needed to manage the new land and opportunities for affected regional workers to obtain them. It must be completed within six months of the relevant arrangement starting and links workforce planning to the people actually affected by the transition. Amendment No. 92 deals with apprenticeships and training opportunities. The amendment requires the department to consider apprenticeships, traineeships and accredited training when planning additional staff for the new land. It must publish the outcome of that consideration. It puts those training opportunities into workforce planning but does not necessarily guarantee particular positions.

Amendment No. 93 concerns business transition case coordination. The amendment requires the Minister to seek coordinated case management where a business applies to multiple State assistance programs. Because of those land transfers, the aim is to reduce unnecessary repeated information requests and make the process easier for affected businesses. Amendment No. 94 is about the reporting of any unpaid transition claims. It requires quarterly public reporting on pending transition assistance applications. We think that is eminently sensible. If the Government is spending taxpayers' money, we have a right to know in a timely manner whether it has been fully expended. That way we can redirect it if needed, or contact people who may have been unsuccessful or may not even have applied. I commend the amendments to the Committee.

T he Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 14:38 :14 ): The Government does not support the amendments for reasons previously outlined.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 14:38 :20 ): I indicate that The Nationals support all of the amendments. I comment on a few but not all of them. Amendment No. 24 is about the recognition of forestry skills in recruitment. As has been canvassed extensively throughout the debate, for a lot of the families on the Mid North Coast, forestry has kept food on the table and a roof over their heads. The industry has made clear that the Government's approach to managing the complete decimation of the industry is not good enough. As many of my colleagues, including the leader of the Nats, Gurmesh Singh, said in the other place, it is about more than money; it is about the identity, skills and long-term planning for forestry workers who deserve meaningful employment. We commend the Shooters for moving the amendments, particularly amendment No. 24, which recognises forestry workers and gives them an opportunity to have their skills recognised. That is important.

The Government has failed to come to the table to listen and to learn from the industry, but this sensible amendment ensures workers with demonstrated forestry skills and transferable practical skills are considered, even if those skills were obtained outside the department. Likewise, amendment No. 25 provides more practical support for impacted forestry workers to ensure that contractors are considered in transition support. Because it is not just those working directly in the timber harvesting operations; it is the haulage drivers, the harvest crews, the mill workers. It is important that they are covered as well, which is why we support that amendment.

Amendment No. 26 relates to the notice before the closure of training applications. Again, the Hon. Mark Banasiak covered this well. The amendment keeps the lines of communication open with impacted forestry workers, ensuring that they are given at least 60 days notice before the closing of applications for retraining programs. As I said earlier, the transition for forestry workers is about more than financial compensation; it is about giving them the appropriate support as they navigate what is absolutely an incredibly difficult time for them thanks to the actions of the Labor Government. Lastly, I turn to amendments Nos 91 and 92. I note the importance of the local workforce skills assessment and also apprenticeships and traineeships. It is important that apprentices and trainees are considered in every staffing plan, and the outcome is published. These amendments provide for that. If the Government is serious about this, it should be trying to keep young people in the region. We are happy to support the amendments.
The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 14:41 :07 ): For the reasons the Government has given, the Liberals do not support the amendments.

The Hon. WES FANG ( 14:41 :17 ): As the Hon. Sarah Mitchell has indicated, The Nationals support the amendments. Amendment No. 23 is incredibly important for us to support. It relates to the reasons for terminations of timber supply agreements. We have heard from a lot of impacted timber harvesters and mills that cancelled supply agreements have created heartache, grief and other issues. The member has moved the amendment in good faith, and has done so with an understanding of the level of concern there is about the way the Government basically tore up an industry's livelihood overnight. There is a need for us to recognise that. The Government should personally apologise and make penance or seek forgiveness for what it did to the forestry industry. I also make the point, yet again, that the forestry Minister has not made a contribution in debate on this bill or any of the amendments.

It is interesting that the Minister for the Environment is in this Chamber on behalf of the Government, but we have not heard a single word from the forestry Minister. Where was that Minister when the industry was torn apart? Where is that Minister while we are debating this bill? The forestry Minister has been absolutely silent on this bill, the jobs and the amendments that we are debating. It would have been good if the Minister was in the Chamber to fight for things or even provide clarity around why timber supply agreements may be withdrawn. That is on the Minister responsible for forestry. We cannot compel the Minister to come in to the Chamber and make a contribution, even though this is clearly within the Minister's bailiwick and something that the they should have sought to make a contribution on. Other than that, my colleague the Hon. Sarah Mitchell made salient and sensible points. I encourage members to support the amendments.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 14:43 :52 ): It was remiss of me not to acknowledge my colleague in the other place the member for Port Macquarie for his advocacy on behalf of his community and the incredible work that he has done to ensure that the views of his constituents in terms of their livelihoods and businesses have been represented. We believe deeply that the workers and small to medium-sized businesses that have been affected need support. Again, we appreciate the intention of the amendments, but I place on record that the member for Port Macquarie has done a really important job representing the views and interests of his community.

Amendments Nos 51 to 55 deal with monitoring the environmental benefits and impacts created by the transfer of land tenure. The Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party think that is important because we believe in data‑driven decisions. If we change something, we should always measure before and after so that we can see whether we have improved or not and whether we need to adjust our management strategies. That is good practice. It is called adaptive management, which we think it is sensible to adopt. Amendment No. 59 deals with what I alluded to before regarding boundary disputes about fencing. We believe having a central contact officer, person or department solely around that issue is important, particularly as we transition to this new land tenure. In the beginning, there may be a greater likelihood of disputes.

Amendment No. 60 requires the Minister to tell both Houses about significant errors found in the bill's land descriptions and any proposed corrections. That statement must be tabled within 20 sitting days of each House. Obviously, the bill brings a big change regarding land tenure. If there are any errors or issues that we need to correct, it is better that we do so promptly and not in a big omnibus, miscellaneous bill. We all love those! Amendment No. 61 makes it clear that editing an online map does not itself change the legal boundary, land description or reservation category. Materially misleading departmental maps must be corrected promptly, and changes made under the actual statutory power would still be recognised.

Amendment No. 62 requires superseded departmental land maps to remain publicly available with dates and explanations of significant changes. Any sensitive personal or cultural information obviously must be excluded. We think that is a sensible amendment. Amendment No. 95 requires consultation with affected councils about roads, waste services, emergency services and visitor facilities. A summary of unresolved responsibilities must be published within 12 months of the relevant arrangements starting, and it makes outstanding practical responsibilities visible to the community. Often when there are land tenure changes, as we found in the inquiry into access to public lands, a lot of agencies do not even know that they own land or what they are, or are not, responsible for. We think a register of some sort would be good in that instance and might actually become best practice in all land tenure changes.

Amendment No. 99 makes it clear that an administrative guideline without its own legal force cannot itself cancel an existing interest, change a statutory boundary or create an offence. This amendment is about protecting the powers of this House, particularly with the Henry VIII clause. Amendment No. 100 says that no regulation may amend the Act. That amendment prevents regulations under clause 43 from changing the Act or its schedules, including indirectly through savings or transitional provisions. That is so regulations will not be able to rewrite what Parliament has passed, potentially, in this sitting. It does not remove the bill's separate schedule changing order powers. I commend the amendments to the Committee.
The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environme nt, and Minister for Heritage) ( 14:57 :00 ): The Government prefers the bill as it is.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 14:57 :03 ): The Nationals support all of the amendments. We are happy to support the transparency measures in amendments Nos 51 to 55. These amendments are about putting honest monitoring in place as to how koala numbers are counted, whether surveys are comparable, and the monitoring of other native species as well. If we are going to monitor koalas, it makes sense to monitor gliders, owls, frogs and whatever other native species may be in the park. We also support amendments Nos 54 and 55, which are about waterway monitoring and the extraction register.

Amendments Nos 59 to 62 are important because the boundaries of the park have already shifted throughout the process, even here in the Parliament. It is important for landholders to have certainty that the line on the map is the legal perimeter of the park. Making sure there is a boundary dispute contact officer—one named contact—and having timely acknowledgement of inquiries are important. It is also important that any schedule errors are tabled in Parliament. Amendment No. 61 ensures any incorrect online maps are corrected promptly. The Nationals also agree with the archiving of superseded maps under amendment No. 62. Finally, we are happy to support amendments Nos 95, 99 and 100. These sensible amendments ensure that the Parliament has a role to play in relation to the park going forward.

I will try to be brief. Amendments Nos 30 and 46 to 50 deal with what we have heard often from landholders who sit adjacent to national parks—or to any public land, to be frank—which is how the management of pests and weeds can be improved. These amendments seek to do so by the mapping of priority weeds so that they can be dealt with, by neighbours being able to easily report pest damage, by coordinated boundary pest management and by a clear and concise response to newly detected invasive species.

Amendments Nos 31 and 41 to 44 deal with our concerns about fire trail conditions and the response to firefighting in the national park. Amendments Nos 57, 58 and 59 are about biosecurity, which is a big issue that is of great concern in our rural areas. Those amendments go to the protection of agricultural biosecurity, particularly around the boundaries of public land, and procedures for dealing with livestock that has escaped from private land into national park land. Amendments Nos 63 to 77 largely deal with something that our party is passionate about, which is maintaining public access for recreation on public land, and making sure that all public land is as accessible as possible for the varied recreations that people love to enjoy and practice in our State.

It become clear through the Select Committee on Access Restrictions to Public Lands and Waterways that there are real concerns around how we are managing public land access. The committee made some positive recommendations about how we can better manage access. I look forward to tabling that report later in the year and hopefully seeing those recommendations adopted. Those amendments speak to some of the recommendations, without disclosing confidential information about committee deliberations. They go towards making sure our public land is as accessible as possible, within the confines of the goals and objectives we are trying to achieve with different land tenures. With those remarks, I commend the final amendments to the Committee.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Minister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 15:06 :39 ): The Government prefers the bill as it is. We do not support the amendments.

The Hon. SARAH MITCHELL ( 15:06 :45 ): I indicate that The Nationals support these amendments. I make a couple of comments. Firstly, I think other colleagues like the Hon. Scott Barrett are better placed to speak about some of the specifics around them, but amendments Nos 30 and 46 to 50 are about making sure that we have the right measures in place. We support that, particularly when it comes to issues of biosecurity and pests and weeds. For amendments Nos 41 to 44 about fire and emergency readiness, there was a lot of debate on those issues in the second reading debate. I do not intend to re-prosecute those arguments. They are sensible amendments that ensure the right conditions for fire trails, deal with emergency communication gaps and ensure the right consultation with the RFS.

In relation to amendment No. 41, as I mentioned in my contributions to the second reading debate and to debate on earlier amendments, I acknowledge that some amendments were moved by the Opposition in the other place and passed that were about a fire management strategy. But we are still concerned about the fire risk posed by the park. That is a real risk. Amendment No. 41 is sensible. It will ensure that there is up-to-date information about the conditions of fire trails in the event of a bushfire. Amendments Nos 56 to 58 are about biosecurity and will ensure that there is proper consultation before works that might risk farm biosecurity for neighbours and that there are appropriate procedures and processes in place in the event of any livestock maybe getting through a fence. There is also a clause to ensure that neighbours are made aware of any serious incidents.

Lastly, for amendments Nos 63 to 77, a lot of my colleagues in the other place have spoken about our continuing concerns regarding what park access will be available, particularly for locals and, potentially, tourists as well—the four-wheel drivers, trail bike riders, horseriders, mountain bikers, campers and dog walkers. I am sure the Hon. Scott Barrett will talk about that in his contribution to debate on these amendments. I know he enjoys visiting national parks with his sons. I think his son Henry might actually be watching now. If Henry is watching, I say hello from Sarah and everybody else here. Dad might say something in a minute; he is at work, we promise. Again, we think these are sensible amendments to ensure that all user groups who might have an interest in accessing the park get to have their say. We are happy to support them.

The Hon. JACQUI MUNRO ( 15:09 :59 ): The Liberals do not support these amendments for the reasons I have outlined previously. I note the contribution of the Hon. Sarah Mitchell regarding amendments that were accepted in the other place around fire management.

The Hon. SCOTT BARRETT ( 15:10 :19 ): Briefly, I will touch on a couple of things that are wrapped up in these amendments. There is the biosecurity aspect, the access aspect and the aspect of the neighbours of national parks as well. Obviously, there would be a concern if what is in the bill conflicted with the Biosecurity Act, which is where our biosecurity is managed in this State. From my quick read of the bill, I do not believe it does. It strengthens some opportunities we have here. It is a good opportunity for the National Parks and Wildlife Service to prove itself as the gold standard in biosecurity management. Some of the baseline studies that could be done and some of the reporting of biosecurity incursions would be a really good opportunity for the service to show that it manages our invasive species well, gets on top of weed infestations and works well with neighbours.

That leads me to my next point, which is also wrapped up in these amendments. Unfortunately, there is a history of sour relationships with landholders who border national parks. In some areas, I know that has been improved by the really good staff that the National Parks and Wildlife Service can put in the area. It is interesting that when local staff such as former farmers and landholders are themselves put into that system, the relationships seem to be a lot better than in other areas where external people have been brought in. I will not go through them, but I have heard really good stories about some people working in the National Parks and Wildlife Service building those relationships.

If some of these amendments can provide the tools to strengthen those relationships, that is certainly worth supporting and worth trying. As I say, the history is not great as far as the landholders who neighbour national parks go. There are boundary fence issues. Some national parks generally have the policy that they do support boundary fencing, although they are not legislated or required to do so. There is an opportunity to look at exclusion fencing in some of these areas, which would deal with some of the issues, such as pests coming out of national parks but also livestock going into national parks.

The third aspect I touch on—and one of the reasons I will support these amendments—is access. I get that there are parts of national parks that need to be locked up to protect them and keep people out. The example I have given before is that those areas are like that room at grandma's house you were not allowed into that had the good furniture, the good carpet and the old war medals we did not want to damage. Parts of national parks are a bit the same. We do not want four‑wheel drives racing through areas of Wollemi pine, for instance, or fragile sand dunes, perhaps. But other areas are there for us to share, enjoy and make the most of.

We need to make sure we have access to the areas for us to enjoy, which is a big part of what national parks are. We hear people trumpet how good our visitor numbers are in national parks. Let us capitalise on that. Let us get more people in to enjoy our national parks. The more people who go into our national parks and enjoy how great they are, the more people who will associate with national parks. Then we will get more and more people wanting to protect and conserve them. As the Hon. Sarah Mitchell mentioned, I spent last school holidays in national parks with Henry, Darcy and my wife. I am looking forward to doing that again—and looking forward to getting home this afternoon.

Ms SUE HIGGINSON ( 15:14 :07 ): I am reluctant to do this, but I have to call out the utter hypocrisy that has been put forward. I have had to listen to members who really seem not to know what they are talking about denigrate National Parks and Wildlife Service staff by suggesting that some are great and others are not, and that there is a history of bad relationships. Let us for one moment reflect on where that awful myth of bad relationships really comes from. I can perhaps point to the former Leader of The National Party, now part of Pauline Hanson's One Nation, Barnaby Joyce, who has spent decades demonising the National Parks and Wildlife Service across New South Wales. I think of the former Leader of The Nationals in this Parliament, John Barilaro, demonising National Parks and Wildlife Service staff.

As someone who has been involved with national parks for over 30 years, and who has known numerous people who have worked in national parks and watched their incredible work ethic, commitment and skill, I can guarantee that it is not just about controlling invasive species. It is not just about making sure roads are upgraded and suitable for use, and that gates are in good condition. It is about understanding the systems and the ecology of those places. The amendments before us are from a couple of MPs and their staffers who think they know what they are talking about, as if these matters should be in legislation. We know that these amendments—

The Hon. MARK BANASIAK ( 15:32 :03 ): I thank most members for the spirit in which the amendments were dealt with. I am not preparing to relitigate those amendments, but the bill has provisions that may contain unintended drafting errors. Before I get accused of enacting the Hon. Rod Roberts provision, I take members to clause 27 regarding road-widening provisions. The clause allows an order to specify an additional width for a road. It then refers to the land of the specified width when identifying the land that vests in the Minister. Additional width and total width are not the same thing. If a road corridor is 10 metres wide and we add six metres, we would generally expect that to finish with 16 metres.

As a teacher, I am pretty comfortable with that, but the operative wording does not clearly distinguish the six metres being added from the 16 metres we are supposed to end up with. Some might say, "Come on, we all know what that means", but surveyors need to identify an actual boundary. Landholders need to know their rights, and as it is written, it is not clear. Clause 27, when it comes to easements, also states an existing easement or right of way is taken to apply to the widening of a narrowed road. Clause 28 states it is extinguished when an order is made unless the order preserves it. The same road alteration can engage both provisions, so one appears to carry the right across and the other appears to remove it, which seems to be an inherent contradiction.

When it comes to the automatic reservation of roads, clause 26 tells us what happens when a road has the same reservation category on both sides. It also deals with different reservation categories on either side. But what happens when there is a national park on one side and a farm or a State forest on the other? That automatic mechanism does not clearly tell us what happens in that situation. The 10-year deadline is also an issue. The bill allows additional land to be reserved later. The Minister explained that the flexibility is needed to sort out tenure boundaries and other administrative matters, but the road provisions work to a fixed deadline of 10 years after the relevant clause commences. What happens if land is added in year 11, the deadline for making the road order has passed and the automatic reservation date has also passed?

Private property protection also needs a closer look. Clause 6 says private freehold land is not reserved by the Act, but clause 27 provides for land to vest in the Minister when a road is widened. Reservation and vesting are different legal actions. The protection against one does not necessarily answer the question about the other. Could a widening order reach into adjoining private land despite what clause 6 says? There is also another point about boundaries that comes directly from the Minister's speech. Clause 15 expressly protects the size and natural and cultural value of national park estate land. The Minister said that adjustments could not significantly diminish either the national park estate or the State forest estate. However, despite what the Minister says and despite what clause 15 says, there is a reasonable question about whether the State forest estate will be diminished through the passing of this bill. With those remarks, I move:

That the question be amended by omitting "this bill be now read a third time" and instead inserting "this bill be referred to Portfolio Committee No. 7 - Planning and Environment for inquiry and report by 16 November 2026".
I have moved the amendment so those planning technicalities can be resolved.

The Hon. PENNY SHARPE (Minister for Climate Change, Minister for Energy, Min ister for the Environment, and Minister for Heritage) ( 15:35 :33 ): In reply: No, the Government is not going to agree to a referral. This has been well canvassed in the debate. I thank the Hon. Mark Banasiak for being very reasonable to deal with throughout this process, even though we vehemently disagree in relation to the outcome. There is no need for the bill to be sent off to a committee. We should pass the bill and pass it today.
